item.title: 别再让模型现场拼 API：Skillware 把「能力」做成可注册的标准件，而不是提示词里的约定 ｜ Don't Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them: Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign Agents
item.description:
一句话：模型动态写代码、猜 API 载荷、靠提示词记约束——代价是上下文烧光、账单变贵、生产环境不稳。

要点：

  • 要反驳的假设：当前自治系统默认「让语言模型动态写代码、猜 API 载荷、通过提示词工程记住运行约束」，作者认为这个假设很脆弱
  • 代价很具体：**烧掉大量上下文窗口、推高 API 账单、生产环境里不可预测地失败**
  • Skillware 提出一套开放架构框架与**能力注册表（capability registry）**，把「一个 agent 能做什么」与「怎么提示它」正式分开，使能力成为可注册、可复用的标准件

为什么值得看：这与 11-20 期 NVIDIA 把 CAD 转 USD 封成 Agent Skill、11-17 Unity 给 Claude Code/Codex 写官方 skills 是同一趋势的理论表述：**引擎工具的未来形态是可注册能力，不是提示词模板**。做 AI 工具链的团队可以直接照这个分层。

中文摘要：当前的自治系统建立在一个脆弱的假设上：语言模型应当动态地写代码、猜测 API 载荷，并通过提示词工程记住各种运行约束。作者指出这在实践中代价高昂——大量消耗上下文窗口、推高 API 账单，并产生在生产环境里不可预测失败的脆弱 agent。Skillware 因此提出一个开放的架构框架与能力注册表（capability registry），把「一个 agent 能做什么」与「如何用提示词驱动它」正式分离，使能力成为可注册、可复用、可审计的标准件。这与近期引擎厂商把工具封装成 agent skill 的做法同源——区别在于它给出了分层与标准，而不只是一份说明书。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.SE（English）

原文发布：2026-11-05

本期推送：2026-11-23

Don’t Prompt Your Agents. Equip Them.
Skillware as a Modular Standard for Sovereign, Auditable,
and Deterministic Capability Execution for Logical Systems

November 2026 | github.com/arpahls/skillware

Abstract

Current autonomous logical systems rely on a fragile assumption: that language models should dynamically write code, guess API payloads, and memorize operational constraints through prompt engineering. In practice, this burns massive context windows, inflates API bills, and produces fragile agents that fail unpredictably in production.

In this work, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and capability registry that formally separates what an agent wants to do from how that task is executed. Instead of prompting models with loose text instructions or markdown files baptized as “skills”, Skillware equips them with modular, versioned software capability bundles. Much like skill hotkeys in video games, which execute deterministically under fixed world rules rather than conversational negotiation, each bundle combines a typed JSON input contract, deterministic Python code, task directives, bundled datasets, and automated unit tests. In-process adapters translate these capabilities into native tool declarations for any model, from frontier cloud APIs to open-weight, local, and edge runtimes with zero network latency.

Evaluating 23 frontier and open-weight models across 368 benchmark conditions, we show that small local models, even 3B to 8B parameters, equipped with Skillware consistently outperform unequipped frontier models on complex multi-step workflows. They cut token usage by up to 84.8%, slash inference costs by up to 97.3%, and eliminate parameter errors entirely. True agent reliability does not come from larger models or longer prompts, but from equipping logical systems with verified, deterministic software.

Finally, we articulate the trajectory of capability bundles across an invariant continuum of information processing systems. Today, Skillware serves as a modular, installable capability library for digital logical systems. Tomorrow, the exact same framework powers robust capabilities for IoT devices, smart appliances, vehicles, drones, and embodied robotics. Down the line, as brain-computer interfaces advance, this modular architecture provides the foundation to install verified capabilities directly into organic information processors (brains), turning the instant skill acquisition of science fiction into a concrete, auditable engineering discipline.

Keywords: Autonomous Agents · Capability Engineering · Tool-Augmented Language Models · Small Language Models (SLMs) · Deterministic Execution · Token Economics · Agent Software Architecture · Skillware

1  Introduction: The Stochastic Impedance Mismatch

Computer systems research has historically progressed by establishing formal boundaries between distinct abstraction layers: the separation of physical memory from virtual addressing, the isolation of user space from kernel execution, and the decoupling of declarative query specification from relational execution engines [41, 22, 33, 18]. Each transition replaced stochastic, ad-hoc programming conventions with deterministic, verifiable contracts.

The contemporary paradigm of autonomous artificial intelligence agents represents a sharp departure from this historical trajectory. As foundation models have scaled, practitioners have attempted to bridge the gap between linguistic reasoning and real-world execution by coercing auto-regressive language models into serving simultaneously as planners, compilers, runtime engines, and policy arbiters [45, 48, 49, 42]. In this prevailing architectural approach—which we term the prompt-driven execution paradigm—an agent is provided with unstructured natural-language descriptions of external APIs, instructed to synthesize execution code or structured payloads on the fly, and expected to self-regulate its operational boundaries through in-context prompting.

This approach suffers from a foundational stochastic impedance mismatch. Deep transformer architectures compute conditional probability distributions over discrete token sequences:

p(y₁,…,y_T|x)=∏ₜ₌₁ᵀp(yₜ|y_

(1)

While auto-regressive token generation is exceptionally well-suited for semantic interpretation, open-domain summarization, and human-machine dialogue, it possesses no formal mechanisms for enforcing computational invariants. When task complexity scales compositionally, transformer architectures experience severe combinatorial degradation, non-deterministic branching, and state hallucination [13, 44, 21, 20].

1.1  The Crisis of Prompt-Driven Capability

Treating auto-regressive language models as direct computation runtimes introduces five critical systemic bottlenecks:

  • 1.

    Stochastic Non-Determinism: An identical operational intent executed across multiple turns yields variable argument casing, hallucinated parameters, and dropped structural invariants.

  • 2.

    Quadratic Context Dilution: Injecting thousands of tokens of API manuals and directives into system prompts permanently taxes transformer attention (O(L²)), causing models to ignore critical safety predicates [23].

  • 3.

    Egress Insecurity and the Confused Deputy: Natural-language prompts cannot enforce security perimeters; untrusted inbound text easily repurposes ambient model authority into unauthorized side-effects [15, 25].

  • 4.

    Schema Balkanization: Fragile, incompatible tool formats across major cloud providers (e.g., Protobuf, XML, JSON) force developers to maintain brittle prompt shims that break across model releases.

  • 5.

    Cyber-Physical Incompatibility: Multi-second cloud latency and stochastic parameter drift are fundamentally incompatible with real-time physical control and millisecond reflex envelopes [2, 51, 46].

    • These failure modes are not cosmetic developer inconveniences; they form a systemic crisis where critical software workflows become trapped inside a centralized, rented loop. Section 2 provides a comprehensive technical deconstruction of these failures across enterprise, developer, macroeconomic, and cyber-physical layers.

    1.2  The Core Principle: Don’t Prompt. Equip.

    In 1975, Saltzer and Schroeder articulated the foundational tenets of secure and reliable systems: Economy of Mechanism, Fail-Safe Defaults, Least Privilege, and Complete Mediation[41]. In classical computing, operating systems do not generate utility binaries at runtime; they package pre-compiled, verifiable, and isolated software libraries behind typed system calls.

    A compelling systems analogy emerges from role-playing video games (RPGs), where players and non-player companions personalize and customize characters through modular skill systems. In a game engine, activating an ability is never an ambiguous negotiation, a conversational plea, or a probabilistic discussion with the character model. It is a hotkey bound to deterministic engine logic: provided environmental preconditions and background policies hold true—the entity is in combat outside a sanctuary town, targeting a hostile creature rather than an immune town guard, and possessing sufficient resource reserves—the skill executes with a single trigger and produces the exact same state transition every time. The character never invents the physics of the ability at runtime, nor does it negotiate its operational boundaries; it is strictly in the position to trigger the action. Skillware introduces this exact computational discipline to autonomous agents: the language model evaluates semantic context and decides when to trigger a capability, but has zero authority over how the capability executes, how its parameters are validated, or how its constitutional policies are enforced.

    In this paper, we present Skillware, an open architectural framework and registry that formalizes this separation. While the term skillware has historical currency in corporate compliance software and speculative fiction, its coinage and introduction into artificial intelligence and autonomous systems was originated by ARPA Hellenic Logical Systems [37]. Recent academic literature, notably Fan and Lan [14], has acknowledged this origin while exploring theoretical software ontologies for persistent agent behaviors. In this work, we present the production-validated execution standard: self-contained, versioned capability bundles. Each bundle unifies a typed contract (manifest.yaml), a deterministic execution class (skill.py), a cognitive directive (instructions.md), offline assurance verifiers (test_skill.py), and metadata presentation (card.json).

    Through in-process dynamic adapters, Skillware translates declared capabilities into native host formats across all major frontier and local models without IPC or network overhead. We demonstrate that this architecture not only restores determinism to the execution layer of autonomous systems, but enables Small Language Models (SLMs) to achieve superior operational reliability at a fraction of the token and financial cost of unequipped frontier models.

    The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 dissects the capability crisis across technical layers and constituencies. Section 3 formalizes the Skillware bundle and its interface morphism; Section 4 describes runtime discovery, chaining, and operator stores. Section 5 analyzes complexity, empirical scaling, and token economics, and Section 6 positions Skillware against adjacent ecosystems alongside multi-model empirical evaluation under Skillware-Bench. Sections 7 and 8 cover ecosystem integration and adversarial security verification, Section 9 extends the abstraction to cyber-physical scales, and Section 10 concludes.

    2  Deconstructing the Capability Crisis Across Systemic Layers and Constituencies

    The failure of prompt-driven capabilities is not an isolated developer inconvenience; it is an architectural breakdown that propagates across the entire computing stack. To rigorously motivate the design of Skillware, we first analyze the failure modes across four technical layers, examine three insidious non-outage operational crises, and then demonstrate how Skillware resolves these challenges for four vital computing constituencies: software developers, autonomous systems, enterprise operators, and sovereign defense entities.

    2.1  The Four Technical Failure Layers of Prompted Agents

    2.1.1  The Enterprise and Regulatory Layer: The Illusion of Compliance

    In regulated industries—including banking, defense logistics, healthcare, and telecommunications—autonomous operations are bound by statutory compliance regimes such as SOX, HIPAA, GDPR, and OFAC sanctions enforcement.

    When an agent’s capability is enforced solely through natural-language system instructions (e.g., “You are a compliance officer. Check if this Ethereum address is on the OFAC sanctions list before approving transaction”), the system lacks any defensible guarantee of execution. An auto-regressive model may hallucinate that an address is benign, misparse hexadecimal character casing, or fail to access real-time sanctions lists due to network timeouts. Furthermore, irreversible side-effects (such as submitting an on-chain transaction or dispatching an email to 10,000 corporate customers) are executed through direct, unverified model outputs.

    Enterprise sovereignty demands:

  • •

    Inviolable Confirmation Gates: Destructive mutations must require explicit, typed boolean gates (confirmed: true) and preview dry-runs (dry_run: true) enforced at the code level, completely independent of the model’s textual disposition.

  • •

    Deterministic Data Provenance: Critical reference datasets (such as sanctions lists or regulatory taxonomies) must ship bundled beside the execution logic as static, offline assets, eliminating runtime scraping and dynamic tampering.

    • 2.1.2  The Developer Layer: Schema Fragmentation and Prompt Rot

    For software engineers, maintaining prompt-based tool definitions is an operational nightmare known as prompt rot.

    First, foundation model providers lack standardization. Google Gemini requires uppercase Protobuf type declarations (STRING, INTEGER, OBJECT); Anthropic Claude requires its own tool envelope with a JSON Schema input_schema; OpenAI requires its Chat Completions function signatures [4]. When an engineering team updates an API or switches from Claude to Gemini, hundreds of lines of fragile prompt shims must be rewritten and re-evaluated.

    Second, prompt-driven tools violate standard software engineering lifecycle guarantees. There is no concept of a unit test for an instruction string. In contrast, standard software undergoes deterministic continuous integration: unit tests, regression suites, type validation, and dependency pinning. Prompt-based agents deploy completely unverified code directly into execution paths.

    Finally, package management in agent stacks is broken. Equipping an agent with complex capabilities (e.g., cryptographic hashing, EVM RPC handling, or PDF parsing) often pollutes the global application environment, triggering severe dependency conflicts.

    2.1.3  The Macroeconomic Layer: The Token Burn of Disposable Logic

    From an economic perspective, the current industry approach is profoundly unsustainable. When an agent is prompted to solve a task through dynamic code generation or instruction following:

  • •

    Frontier Token Rates for Static Logic: Operators pay upwards of $3.00 to $15.00 per million output tokens for an LLM to re-synthesize common Python logic that has been solved for decades (e.g., regex sanitization, IMAP parsing, or JSON transformations).

  • •

    Quadratic Attention Tax: Stuffing multiple tool schemas and voluminous OpenAPI manifests into the context window consumes thousands of prompt tokens per turn. Over a 50-turn conversational session, an agent can easily consume $20.00 in input tokens simply re-reading the identical tool documentation on every message.

    • Pre-compiled capabilities eliminate this overhead entirely. The model emits a compact JSON function call (e.g., 20 tokens), the host executes the deterministic Python code locally with zero token cost, and the structured response is returned for semantic synthesis.

    2.1.4  The Cyber-Physical Layer: Determinism in Real Space

    The final frontier of autonomy lies outside data centers: in autonomous quadcopters navigating contested airspace, industrial robotic arms assembling microelectronics, and neural prosthetic interfaces restoring motor function to paralyzed patients [8, 46].

    In cyber-physical systems, failure is not a low-confidence text response; it is physical collision, equipment destruction, or physiological trauma. Such systems cannot tolerate 2.5-second cloud round-trip latencies, stochastic API argument hallucination, or network dependency. Physical agency requires instantaneous, deterministic, and sandboxed execution that can run entirely offline on low-power edge compute (such as an NVIDIA Jetson or ARM Cortex SoC).

    2.2  The Chronic Crises of Rented Intelligence: Infrastructure Cascades and Hidden Penalties

    While catastrophic infrastructure outages make headlines and populate vendor status pages, four chronic operational penalties undermine production autonomy behind closed doors:

  • 1.

    The Rented Loop and Infrastructure Cascades: Historically, software development was architecturally decentralized: Git repositories lived locally on disk, and remote servers were merely optional publishing targets. Today, that relationship has inverted into a rented loop: editor completions, pull request reviews, continuous integration, and runtime capabilities depend on centralized model endpoints sharing a common failure domain.

    When an upstream cloud infrastructure degrades—exemplified by the August 2026 cascading incident where sidecar proxy exhaustion, auth collapse, and client-side retry storms paralyzed repositories, CI pipelines, and Copilot on the identical incident clock—the entire cognitive workflow halts. Competing chat interfaces and cloud APIs frequently share identical geographical corridors and cooling zones. When the pipe darkens, an enterprise does not merely experience latency; it loses the digital hands it hired. Real operational autonomy requires that capability execution reside on local silicon, independent of external network availability.

  • 2.

    Subscribed Cognition vs. Amortized Silicon: Operators do not control the cost of automated thinking; they subscribe to it. Token pricing shifts at the whim of foundation model providers seeking margin expansion or sunsetting promotional tiers. A model executing on local silicon incurs predictable electricity consumption; a cloud-rented model sends an altered monthly invoice because a line changed in a vendor spreadsheet.

  • 3.

    Geopolitical and Corporate Blockades: Frontier model access is increasingly politicized and weaponized through geographic blacklists and corporate parentage audits. Developers and enterprises in disfavored jurisdictions can be severed from mission-critical tools overnight without an announcement or a dependency lockfile bump—exemplified by silent platform lockouts affecting millions of global developers under the guise of infrastructure rollouts. When capability is bound to a remote cloud identity, sovereignty is an illusion.

  • 4.

    Unpinned Drift and Closed-Weight Amnesia: In production software, dependencies are pinned to immutable commit hashes. In cloud AI, foundation model endpoints are continuously rerouted, compressed, and safety-tuned behind static API aliases without public version control. Developers across the industry repeatedly document sudden degradation: models become taciturn, omit procedural steps, violate negative constraints, or hallucinate task completion. Because proprietary cloud weights cannot be diffed, operators cannot inspect, reproduce, or rollback behavioral regressions.

    • 2.3  Why Skillware is Better for the Four Core Constituencies

    Having examined the structural layers of failure and the chronic crises of rented cognition, we synthesize how Skillware transforms operational stability across the four core computing constituencies:

    2.3.1  Software Developers: Eliminating Prompt Rot and Restoring Offline Verification

  • •

    Elimination of “Prompt Rot”: In prompt-based architectures, minor adjustments to a system prompt frequently break tool invocation schemas across unrelated domains. Skillware encapsulates each capability behind a typed JSON Schema in manifest.yaml. The tool signature is decoupled from prompt phrasing and validated programmatically at compile- and run-time.

  • •

    Offline Testability (test_skill.py): Standard agent frameworks cannot be unit-tested without calling third-party LLM APIs, incurring latency, monetary costs, and stochastic results. Every Skillware bundle ships with a comprehensive offline test suite (test_skill.py) that verifies that execute() honors manifest.yaml independently of any model invocation.

  • •

    Isolated Package Management: Complex capabilities require distinct external libraries (e.g., web3 for blockchain validation, requests for REST calls, fsspec for cloud storage). Installing a monolithic agent framework frequently results in dependency hell. Skillware enforces granular dependency declarations per skill, mapped automatically to pip extras (e.g., pip install "skillware[defi_evm_tx_handler]"). Missing packages are detected pre-flight, guiding the developer with precise installation hints.

    • 2.3.2  Autonomous Logical Systems: Bounded State and Safe Asynchronous Execution

  • •

    Pre-Flight Parameter Invariants: In a prompt-driven loop, a model hallucinating an invalid argument type (e.g., passing a string where an integer timestamp is required) passes directly into underlying system APIs, causing unhandled runtime crashes. Skillware’s BaseSkill.validate_params() intercepts inputs at the interface boundary, catching schema violations and raising structured, machine-readable SkillwareParamValidationError exceptions that allow the agent to self-correct without crashing.

  • •

    Deterministic Chaining vs. Multi-Agent Banter: When orchestrating multi-step workflows, popular frameworks (e.g., CrewAI, AutoGen) spawn multiple conversing LLM agents [47, 30]. This approach suffers from semantic drift, high latency, and compounding errors. Skillware provides a deterministic directed acyclic graph (DAG) chaining engine (skillware.chains) with explicit state bindings (host., next., prev.) and conditional evaluation gates (when:), executing complex pipelines with zero conversational overhead.

  • •

    Asynchronous Non-Blocking Execution: Real-world systems run high-concurrency event loops. Skillware natively implements aexecute(), automatically offloading synchronous blocking calls to worker threads while preserving native non-blocking coroutine support for I/O-intensive tools.

    • 2.3.3  Enterprise Operators: Deterministic Logic, Confirmation Gates, and Secret Isolation

  • •

    Zero Unreviewed Code Execution: Under Skillware, an agent never writes code on the fly to interact with sensitive databases. All operational logic resides in pre-compiled, peer-reviewed, static Python files. The model’s authority is constrained strictly to selecting the appropriate capability and parameterizing it.

  • •

    Inviolable Confirmation and Dry-Run Gates: For irreversible mutations (e.g., executing high-value bank transfers or dispatching executive communications), Skillware skills implement mandatory boolean validation gates (confirmed: true) and preview modes (dry_run: true). If the model omits confirmation, the capability refuses execution at the code level, regardless of how persuasively the agent was prompted.

  • •

    Zero-Leak Secret Management: Storing credentials in process-global environment variables (os.environ) exposes keys to accidental leakage via exception tracebacks or unauthorized memory inspection. Skillware’s SecretProvider protocol (EnvSecretProvider, MappingSecretProvider, CallableSecretProvider) injects credentials directly into the skill instance via BaseSkill.credential(), allowing hosts to bridge enterprise KMS or HashiCorp Vault backends with zero global state pollution.

    • 2.3.4  Sovereign Infrastructure: Air-Gapped Autonomy, Supply-Chain Provenance, and Forensic Auditability

  • •

    Air-Gapped Sovereignty: Contemporary cloud agent APIs require streaming operational telemetry, military communications, and critical infrastructure telemetry to foreign-controlled data centers. Skillware skills, when paired with locally hosted Small Language Models (SLMs), execute 100% offline on sovereign hardware with zero external network connectivity.

  • •

    Issuer Attribution and Supply-Chain Visibility: In high-assurance defense applications, third-party software must be attributable. Every Skillware manifest declares its issuer (name, GitHub handle, organization), and the loader resolves skills through an explicit tier order (project\succexternal\succbundled) with automated shadow-conflict detection, so that any skill overriding a maintainer-reviewed bundled skill is surfaced to the operator rather than silently substituted.

  • •

    Non-Repudiable Auditing: Through its synergy with AURA Harness (Section 7), Skillware operations emit SHA-256 hash-chained JSONL audit receipts, providing tamper-evident forensic logs that record what actions an autonomous system took, when, and under what policy constraints.

    • 3  The Skillware Architecture: Formal Specification and In-Process Adaptation

    To replace informal prompt conventions with a mathematically verifiable foundation, Skillware formalizes an Agent Skill as a self-contained, version-controlled filesystem bundle that encapsulates code, contracts, instructions, and tests into a unified, installable unit (Figure 1).

    3.1  Formal Mathematical Definition of an Agent Skill

    Definition 1(Agent Skill Bundle).

    An Agent Skill K is defined as a 5-tuple:

    K=⟨ℂ,𝔼,D,A,ℙ⟩

    		(2)

    where:

  • 1.

    ℂ=⟨Sᵢₙ,Sₒᵤₜ,Π_const,Iᵢₛₛ,ℝ_dep⟩ is the Contract (manifest.yaml) [18, 37], comprising the input parameter JSON Schema Sᵢₙ, the structured output schema Sₒᵤₜ, the immutable constitutional boundary predicates Π_const, the cryptographic publisher identity Iᵢₛₛ, and dependency specifications ℝ_dep. In Skillware v0.6.0, contract validity is enforced via an internal meta-schema engine (skillware.core.manifest_schema) that pre-validates action signatures, parameter types, and security constraints prior to runtime ingestion.

  • 2.

    𝔼:Sᵢₙ×Θₑₙᵥ→Sₒᵤₜ∪{⊥} is the deterministic Effect (skill.py), a state transition mapping valid input arguments under environment secrets Θₑₙᵥ to typed output envelopes, or failing closed to an error state ⊥.

  • 3.

    D∈Σ^* is the cognitive Directive (instructions.md), a structured natural-language guide instructing the foundation model on operational preconditions, output semantics, and cognitive heuristics.

  • 4.

    A:(𝔼×ℂ)→{0,1} is the offline Assurance verifier (test_skill.py), an executable predicate guaranteeing that the Effect satisfies the Contract independently of external model APIs:

    A(𝔼,ℂ)=1\iff∀p∈Sᵢₙ, 𝔼(p,Θ)∈Sₒᵤₜ ∧ Π_const(𝔼,p)=true

    		(3)
  • 5.

    ℙ is the Presentation descriptor (card.json), providing metadata for UI catalogs, registry discovery, and operator dashboards.

    • Optional assets extend the bundle: a static CorpusB_data (kb/, data/) containing local authoritative lookup datasets, and machine-readable Referencesℝ_ref (schemas/) providing auxiliary domain taxonomies.

    3.2  The Five Core Roles of a Skill Bundle

    Every skill registered within the Skillware ecosystem resides within a categorized directory (skills///) and satisfies five distinct foundational roles implemented via fixed filenames (Figure 2):

  • 1.

    Contract (manifest.yaml): The single source of truth defining the capability’s external boundary. It specifies JSON Schema-compliant input parameters (parameters:), structured return types (returns:), execution prerequisites (requires:), publisher identity (issuer: containing name, email, GitHub handle, and organization), and an immutable Constitution—a set of hard rules defining what the capability will and will not do (e.g., “Offline only; no external network transmission”, “Never execute transfers without explicit confirmed flag”).

  • 2.

    Effect (skill.py): The deterministic runtime engine. Inheriting from the framework’s BaseSkill class, this module implements synchronous execute(params) and non-blocking asynchronous aexecute(params) entry points. It contains the real, pre-reviewed Python logic—ranging from cryptographic ledger operations and financial compliance to biological sequence processing (bio/sequence_ops) and specialized numerical routines—completely insulated from stochastic LLM code generation.

  • 3.

    Directive (instructions.md): The cognitive operational manual. This document is injected into the model’s system context, teaching the reasoning engine when to call the skill, how to interpret its JSON responses, and where its operational boundaries lie, without usurping the host agent’s global personality.

  • 4.

    Assurance (test_skill.py): The automated verification suite. Every skill must ship with comprehensive offline tests ensuring that the Effect honors the Contract. These tests are executed automatically via the CLI (skillware test) and in continuous integration before any skill is admitted into the registry.

  • 5.

    Presentation (card.json): UI and registry catalog metadata. It defines visual icons, branding palettes, and human-readable badges, ensuring seamless integration into visual dashboards and agent discovery marketplaces.

  • 6.

    Corpus and References (kb/, data/, schemas/): Bundled static assets, such as offline sanctions lists, geographic boundary databases, or MIME schemas, enabling self-contained, air-gapped execution without external scraping.

    3.3  The BaseSkill Class and Parameter Invariants

    Every capability subclassing BaseSkill inherits an inviolable parameter enforcement mechanism. Listing 2 shows the core implementation from skillware.core.base_skill:

    Notice the defensive invariants embedded directly within BaseSkill:

  • •

    Schema Pre-flight Validation: When a model emits a tool call, validate_params() intercepts the arguments against the manifest’s JSON Schema before any business logic executes. If the model hallucinates a malformed type, execution immediately halts with an explainable SkillwareParamValidationError, protecting underlying systems from corrupt state.

  • •

    Safe Async/Sync Bridging: Recognizing that modern agent runtimes alternate between synchronous script loops and high-concurrency asyncio event loops, BaseSkill provides an internal _run_coroutine_sync() bridge that safely executes coroutines even within pre-existing event loops via isolated thread pools.

    • 3.4  Universal Interface Morphism

    A primary source of developer fatigue is the need to maintain separate tool declarations for every foundation model API. Skillware solves this through the mathematical concept of an Interface MorphismΦₕₒₛₜ:

    Φₕₒₛₜ:ℂ\longrightarrowTₕₒₛₜ

    		(4)

    which transmutes the unified Contract ℂ into the target host’s specific type signature Tₕₒₛₜ entirely in-process:

  • 1.

    Google Gemini (Φ_gemini): Google’s google-genai SDK requires uppercase Protobuf type declarations (e.g., "type": "STRING" rather than standard JSON Schema’s "type": "string"). SkillLoader.to_gemini_tool() recursively traverses the properties tree, sanitizing tool names and upper-casing all primitive and nested types to produce valid types.Tool(function_declarations=[…]) objects.

  • 2.

    Anthropic Claude (Φ_claude): Transmutes the schema into Claude’s tools specification, enforcing alphanumeric name sanitization and embedding properties in input_schema.

  • 3.

    OpenAI & DeepSeek (Φₒₚₑₙₐᵢ,Φ_deepseek): Maps the contract to Chat Completions function signatures ("type": "function", "function": {…}).

  • 4.

    AWS Bedrock Converse (Φ_bedrock): Packages parameters into Bedrock’s toolSpec JSON schema envelopes.

  • 5.

    Ollama Local Models (Φₒₗₗₐₘₐ): For edge models lacking native function-calling APIs, to_ollama_prompt() compiles the schema into clean, deterministic markdown specifications that small open-weights models (e.g., Llama-3-8B) can reliably interpret and execute.

    • Crucially, because Φₕₒₛₜ is executed in-process through native Python class instances, it introduces zero network serialization latency, zero IPC sockets, and zero inter-process dependencies.

    4  Runtime Operations, Deterministic Chaining, and Operator Control

    Real-world autonomous systems do not operate with isolated single-shot tool calls. Production workflows require multi-capability sessions, deterministic step sequencing, and strict access governance. Skillware provides a comprehensive runtime management stack to handle these operational demands with mathematical predictability.

    4.1  SkillContext: Hierarchical Discovery and Shadow Guards

    To manage multi-capability environments, Skillware introduces SkillContext, a centralized session controller that governs capability discovery, trust tiers, and prompt overhead.

    SkillContext establishes an explicit path-resolution hierarchy to discover and load capability bundles:

    Tᵣₑₛₒₗᵥₑ=project \succ external \succ bundled \succ override

    		(5)

    where local project-specific skills (./skills/) take precedence over external organizational libraries (SKILLWARE_SKILL_PATH), which in turn take precedence over the immutable core skills bundled inside the framework’s wheel.

    Automated Shadow-Conflict Detection: In enterprise settings, an adversary or misconfigured repository might attempt to introduce a malicious skill that shadows a core security component (e.g., masking security/prompt_injection_firewall). During initialization, the loader’s find_shadow_conflicts() algorithm conducts an exhaustive cross-tier audit. If path shadowing is detected, the framework halts execution and alerts the operator before any code is imported, guaranteeing supply-chain integrity.

    Context Overhead Modes: To eliminate context window bloat, SkillContext supports three discrete modes:

  • •

    Mode Directives (mode="directives"): Injects full instructions.md documentation for all loaded skills (1,000–3,500 tokens per skill).

  • •

    Mode Brief (mode="brief"): Compresses every skill’s contract into an ultra-lean, one-line signature (25–35 tokens per skill).

  • •

    Mode Tools Only (mode="tools_only"): Exposes tool declarations directly to the API with zero tokens added to the system prompt.

    • By structuring discovery around these three operating modes, SkillContext implements a progressive disclosure lifecycle: the host runtime ingests minimal brief signatures (≈30 tokens per skill) during intent routing (mode="brief"), unlocks typed JSON Schema parameters only when a capability candidate is emitted (mode="tools_only"), validates all constraints pre-flight via prepare(), and lazy-loads deterministic Python execution logic via execute() exclusively upon verified invocation. Full markdown instructions (mode="directives") are unlocked on demand only when task ambiguity or organizational policy mandates deeper cognitive guidance.

    Zero-Token Dynamic Discovery via SkillMatcher: In version 0.6.0, Skillware integrates the SkillMatcher engine (skillware.core.matcher) and the unified skillware find discovery CLI. Rather than forcing foundation models to maintain dozens of tool definitions inside their active context windows—which triggers quadratic attention compute and increases routing hallucinations—SkillMatcher performs client-side intent routing across registered capability manifests using a hybrid BM25 lexical scorer and cosine embedding metric. By matching task semantics to candidate contracts in under 2 ms on local silicon, the runtime retrieves and activates solely the relevant bundle, enabling sub-second cold starts and slashing resident context overhead to zero until execution time.

    4.2  Formal Semantics of the Deterministic Chaining Engine

    To eliminate the stochastic fragility and token waste of multi-agent conversational banter (e.g., in CrewAI or AutoGen [47, 30]), Skillware provides the Named Skill Chaining Engine (skillware.chains). A chain is a statically defined Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) executed deterministically by the runtime (Figure 3).

    Definition 2(Chain State Transition Function).

    Let Σ represent the execution state space, where σₖ=⟨host,prev,next⟩∈Σ records host inputs, prior outputs, and intermediate pipeline buffers. A chain step k is defined as a 4-tuple:

    Stepₖ=⟨κₖ,Bᵢₙ,Mₒᵤₜ,Π_when⟩

    		(6)

    where κₖ is the target Skillware bundle, Bᵢₙ is the dot-notation parameter binding, Mₒᵤₜ is the output mapping, and Π_when:Σ→{0,1} is the conditional activation predicate.

    The state transition operator Γ:(Step×Σ)→Σ evaluates as:

    Γ(Stepₖ,σₖ)=\begincasesσₖ⊕Mₒᵤₜ(𝔼ₖ(pₖ))&ifΠ_when(σₖ)=1 σₖ&ifΠ_when(σₖ)=0\endcases

    		(7)

    where pₖ=resolve(Bᵢₙ,σₖ) resolves argument bindings from host and prior states.

    Listing 3 illustrates a concrete named chain defined in .skillware.yaml:

    As formalized in Equation 7 and Listing 3, if a safety scanner flags an untrusted input (Π_when=0), the downstream task is skipped instantly with zero token expenditure and zero model latency, eliminating conversational drift.

    4.3  Operator Infrastructure: Segregated Identity and State

    A foundational principle of secure systems is the physical segregation of operational state from cognitive processing. Skillware enforces this through local-first operator stores under ~/.config/skillware/ that survive framework upgrades:

  • 1.

    Local-First Address Book (addressbook.yaml): Real-world workflows require resolving colloquial aliases (e.g., “Send draft to the CFO”). Instead of exposing full corporate contact directories to cloud model prompts, Skillware’s office/gmail_handler resolves aliases deterministically on disk via operations (add, update, upsert, remove). The foundation model never receives sensitive personnel directories.

  • 2.

    EVM Network Ledger (evm.yaml): Encapsulates private RPC nodes, smart contract ABIs, chain IDs, and gas ceilings locally. The agent cannot be manipulated into routing transactions through hostile or unmonitored RPC relays.

  • 3.

    Multi-Profile Signatures and Append-Only Ledgers: Outbound email workflows utilize localized signature profiles (mail_signature.txt, mail_signature.html, profiles default, formal) and commit every dispatch event to an immutable append-only ledger (gmail_send_ledger.json) with incremental scan cursors (gmail_scan_state.json), providing defensible, non-repudiable transaction histories.

  • 4.

    Dedicated Machine Personas: The Skillware constitution mandates dedicated operational identities: agents operate under dedicated, segregated Gmail mailboxes using App Passwords, and dedicated on-chain wallets with strictly capped gas allowances—never human primary accounts.

  • 5.

    Zero-Leak Secret Providers: Under the SecretProvider interface (EnvSecretProvider, MappingSecretProvider, CallableSecretProvider), capabilities resolve API tokens dynamically via enterprise Key Management Services (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) or ephemeral STS tokens. Secrets are never exposed to process-global environment variables or logged in unhandled exception traces.

    • 4.4  Agent Loops: The Tool Execution Cycle

    In production applications, Skillware integrates cleanly into standard conversational agent loops without requiring external orchestration frameworks. Listing 4 illustrates the canonical in-process execution cycle:

    This pattern guarantees that the model never touches external APIs directly; every argument is validated pre-flight, and execution happens deterministically in-process.

    To visualize this execution cycle in practice, Figure 4 contrasts a live multi-step invocation under speculative Python generation against Skillware’s deterministic execution. In the prompt-driven regime, the model attempts to synthesize disposable code across multiple turns: handling binary IMAP streams triggers buffer truncations, unhandled UnicodeDecodeError crashes, and repeated subprocess spawns that burn 28,041 tokens and 41.8 s of latency before resolution. Under Skillware, the identical operational objective is dispatched via typed schema calls (search_messages→download_attachment) in 3.7 mean turns and 11.7 s (6,194 tokens), with zero runtime script synthesis and zero workspace debugging loops.

    This multi-turn failure dynamic reveals a deeper structural pathology in prompt-driven autonomy: the Context Poisoning Cliff (Figure 5). In traditional software engineering, allowing an agent multiple retry attempts generally increases cumulative problem-solving probability (Pass@k). In generative LLM agents, however, this assumption fails catastrophically. As documented across 368 unassisted trials under Skillware-Bench, attempts 1–4 exhibit strong error-recovery dynamics (85.0%--100.0% pass rate). However, as failed script attempts, compiler tracebacks, and hallucinated fixes accumulate in the context window, the model’s effective attention degrades. By Attempt 8, the marginal pass rate collapses to 50.0%, plunging to 33.3% at Attempt 9, and reaching a terminal 0.0% failure loop at 12+ attempts. The agent becomes context-poisoned by its own historical errors, perseverating on invalid syntax patterns. By replacing speculative code generation with pre-verified deterministic bundles, Skillware completely excises this hazard curve, guaranteeing that agents never enter degenerate multi-turn script debugging loops.

    4.5  Execution Telemetry: Call Survival Flow and Run-to-Run Determinism

    The architectural combination of typed pre-flight validation and deterministic execution has profound empirical consequences for agent reliability.

    Figure 6 traces the survival lifecycle of 1,000 emitted tool calls per arm. In prompt-driven systems, unconstrained parameter generation leads to a high incidence of invalid signatures (11.8%), triggering multi-turn repair loops or catastrophic task abandonment (57 aborts). In contrast, Skillware’s typed gates ensure 99.6% initial validity, elevating clean first-pass completion from 71.2% to 94.1% and reducing total aborts by 87.7%.

    Furthermore, as illustrated in Figure 7, Skillware eliminates the stochastic volatility that plagues production deployments. Across 40 seeded replays under identical prompts and seeds, unequipped baseline execution score variance remains wide (σ=4.1), whereas Skillware-equipped execution contracts by a factor of 5.1× (σ=0.8). Deterministic capability execution guarantees that repeated invocations yield reproducible, verifiable outcomes across time.

    5  The SLM Parameter Paradox and Bounded Computational Complexity

    A central premise of contemporary foundation model research is that reliability scales monotonically with parameter count [45]. In the domain of tool-using autonomous systems, however, empirical evidence demonstrates that this scaling hypothesis is flawed. Pioneering research in compact model families—from synthetic textbook curricula [16] to local on-device models such as Phi-3 [1] and TinyLlama [50]—confirms that reasoning efficiency depends primarily on context purity and structured interfaces rather than parameter bloat. When capability is decoupled from linguistic reasoning, we observe the Small Language Model (SLM) Parameter Paradox: Compact models (3B–8B parameters) equipped with deterministic Skillware bundles consistently surpass massive unequipped frontier models (70B–1.8T parameters) in functional accuracy, execution latency, and economic sustainability.

    5.1  Computational Complexity of Prompted vs. Equipped Agents

    The architectural inefficiency of prompt-driven tools can be formalized through transformer attention complexity. In standard self-attention, computational and memory complexity scales quadratically with total sequence length L[23]:

    Ωₐₜₜₑₙₜᵢₒₙ=O(L²·d_model)

    		(8)

    When an agent framework injects T_sys≈4,000 tokens of OpenAPI documentation and procedural instructions into the system prompt, this overhead permanently inflates L across every turn of a multi-turn session. For an M-turn interaction, the cumulative attention computation expended merely re-reading static API specifications scales as ∑ₘ₌₁^MO((m·Lₜᵤᵣₙ+T_sys)²).

    In contrast, Skillware partitions computation into two distinct regimes:

  • 1.

    Semantic Mapping (Stochastic): The language model is tasked strictly with mapping user intent into parameter selection:

    f_SLM:Xᵤₛₑᵣ\longrightarrowp∈Sᵢₙ

    		(9)

    Under mode="brief", tool signatures consume T_brief≤35 tokens, keeping sequence length L minimal and bounded.

  • 2.

    Logic Execution (Deterministic): The actual computation is evaluated by compiled Python code:

    𝔼(p,Θ)\longrightarrowr∈Sₒᵤₜ

    		(10)

    which executes with O(1) model token expenditure and near-instantaneous CPU execution time.

    • By excising resident procedural logic from active context and executing it just-in-time on local silicon, Skillware achieves an 84.0% reduction in resident prompt volume (Figure 8).

    5.2  Soft Skills vs. Hard Skills: The Moat of Executable Software

    To understand why small models triumph when properly equipped, one must distinguish between Soft Skills and Hard Skills:

  • •

    Soft Skills (Prompt-Based Directives): A markdown file or instruction block (exemplified by SKILL.md conventions) provides natural-language procedural guidance. The language model is forced to parse extensive prose, synthesize ad-hoc bash or python snippets, interpret terminal exit codes, and self-correct when code fails. This paradigm requires massive frontier models to carry the reasoning load, burns thousands of prompt tokens per turn, and collapses entirely on compact 7B/8B open-weights models that struggle with zero-shot code generation under context pressure. Furthermore, when the host API endpoint degrades or closes, the soft skill evaporates.

  • •

    Hard Skills (Skillware Capability Bundles): In this paradigm, capabilities are structured not as arbitrary markdown files with procedural prompt instructions, but as versioned, ontological software artifacts with an engineered lifecycle [14]. The operational task is pre-compiled as verified, tested Python software residing directly on disk, bound by an immutable JSON Schema contract and local unit tests. The language model is relieved of code generation entirely; its sole responsibility is parameter selection. Because execution occurs deterministically in native code, functional output is invariant across model scale: GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, or an 8B SLM running locally on Ollama produce the exact same validated JSON output, the exact same error handling, and the exact same forensic audit trail.

    • Frontier language models fail at multi-step tasks not because they lack linguistic comprehension, but because transformers cannot reliably compute non-linear symbolic transformations over auto-regressive state [13, 44]. Tasks such as validating an Ethereum checksum address, calculating an SHA-256 state root, computing OFAC fuzzy sanctions distances, or traversing an IMAP MIME multipart tree require exact computational steps. While massive API calling harnesses (such as Gorilla [34] and ToolLLM [40]) attempt to train models to memorize thousands of API signatures, they still suffer from parameter drift and execution stochasticity.

    Compiled software is the ultimate moat. By packaging exact algorithmic routines in skill.py and immutable reference taxonomies in Corpus, an 8B parameter model achieves 100% algorithmic execution accuracy without burning parameters on disposable logic.

    5.3  Empirical Cost Economics: Multi-Turn Scaling

    To rigorously quantify the economic divergence between paradigms, we evaluate a production pipeline executing three coordinated skills (Email Communication, Corporate Registry Verification, and Context Compression) across N=1,000 multi-turn sessions.

    The cost functions are governed by:

    ℂₚᵣₒₘₚₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^N(T_sys+T_ctx⁽ⁱ⁾)Pᵢₙ+T_code⁽ⁱ⁾Pₒᵤₜ(11)
    ℂ_skillware=∑ᵢ₌₁^N(T_brief+T_ctx⁽ⁱ⁾)Pᵢₙ+T_call⁽ⁱ⁾Pₒᵤₜ+0_logic(12)

    As documented in Figure 9:

  • •

    Dynamic Code Generation (Frontier LLM): Costs $15.58 per 1,000 turns due to voluminous prompt context and high output token synthesis fees.

  • •

    Skillware Directives (Frontier LLM): Reduces cost to $9.11 by replacing synthesized code with concise JSON tool calls.

  • •

    Skillware Brief Mode (Frontier LLM): Compresses tool documentation into 30-token signatures, dropping cost to $2.89.

  • •

    Skillware + Local 8B SLM: Completely eliminates cloud API costs, running locally on commodity consumer hardware (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090 or Apple M-series silicon) at an amortized energy cost of $0.42 per 1,000 turns—a 97.3% operational expenditure reduction.

    • This economic divergence is further dissected in Figures 10 and 11. At the granular per-call level, an unequipped agent consumes a median of 5,520 tokens to complete a successful tool invocation, driven by redundant schema prefill (1,840 tokens), retry friction (940 tokens), and code debugging loops (780 tokens). Equipping the agent with Skillware contracts per-call consumption to 1,620 tokens—a net savings of 70.6%.

    Crucially, as shown in Figure 11, Skillware eliminates the output completion bloat characteristic of prompted models: while vanilla agents expend 64.3% of their generated tokens emitting fragile script boilerplate and 21.2% on apologies or replanning, Skillware-equipped agents generate only 556 tokens per task, with 86.4% dedicated directly to actionable, structured tool dispatch.

    The macro-level consequences of this token compression are demonstrated in Figure 12, which measures cumulative task pass rates as a function of strict token budget caps across all 736 experimental conditions. Under tight token constraints (1,000 to 4,000 tokens), unequipped models fail over 58% of trials due to prompt prefill overhead and script re-synthesis. In contrast, Skillware achieves an 82.3% pass rate at a modest budget of 8,000 tokens. Remarkably, this exceeds the terminal pass rate achieved by unassisted vanilla models even when granted an unconstrained budget of 64,000 tokens (81.5%)—demonstrating a decisive 8× token budget efficiency advantage.

    5.4  The Empirical Parameter Paradox: Asymmetric Lift Across Model Scales

    While the cost functions in Equations (11)–(12) demonstrate dramatic operational expense reductions, empirical testing reveals an even more profound structural phenomenon: the marginal performance lift from Skillware is inversely proportional to baseline model scale.

    To evaluate this scaling effect, we benchmarked models across parameter scales ranging from compact 3B on-device models to 1.8T frontier mixture-of-experts under the Skillware-Bench evaluation harness [36]. Figure 13 plots the empirical Task Resolution and Governance Score across model scales for both the prompt-driven baseline and the Skillware-equipped configuration.

    Under the baseline prompt-driven regime, performance collapses precipitously when parameter scale drops below 70B: an unequipped 8B model (such as Llama 3.2 8B or Qwen 2.5/3.5 7B) achieves a composite score of only 56.0, failing basic procedural sequences, emitting hallucinated shell code, and missing required constitutional dry-run previews. Because transformer attention cannot natively execute stateful symbolic transformations without extensive parameter capacity, compact models struggle under the dual cognitive burden of reasoning and ad-hoc code compilation.

    Equipping compact models with Skillware fundamentally alters this scaling relationship:

  • 1.

    Asymmetric Marginal Lift: While frontier models gain +18.0 to +20.0 points, 8B SLMs gain +32.0 points (56.0→88.0), achieving a higher marginal return on capability equipping than massive foundation models.

  • 2.

    The Parity Inversion: At 88.0 composite points, an open-weight 8B SLM running locally on commodity consumer hardware systematically outperforms unequipped frontier foundation models, including unequipped Claude Sonnet 5 (80.0 composite points, corresponding to an 87.5% binary pass rate on standard tasks) and GPT-5 (79.0).

  • 3.

    Inductive Schema Alignment in SLMs: Compact models specifically instruction-tuned for tool execution (such as Llama 3.2 and Qwen 2.5/3.5) exhibit minimal conversational sycophancy or disclaimers. When relieved of the need to synthesize logic and restricted strictly to schema-constrained parameter selection (f_SLM:Xᵤₛₑᵣ→p∈Sᵢₙ), their parameter efficiency is maximized, yielding deterministic execution with zero cloud API dependency.

    • 5.5  Thermodynamic Efficiency, Data Sovereignty, and Air-Gapped Operation

    Beyond financial balance sheets, prompt-driven cloud execution exacts a staggering thermodynamic toll. Running multi-thousand-token prompts through multi-hundred-billion parameter cloud clusters can consume upwards of 29 watt-hours per complex interaction, requiring substantial electricity and evaporative datacenter cooling water. Firing massive frontier clusters to dynamically re-synthesize common string manipulations or JSON mappings is an unsustainable misallocation of planetary compute resources.

    Local silicon running quantized 3B–8B models (e.g., Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, or Phi-3) executing compiled Python capabilities reduces active power draw to fractions of a watt-hour per call.

    Furthermore, for sovereign defense entities, intelligence agencies, and healthcare institutions, cloud-based foundation models present an unacceptable operational risk: streaming proprietary code, medical records, or defense telemetry across external boundaries violates statutory privacy mandates and risks immediate revocation under geopolitical embargoes. Because Skillware bundles resolve all contracts, code, and lookup corpora locally, an operator can pin open-weights models and hard capabilities inside a 100% air-gapped, zero-egress perimeter. The system remains fully operational, completely auditable, and impervious to remote cloud outages.

    6  Systematic Comparative Analysis:
    Skillware vs. The Autonomous Systems Ecosystem

    A persistent impediment to scientific clarity in the autonomous systems literature is the conflation of transport protocols, conversational orchestrators, and capability standards. In this section, we present an analytical taxonomy contrasting Skillware against alternative paradigms, followed by an empirical case study.

    6.1  Taxonomic Framework: Seven Architectural Dimensions

    To establish rigorous scientific boundaries, we systematically analyze Skillware against prevailing alternative paradigms across seven foundational architectural dimensions:

  • 1.

    Primary Abstraction: Skillware formalizes know-how as an immutable 5-role capability bundle containing code (skill.py), contracts (manifest.yaml), directives (instructions.md), tests (test_skill.py), and corpus data. In contrast, MCP operates as an external client-server wire protocol; Cursor and agent coding frameworks rely on informal markdown prose (SKILL.md); LangChain provides Python class wrappers around ad-hoc libraries; and AutoGen/CrewAI rely on conversational agent personas.

  • 2.

    Runtime Topology and Latency: Skillware executes in-process within CPython, requiring zero prompt tokens for logic execution and completing in sub-millisecond time. In contrast, MCP requires managing out-of-process daemon processes over stdio or HTTP sockets (8–15 ms latency); prompt directives force multi-turn auto-regressive code synthesis; and multi-agent meshes burn thousands of tokens in circular multi-turn chatter.

  • 3.

    Contract Enforcement: Skillware enforces strict compile-time JSON Schema meta-validation and BNF parameter typing before execution. In contrast, prompt directives provide informal natural-language descriptions with zero type checking, and conversational frameworks rely on unconstrained text parsing prone to semantic drift.

  • 4.

    Model Portability: Skillware provides universal in-process adapters that dynamically transmute tool contracts into native dialects (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Ollama). Alternative approaches either require host-specific MCP client implementations, lock capabilities to specific IDE environments, or mandate framework-bound runtime engines.

  • 5.

    Assurance and Offline Verification: Every Skillware bundle ships with a hermetic offline test suite (test_skill.py) verifying that the Effect satisfies the Contract with zero third-party API calls. Prompt directives cannot be tested without calling live LLMs, and multi-agent meshes yield stochastic evaluations that resist reproducible verification.

  • 6.

    Governance and Security Boundaries: Skillware enforces inviolable code-level confirmation gates (confirmed: true) and air-gapped sandboxing. Prompt-based capabilities are vulnerable to indirect injection, and framework tools frequently grant unbounded process-global environment access.

  • 7.

    Sovereignty and Supply Chain: Skillware operates 100% offline on local silicon with cryptographic issuer attribution and SHA-256 Merkle audit trails. Cloud-dependent paradigms leak telemetry to third parties and suffer from unpinned remote model drift.

    • 6.2  Skillware vs. Model Context Protocol (MCP)

    Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) specifies a client-server architecture using JSON-RPC over stdio or Server-Sent Events (SSE) to connect AI applications to data sources and tools [4].

    While MCP provides a valuable language-agnostic wire transport protocol for connecting desktop environments (e.g., Claude Desktop) to local or remote microservices, its client-server topology introduces severe friction for in-process application runtimes:

  • 1.

    Process Supervisory Overhead: Operating an agent with dozens of capabilities under MCP requires spawning, monitoring, and managing separate daemon child processes. In production, child process crashes, broken pipes, and socket disconnects create brittle points of failure.

  • 2.

    IPC Serialization Latency: Transferring large binary payloads (e.g., high-resolution drone imagery, local database dumps, or memory buffers) over stdio or HTTP sockets incurs serialization penalties that do not exist within Skillware’s in-process CPython execution, where data is passed directly via memory references.

    • Skillware and MCP are orthogonal and complementary layers: MCP is a wire transport protocol; Skillware is an in-process capability standard. A developer can wrap any Skillware bundle in an MCP server with minimal boilerplate, but Skillware eliminates the overhead of managing background server daemons when building native Python applications.

    6.3  Skillware vs. Agent Skills (SKILL.md)

    The emerging Agent Skills format (originating from Anthropic and now adopted by developer agents such as Cursor and Claude Code) organizes agent instructions as SKILL.md files containing markdown guidance and optional shell scripts [3].

    While SKILL.md serves as an effective procedural reference for human developers and IDE coding agents, it lacks the formal guarantees necessary for autonomous production systems:

  • •

    Absence of Formal Typed Contracts:SKILL.md relies on the model to read natural-language text and synthesize command-line invocations. It provides no typed JSON Schema parameter guarantees, no programmatic output typing, and no automated pre-flight parameter validation.

  • •

    Lack of Universal Model Adaptation:SKILL.md relies on host-specific client harnesses. In contrast, Skillware’s universal interface adapters (to_gemini_tool, to_claude_tool, to_openai_tool) dynamically transmute a single manifest.yaml into the exact native tool specification required by any major model API at runtime.

  • •

    Ephemeral Text vs. Versioned Software Ontology: Rather than reducing operational capabilities to markdown files with natural-language instructions, Skillware formalizes capability execution as an engineered software ontology for persistent behavioral artifacts. While Fan and Lan [14] cite the ARPA Skillware open architecture [37] and explore a theoretical ontology for persistent agent behaviors, this work provides the concrete, production-validated execution standard: self-contained five-role capability bundles bound by version-controlled manifests, isolated dependency environments, and deterministic offline assurance verifiers.
