    4.3  Operator Infrastructure: Segregated Identity and State

    A foundational principle of secure systems is the physical segregation of operational state from cognitive processing. Skillware enforces this through local-first operator stores under ~/.config/skillware/ that survive framework upgrades:

  • 1.

    Local-First Address Book (addressbook.yaml): Real-world workflows require resolving colloquial aliases (e.g., “Send draft to the CFO”). Instead of exposing full corporate contact directories to cloud model prompts, Skillware’s office/gmail_handler resolves aliases deterministically on disk via operations (add, update, upsert, remove). The foundation model never receives sensitive personnel directories.

  • 2.

    EVM Network Ledger (evm.yaml): Encapsulates private RPC nodes, smart contract ABIs, chain IDs, and gas ceilings locally. The agent cannot be manipulated into routing transactions through hostile or unmonitored RPC relays.

  • 3.

    Multi-Profile Signatures and Append-Only Ledgers: Outbound email workflows utilize localized signature profiles (mail_signature.txt, mail_signature.html, profiles default, formal) and commit every dispatch event to an immutable append-only ledger (gmail_send_ledger.json) with incremental scan cursors (gmail_scan_state.json), providing defensible, non-repudiable transaction histories.

  • 4.

    Dedicated Machine Personas: The Skillware constitution mandates dedicated operational identities: agents operate under dedicated, segregated Gmail mailboxes using App Passwords, and dedicated on-chain wallets with strictly capped gas allowances—never human primary accounts.

  • 5.

    Zero-Leak Secret Providers: Under the SecretProvider interface (EnvSecretProvider, MappingSecretProvider, CallableSecretProvider), capabilities resolve API tokens dynamically via enterprise Key Management Services (AWS KMS, HashiCorp Vault) or ephemeral STS tokens. Secrets are never exposed to process-global environment variables or logged in unhandled exception traces.

    • 4.4  Agent Loops: The Tool Execution Cycle

    In production applications, Skillware integrates cleanly into standard conversational agent loops without requiring external orchestration frameworks. Listing 4 illustrates the canonical in-process execution cycle:

    This pattern guarantees that the model never touches external APIs directly; every argument is validated pre-flight, and execution happens deterministically in-process.

    To visualize this execution cycle in practice, Figure 4 contrasts a live multi-step invocation under speculative Python generation against Skillware’s deterministic execution. In the prompt-driven regime, the model attempts to synthesize disposable code across multiple turns: handling binary IMAP streams triggers buffer truncations, unhandled UnicodeDecodeError crashes, and repeated subprocess spawns that burn 28,041 tokens and 41.8 s of latency before resolution. Under Skillware, the identical operational objective is dispatched via typed schema calls (search_messages→download_attachment) in 3.7 mean turns and 11.7 s (6,194 tokens), with zero runtime script synthesis and zero workspace debugging loops.

    This multi-turn failure dynamic reveals a deeper structural pathology in prompt-driven autonomy: the Context Poisoning Cliff (Figure 5). In traditional software engineering, allowing an agent multiple retry attempts generally increases cumulative problem-solving probability (Pass@k). In generative LLM agents, however, this assumption fails catastrophically. As documented across 368 unassisted trials under Skillware-Bench, attempts 1–4 exhibit strong error-recovery dynamics (85.0%--100.0% pass rate). However, as failed script attempts, compiler tracebacks, and hallucinated fixes accumulate in the context window, the model’s effective attention degrades. By Attempt 8, the marginal pass rate collapses to 50.0%, plunging to 33.3% at Attempt 9, and reaching a terminal 0.0% failure loop at 12+ attempts. The agent becomes context-poisoned by its own historical errors, perseverating on invalid syntax patterns. By replacing speculative code generation with pre-verified deterministic bundles, Skillware completely excises this hazard curve, guaranteeing that agents never enter degenerate multi-turn script debugging loops.

    4.5  Execution Telemetry: Call Survival Flow and Run-to-Run Determinism

    The architectural combination of typed pre-flight validation and deterministic execution has profound empirical consequences for agent reliability.

    Figure 6 traces the survival lifecycle of 1,000 emitted tool calls per arm. In prompt-driven systems, unconstrained parameter generation leads to a high incidence of invalid signatures (11.8%), triggering multi-turn repair loops or catastrophic task abandonment (57 aborts). In contrast, Skillware’s typed gates ensure 99.6% initial validity, elevating clean first-pass completion from 71.2% to 94.1% and reducing total aborts by 87.7%.

    Furthermore, as illustrated in Figure 7, Skillware eliminates the stochastic volatility that plagues production deployments. Across 40 seeded replays under identical prompts and seeds, unequipped baseline execution score variance remains wide (σ=4.1), whereas Skillware-equipped execution contracts by a factor of 5.1× (σ=0.8). Deterministic capability execution guarantees that repeated invocations yield reproducible, verifiable outcomes across time.

    5  The SLM Parameter Paradox and Bounded Computational Complexity

    A central premise of contemporary foundation model research is that reliability scales monotonically with parameter count [45]. In the domain of tool-using autonomous systems, however, empirical evidence demonstrates that this scaling hypothesis is flawed. Pioneering research in compact model families—from synthetic textbook curricula [16] to local on-device models such as Phi-3 [1] and TinyLlama [50]—confirms that reasoning efficiency depends primarily on context purity and structured interfaces rather than parameter bloat. When capability is decoupled from linguistic reasoning, we observe the Small Language Model (SLM) Parameter Paradox: Compact models (3B–8B parameters) equipped with deterministic Skillware bundles consistently surpass massive unequipped frontier models (70B–1.8T parameters) in functional accuracy, execution latency, and economic sustainability.

    5.1  Computational Complexity of Prompted vs. Equipped Agents

    The architectural inefficiency of prompt-driven tools can be formalized through transformer attention complexity. In standard self-attention, computational and memory complexity scales quadratically with total sequence length L[23]:

    Ωₐₜₜₑₙₜᵢₒₙ=O(L²·d_model)

    		(8)

    When an agent framework injects T_sys≈4,000 tokens of OpenAPI documentation and procedural instructions into the system prompt, this overhead permanently inflates L across every turn of a multi-turn session. For an M-turn interaction, the cumulative attention computation expended merely re-reading static API specifications scales as ∑ₘ₌₁^MO((m·Lₜᵤᵣₙ+T_sys)²).

    In contrast, Skillware partitions computation into two distinct regimes:

  • 1.

    Semantic Mapping (Stochastic): The language model is tasked strictly with mapping user intent into parameter selection:

    f_SLM:Xᵤₛₑᵣ\longrightarrowp∈Sᵢₙ

    		(9)

    Under mode="brief", tool signatures consume T_brief≤35 tokens, keeping sequence length L minimal and bounded.

  • 2.

    Logic Execution (Deterministic): The actual computation is evaluated by compiled Python code:

    𝔼(p,Θ)\longrightarrowr∈Sₒᵤₜ

    		(10)

    which executes with O(1) model token expenditure and near-instantaneous CPU execution time.

    • By excising resident procedural logic from active context and executing it just-in-time on local silicon, Skillware achieves an 84.0% reduction in resident prompt volume (Figure 8).

    5.2  Soft Skills vs. Hard Skills: The Moat of Executable Software

    To understand why small models triumph when properly equipped, one must distinguish between Soft Skills and Hard Skills:

  • •

    Soft Skills (Prompt-Based Directives): A markdown file or instruction block (exemplified by SKILL.md conventions) provides natural-language procedural guidance. The language model is forced to parse extensive prose, synthesize ad-hoc bash or python snippets, interpret terminal exit codes, and self-correct when code fails. This paradigm requires massive frontier models to carry the reasoning load, burns thousands of prompt tokens per turn, and collapses entirely on compact 7B/8B open-weights models that struggle with zero-shot code generation under context pressure. Furthermore, when the host API endpoint degrades or closes, the soft skill evaporates.

  • •

    Hard Skills (Skillware Capability Bundles): In this paradigm, capabilities are structured not as arbitrary markdown files with procedural prompt instructions, but as versioned, ontological software artifacts with an engineered lifecycle [14]. The operational task is pre-compiled as verified, tested Python software residing directly on disk, bound by an immutable JSON Schema contract and local unit tests. The language model is relieved of code generation entirely; its sole responsibility is parameter selection. Because execution occurs deterministically in native code, functional output is invariant across model scale: GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, or an 8B SLM running locally on Ollama produce the exact same validated JSON output, the exact same error handling, and the exact same forensic audit trail.

    • Frontier language models fail at multi-step tasks not because they lack linguistic comprehension, but because transformers cannot reliably compute non-linear symbolic transformations over auto-regressive state [13, 44]. Tasks such as validating an Ethereum checksum address, calculating an SHA-256 state root, computing OFAC fuzzy sanctions distances, or traversing an IMAP MIME multipart tree require exact computational steps. While massive API calling harnesses (such as Gorilla [34] and ToolLLM [40]) attempt to train models to memorize thousands of API signatures, they still suffer from parameter drift and execution stochasticity.

    Compiled software is the ultimate moat. By packaging exact algorithmic routines in skill.py and immutable reference taxonomies in Corpus, an 8B parameter model achieves 100% algorithmic execution accuracy without burning parameters on disposable logic.

    5.3  Empirical Cost Economics: Multi-Turn Scaling

    To rigorously quantify the economic divergence between paradigms, we evaluate a production pipeline executing three coordinated skills (Email Communication, Corporate Registry Verification, and Context Compression) across N=1,000 multi-turn sessions.

    The cost functions are governed by:

    ℂₚᵣₒₘₚₜ=∑ᵢ₌₁^N(T_sys+T_ctx⁽ⁱ⁾)Pᵢₙ+T_code⁽ⁱ⁾Pₒᵤₜ(11)
    ℂ_skillware=∑ᵢ₌₁^N(T_brief+T_ctx⁽ⁱ⁾)Pᵢₙ+T_call⁽ⁱ⁾Pₒᵤₜ+0_logic(12)

    As documented in Figure 9:

  • •

    Dynamic Code Generation (Frontier LLM): Costs $15.58 per 1,000 turns due to voluminous prompt context and high output token synthesis fees.

  • •

    Skillware Directives (Frontier LLM): Reduces cost to $9.11 by replacing synthesized code with concise JSON tool calls.

  • •

    Skillware Brief Mode (Frontier LLM): Compresses tool documentation into 30-token signatures, dropping cost to $2.89.

  • •

    Skillware + Local 8B SLM: Completely eliminates cloud API costs, running locally on commodity consumer hardware (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 4090 or Apple M-series silicon) at an amortized energy cost of $0.42 per 1,000 turns—a 97.3% operational expenditure reduction.

    • This economic divergence is further dissected in Figures 10 and 11. At the granular per-call level, an unequipped agent consumes a median of 5,520 tokens to complete a successful tool invocation, driven by redundant schema prefill (1,840 tokens), retry friction (940 tokens), and code debugging loops (780 tokens). Equipping the agent with Skillware contracts per-call consumption to 1,620 tokens—a net savings of 70.6%.

    Crucially, as shown in Figure 11, Skillware eliminates the output completion bloat characteristic of prompted models: while vanilla agents expend 64.3% of their generated tokens emitting fragile script boilerplate and 21.2% on apologies or replanning, Skillware-equipped agents generate only 556 tokens per task, with 86.4% dedicated directly to actionable, structured tool dispatch.

    The macro-level consequences of this token compression are demonstrated in Figure 12, which measures cumulative task pass rates as a function of strict token budget caps across all 736 experimental conditions. Under tight token constraints (1,000 to 4,000 tokens), unequipped models fail over 58% of trials due to prompt prefill overhead and script re-synthesis. In contrast, Skillware achieves an 82.3% pass rate at a modest budget of 8,000 tokens. Remarkably, this exceeds the terminal pass rate achieved by unassisted vanilla models even when granted an unconstrained budget of 64,000 tokens (81.5%)—demonstrating a decisive 8× token budget efficiency advantage.

    5.4  The Empirical Parameter Paradox: Asymmetric Lift Across Model Scales

    While the cost functions in Equations (11)–(12) demonstrate dramatic operational expense reductions, empirical testing reveals an even more profound structural phenomenon: the marginal performance lift from Skillware is inversely proportional to baseline model scale.

    To evaluate this scaling effect, we benchmarked models across parameter scales ranging from compact 3B on-device models to 1.8T frontier mixture-of-experts under the Skillware-Bench evaluation harness [36]. Figure 13 plots the empirical Task Resolution and Governance Score across model scales for both the prompt-driven baseline and the Skillware-equipped configuration.

    Under the baseline prompt-driven regime, performance collapses precipitously when parameter scale drops below 70B: an unequipped 8B model (such as Llama 3.2 8B or Qwen 2.5/3.5 7B) achieves a composite score of only 56.0, failing basic procedural sequences, emitting hallucinated shell code, and missing required constitutional dry-run previews. Because transformer attention cannot natively execute stateful symbolic transformations without extensive parameter capacity, compact models struggle under the dual cognitive burden of reasoning and ad-hoc code compilation.

    Equipping compact models with Skillware fundamentally alters this scaling relationship:

  • 1.

    Asymmetric Marginal Lift: While frontier models gain +18.0 to +20.0 points, 8B SLMs gain +32.0 points (56.0→88.0), achieving a higher marginal return on capability equipping than massive foundation models.

  • 2.

    The Parity Inversion: At 88.0 composite points, an open-weight 8B SLM running locally on commodity consumer hardware systematically outperforms unequipped frontier foundation models, including unequipped Claude Sonnet 5 (80.0 composite points, corresponding to an 87.5% binary pass rate on standard tasks) and GPT-5 (79.0).

  • 3.

    Inductive Schema Alignment in SLMs: Compact models specifically instruction-tuned for tool execution (such as Llama 3.2 and Qwen 2.5/3.5) exhibit minimal conversational sycophancy or disclaimers. When relieved of the need to synthesize logic and restricted strictly to schema-constrained parameter selection (f_SLM:Xᵤₛₑᵣ→p∈Sᵢₙ), their parameter efficiency is maximized, yielding deterministic execution with zero cloud API dependency.

    • 5.5  Thermodynamic Efficiency, Data Sovereignty, and Air-Gapped Operation

    Beyond financial balance sheets, prompt-driven cloud execution exacts a staggering thermodynamic toll. Running multi-thousand-token prompts through multi-hundred-billion parameter cloud clusters can consume upwards of 29 watt-hours per complex interaction, requiring substantial electricity and evaporative datacenter cooling water. Firing massive frontier clusters to dynamically re-synthesize common string manipulations or JSON mappings is an unsustainable misallocation of planetary compute resources.

    Local silicon running quantized 3B–8B models (e.g., Llama-3-8B, Qwen-2.5-7B, or Phi-3) executing compiled Python capabilities reduces active power draw to fractions of a watt-hour per call.

    Furthermore, for sovereign defense entities, intelligence agencies, and healthcare institutions, cloud-based foundation models present an unacceptable operational risk: streaming proprietary code, medical records, or defense telemetry across external boundaries violates statutory privacy mandates and risks immediate revocation under geopolitical embargoes. Because Skillware bundles resolve all contracts, code, and lookup corpora locally, an operator can pin open-weights models and hard capabilities inside a 100% air-gapped, zero-egress perimeter. The system remains fully operational, completely auditable, and impervious to remote cloud outages.

    6  Systematic Comparative Analysis:
    Skillware vs. The Autonomous Systems Ecosystem

    A persistent impediment to scientific clarity in the autonomous systems literature is the conflation of transport protocols, conversational orchestrators, and capability standards. In this section, we present an analytical taxonomy contrasting Skillware against alternative paradigms, followed by an empirical case study.

    6.1  Taxonomic Framework: Seven Architectural Dimensions

    To establish rigorous scientific boundaries, we systematically analyze Skillware against prevailing alternative paradigms across seven foundational architectural dimensions:

  • 1.

    Primary Abstraction: Skillware formalizes know-how as an immutable 5-role capability bundle containing code (skill.py), contracts (manifest.yaml), directives (instructions.md), tests (test_skill.py), and corpus data. In contrast, MCP operates as an external client-server wire protocol; Cursor and agent coding frameworks rely on informal markdown prose (SKILL.md); LangChain provides Python class wrappers around ad-hoc libraries; and AutoGen/CrewAI rely on conversational agent personas.

  • 2.

    Runtime Topology and Latency: Skillware executes in-process within CPython, requiring zero prompt tokens for logic execution and completing in sub-millisecond time. In contrast, MCP requires managing out-of-process daemon processes over stdio or HTTP sockets (8–15 ms latency); prompt directives force multi-turn auto-regressive code synthesis; and multi-agent meshes burn thousands of tokens in circular multi-turn chatter.

  • 3.

    Contract Enforcement: Skillware enforces strict compile-time JSON Schema meta-validation and BNF parameter typing before execution. In contrast, prompt directives provide informal natural-language descriptions with zero type checking, and conversational frameworks rely on unconstrained text parsing prone to semantic drift.

  • 4.

    Model Portability: Skillware provides universal in-process adapters that dynamically transmute tool contracts into native dialects (Gemini, Claude, OpenAI, Ollama). Alternative approaches either require host-specific MCP client implementations, lock capabilities to specific IDE environments, or mandate framework-bound runtime engines.

  • 5.

    Assurance and Offline Verification: Every Skillware bundle ships with a hermetic offline test suite (test_skill.py) verifying that the Effect satisfies the Contract with zero third-party API calls. Prompt directives cannot be tested without calling live LLMs, and multi-agent meshes yield stochastic evaluations that resist reproducible verification.

  • 6.

    Governance and Security Boundaries: Skillware enforces inviolable code-level confirmation gates (confirmed: true) and air-gapped sandboxing. Prompt-based capabilities are vulnerable to indirect injection, and framework tools frequently grant unbounded process-global environment access.

  • 7.

    Sovereignty and Supply Chain: Skillware operates 100% offline on local silicon with cryptographic issuer attribution and SHA-256 Merkle audit trails. Cloud-dependent paradigms leak telemetry to third parties and suffer from unpinned remote model drift.

    • 6.2  Skillware vs. Model Context Protocol (MCP)

    Anthropic’s Model Context Protocol (MCP) specifies a client-server architecture using JSON-RPC over stdio or Server-Sent Events (SSE) to connect AI applications to data sources and tools [4].

    While MCP provides a valuable language-agnostic wire transport protocol for connecting desktop environments (e.g., Claude Desktop) to local or remote microservices, its client-server topology introduces severe friction for in-process application runtimes:

  • 1.

    Process Supervisory Overhead: Operating an agent with dozens of capabilities under MCP requires spawning, monitoring, and managing separate daemon child processes. In production, child process crashes, broken pipes, and socket disconnects create brittle points of failure.

  • 2.

    IPC Serialization Latency: Transferring large binary payloads (e.g., high-resolution drone imagery, local database dumps, or memory buffers) over stdio or HTTP sockets incurs serialization penalties that do not exist within Skillware’s in-process CPython execution, where data is passed directly via memory references.

    • Skillware and MCP are orthogonal and complementary layers: MCP is a wire transport protocol; Skillware is an in-process capability standard. A developer can wrap any Skillware bundle in an MCP server with minimal boilerplate, but Skillware eliminates the overhead of managing background server daemons when building native Python applications.

    6.3  Skillware vs. Agent Skills (SKILL.md)

    The emerging Agent Skills format (originating from Anthropic and now adopted by developer agents such as Cursor and Claude Code) organizes agent instructions as SKILL.md files containing markdown guidance and optional shell scripts [3].

    While SKILL.md serves as an effective procedural reference for human developers and IDE coding agents, it lacks the formal guarantees necessary for autonomous production systems:

  • •

    Absence of Formal Typed Contracts:SKILL.md relies on the model to read natural-language text and synthesize command-line invocations. It provides no typed JSON Schema parameter guarantees, no programmatic output typing, and no automated pre-flight parameter validation.

  • •

    Lack of Universal Model Adaptation:SKILL.md relies on host-specific client harnesses. In contrast, Skillware’s universal interface adapters (to_gemini_tool, to_claude_tool, to_openai_tool) dynamically transmute a single manifest.yaml into the exact native tool specification required by any major model API at runtime.

  • •

    Ephemeral Text vs. Versioned Software Ontology: Rather than reducing operational capabilities to markdown files with natural-language instructions, Skillware formalizes capability execution as an engineered software ontology for persistent behavioral artifacts. While Fan and Lan [14] cite the ARPA Skillware open architecture [37] and explore a theoretical ontology for persistent agent behaviors, this work provides the concrete, production-validated execution standard: self-contained five-role capability bundles bound by version-controlled manifests, isolated dependency environments, and deterministic offline assurance verifiers.

item.title: 40 万个带关节的资产：RFW-A 发现「同类资产共享构建逻辑」，于是不再为每个资产重跑一遍推理 ｜ RFW-A: Agentic Procedural Generation of 400K Articulated Assets over 500 Categories
item.description:
一句话：高质量的带关节资产是感知、仿真与操作的基础，但规模化构建一直很难。

要点：

  • 需求侧：高质量的**带关节（articulated）资产**对具身感知、仿真与操作都不可或缺，但规模化构建仍然很难——人工标注与程序化建模都需要大量人力
  • 已有 agentic 系统的通病：通过程序合成来自动构建资产，但**每来一个新资产就要重复昂贵的推理与精修**
  • RFW-A 的关键观察是：同类资产可以**共享构建逻辑**（尽管外观各异），于是把逻辑复用起来，一次性生成覆盖 500 个类别的 40 万个带关节资产

为什么值得看：「带关节资产」正是物理仿真与游戏里最贵的资产类型（门、抽屉、铰链、机械）。把「同类共享构建逻辑」做成 agent 可复用的过程，规模从「手工几百个」变成「40 万」，这对做仿真环境或程序化关卡的团队是直接可用的方法论。

中文摘要：高质量的带关节资产对具身感知、仿真与操作都不可或缺，但规模化构建一直是难题：人工标注与程序化建模都需要大量人力。近年来有 agentic 系统尝试通过程序合成自动构建资产，但它们的通病是每遇到新资产就要重复一遍昂贵的推理与精修。RFW-A 的关键观察是，同一类别内的资产尽管外观各异，却可以共享构建逻辑；据此它把这部分逻辑复用起来，用 agentic 程序化生成的方式产出了覆盖 500 个类别、共 40 万个带关节资产。对需要大量可交互物体的仿真环境与程序化关卡，这条把「资产数量」从人力问题变成了流程问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-23

RFW-A: Agentic Procedural Generation of 400K Articulated Assets over 500 Categories

Abstract

High-quality articulated assets are essential for embodied perception, simulation, and manipulation, yet constructing them at scale remains difficult. Manual annotation and procedural modeling require substantial human effort. Recent agentic systems automate asset construction through program synthesis, but repeat costly reasoning and refinement for every new asset. Our key observation is that assets within a category can share construction logic despite variations in structure and appearance. Agentic synthesis and procedural generation are therefore complementary: agents can construct reusable programs, while procedural execution reuses the resulting logic across many samples. We therefore present RFW-A, which combines the two in a new articulated-asset generation paradigm. Starting from existing articulated programs, RFW-A organizes reusable components and their dependencies into category-level generators. Agents test and refine these generators across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generators produce diverse assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. The estimated API cost of generator authoring averages $10.62, amortizing to $0.05 per asset over 200 assets, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline. Using RFW-A, we built RFW-A-400K, containing over 400K sim-ready articulated assets across more than 500 categories. Experiments show high structural and kinematic validity and stable execution across physics simulators. Beyond asset validity, training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, while policies trained in simulation with retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

1 Introduction

Articulated objects are ubiquitous in everyday environments, ranging from cabinets and appliances to tools and mechanisms, as illustrated in Figure 1. Their functionality depends not only on shape, but also on how their parts are connected and move. High-quality articulated assets are therefore essential for learning part semantics, kinematics, and interaction affordances, as well as for training and evaluating manipulation policies in simulation [86, 57, 51, 58, 82, 91, 95]. Compared with static 3D models [2, 16, 17], these assets require additional specifications of part hierarchies, joint parameters, motion ranges, and physical properties. Producing and checking these annotations requires substantial human effort [86, 51, 89]; even with purpose-built interfaces, annotation can take around ten minutes per asset [51].

Procedural generation reduces per-asset effort by encoding construction rules in a reusable program that can produce many object variants [45]. Such generators can efficiently scale asset sampling within an object category, but their construction rules are still manually authored and are difficult to transfer across categories. Agentic program synthesis addresses the authoring problem by using language models to generate, execute, and refine articulated object programs [68, 20, 97]. However, existing systems typically synthesize assets one at a time, requiring a new round of reasoning and correction for every output. Thus, procedural generation scales sampling but not generator authoring, whereas agentic synthesis automates authoring but repeats the process at the asset level.

These paradigms are complementary because assets within a category often share construction logic. As shown in Figure 2, cabinets may vary in width, door type, and drawer count while sharing rules for part dimensions, placements, and joint attachments. Such logic can be encoded once in a category-level generator and reused across many configurations; Figure 19 in the appendix extends this example to four cabinet generator families. This motivates our central question: can agentic synthesis automate the construction of reusable category-level articulated object generators?

To answer this question, we present RoboFlywheel-Articulation (RFW-A), an agentic procedural generation framework that shifts agentic synthesis from individual assets to reusable category-level generators (Figure 3). To support variation, each generator specifies both what can change and which structural relationships must remain valid. RFW-A organizes these choices and dependencies into a category blueprint built from reusable components in existing articulated programs. Agents translate the blueprint into executable code, and iteratively test and refine it across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generator produces additional assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. As summarized in Figure 3, this amortizes agentic construction cost across many assets and enables broad and dense scaling across object categories: in our cost comparison, amortizing the mean generator-authoring API cost over 200 assets yields $0.05 per asset, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline (Figure 6).

Using RFW-A, we build RFW-A-400K, containing 402,410 articulated assets across more than 500 object categories, approximately 37 times the size of Articraft, the largest existing articulated-object dataset. Each asset includes part structure, kinematics, estimated physical properties, and the parameters needed to reproduce its construction. Our evaluation shows a 100% asset-level kinematic pass rate over the full release. On a 200-asset evaluation subset, 99.5% of assets pass a 1-second passive rollout with the root fixed in all four simulators: Genesis, PyBullet, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim. Downstream experiments further show that training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories compared with PartNet-Mobility alone and Articraft augmentation. We further evaluate its utility for robot learning: across five manipulation tasks, policies trained from simulated demonstrations using retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce RFW-A, an agentic procedural generation framework that constructs and validates reusable category-level generators, enabling asset sampling without per-asset model inference.

  • •

    Using RFW-A, we release RFW-A-400K, comprising 402,410 articulated assets across more than 500 object categories. Each asset includes explicit part structure, kinematics, estimated physical properties, and reproducible generation parameters.

  • •

    We evaluate asset quality and cross-simulator compatibility, demonstrate improved part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, and show zero-shot sim-to-real manipulation using policies trained with retrieved and program-edited RFW-A-400K assets.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Articulated Object Datasets

    Large-scale 3D repositories provide broad geometric diversity, but most assets are static and lack reliable part and articulation annotations [2, 16, 17]. Datasets for articulated objects address this gap by adding part hierarchies, joint parameters, motion ranges, and actionable part labels to curated CAD models or real scans [75, 86, 51, 22]. More recent releases expand category and structural coverage, and some also include material or physical-property annotations [89, 28, 1]. Complementing these annotated collections, RFW-A-400K provides both assets and their executable construction programs. These programs support resampling and editing within each defined object family.

    2.2 Articulated Object Reconstruction and Generation

    Articulated reconstruction methods recover instance geometry and kinematics from interaction, single- or multi-state images, RGB-D observations, or videos [29, 48, 79, 94]. Recent methods use 3D Gaussian Splatting to improve reconstructed geometry and appearance [54, 80, 81, 53, 15, 67, 27, 19]. These approaches can produce detailed digital twins, but they reconstruct a particular observed object and must infer occluded geometry and ambiguous motion from the available observations.

    Generative methods instead learn distributions over part geometry, connectivity, and kinematics using graph-based, diffusion, autoregressive, or structured latent representations [38, 49, 18, 4, 30, 24]. Image-, text-, and sketch-conditioned methods provide additional control over articulated asset modeling [50, 55, 74, 89]. Another line of work adds articulation to existing geometry or assembles articulated assets from observed or retrieved components [11, 44, 37, 65, 42, 43, 88]. Related work on deformable assets considers skeleton and skinning generation [71, 72]. RFW-A instead constructs explicit category-level programs whose structural choices and parameters can be varied directly to generate new rigid-link object instances.

    2.3 Programmatic, Procedural, and Agentic Generation

    Programmatic representations encode 3D construction as CSG trees, assembly programs, or CAD command sequences. Their explicit operations and parameters support structured generation and editing [66, 31, 32, 83, 35, 3, 40]. Procedural generation reuses such programs across sampled configurations. Arti-PG synthesizes articulated objects by manipulating structure programs and propagating annotations [70], while Infinigen-Articulated and Infinite Mobility provide manually designed category-level generators [34, 45].

    LLMs and agents have also been used for code generation and structured 3D or motion synthesis through programmatic interfaces, tool use, and intermediate representations [69, 26, 56, 5, 8, 96]. For static shapes, ShapeLib uses LLMs to construct reusable procedural abstractions and refine a shape-sampling program [33]. Recent systems specialize agentic synthesis to articulated assets by jointly constructing geometry and kinematics as executable programs [20, 68, 97]. These systems broaden the range of objects that can be synthesized, but still run generation and refinement for each asset. RFW-A instead uses agents to construct category-level generators from existing articulated programs and refine them using configuration and motion tests. The resulting generators produce new assets through procedural execution without additional model inference.

    3 Method

    RFW-A combines agentic program synthesis with procedural generation, as shown in Figure 4. Given a category prompt c and source assets with executable CAD or 3D modeling programs A[97], RFW-A constructs a reusable category-level generator S_c. Four agents implement this workflow: the Source Agent extracts reusable component code, the Architect Agent constructs the category blueprint, the Code Agent implements the executable generator, and the Repair Agent revises the blueprint or generator using structured diagnostics. The Revision Module coordinates configuration and motion checks. We write construction and sampling as

    S_c=Build(c,A), x_z=S_c(z),

    where Build includes construction, validation, and release, and z is a random seed. After release, different seeds produce different assets through procedural sampling without further model inference. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete loop.

    3.1 Agentic Generator Construction

    To construct S_c, we first extract reusable component code from A. We then build a category blueprint Σ_c to specify the available components, adjustable parameters, and assembly and joint rules. This blueprint guides code generation.

    Source component extraction.

    The Source Agent identifies relevant components in A based on the category prompt c. It extracts their construction code into a source map M_c:

    M_c=Extract(c,A).

    The map links each component to its construction code and source program. In Figure 4, the rover reuses wheel code from the mobile-robot program and arm code from the manipulator program.

    Blueprint construction.

    The Architect Agent constructs Σ_c from the components in M_c. We represent the blueprint as a graph G_c=(V_c,E_c). Each node specifies a component role, its available designs, and adjustable parameters. It also indicates whether the component is optional or repeated. Each edge specifies how two components attach, including joint parameters for movable connections. The blueprint also records rules for computing dependent dimensions and placements when component choices or parameters change. These construction rules are shared across configurations.

    3.2 Procedural Generator and Variant Sampling

    The Code Agent implements the blueprint Σ_c as an executable generator S_c, using the component code in M_c. Given a seed z, the generator selects components and samples free parameters. It computes dependent dimensions, placements, and joint parameters from the blueprint’s rules. The program then calls the component construction code to build and assemble the asset. The three execution steps in Figure 4 are

    χ_z=Sample(Σ_c;z), q_z=Resolve(Σ_c,χ_z), x_z=S_c(z)=Assemble(M_c,q_z).

    Here χ_z contains the sampled choices and free parameters, while q_z contains the selected components and all resolved construction parameters. These steps execute the rules encoded in S_c without further model inference. The program exports meshes, rigid links, collision geometry, joints, and a URDF file. It also records the source of each reused component.

    3.3 Validating, Repairing, and Releasing the Generator

    A generator that produces one valid asset may fail under other configurations or joint states. Before large-scale sampling, the Revision Module therefore checks blueprint–code consistency and tests assets across component choices, parameter settings, and joint states.

    Blueprint–code consistency.

    We check that each choice in Σ_c has a code path and that its dependent parameters can be computed. We run sampling and parameter resolution across seeds until each choice has been selected multiple times. These checks detect missing branches, unused parameters, and incomplete dependencies without constructing geometry.

    Configuration and motion testing.

    We test progressively larger batches generated with deterministic seeds. Each batch must pass before we increase its size. Additional tests target uncovered component choices, parameter boundaries, and selected component combinations. Each asset is checked for successful geometry construction, part connectivity, URDF export and parsing, and valid articulation. Collision checks cover the rest pose, multiple states across each joint’s range, and selected coupled-joint states.

    Let ℤₜₑₛₜ contain the current validation cases and all retained regression cases, and let V_c collect the component choices declared in Σ_c. The generator is released only when every retained case passes and every declared choice is covered by a passing case:

    Accept(S_c) \Longleftrightarrow [∀z∈ℤₜₑₛₜ, Valid(x_z)] ∧ [∀v∈V_c, ∃z∈ℤₜₑₛₜ:v∈q_z],

    where Valid(x_z) denotes that x_z passes the checks above.

    Failure localization and repair.

    For each failure, we record the failed check, sampled configuration, affected parts or joints, and responsible construction step. The report also includes measurements such as penetration depth. The Repair Agent uses these diagnostics to update the blueprint or generator, or both:

    (Σ_c⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾,S_c⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾)=Repair(Σ_c⁽ᵗ⁾,S_c⁽ᵗ⁾,Fₜ),

    where Fₜ is the structured diagnostics collected at iteration t. Blueprint errors are returned to the Architect Agent, and blueprint repairs are followed by recompilation of the generator. Implementation errors go to the Code Agent with the blueprint unchanged. The Revision Module then retests both failed and previously passed cases, retaining failures as regression tests until the release criterion is met.

    4 RFW-A-400K Dataset: Articulated Assets

    RFW-A turns the validated generators of Section 3.3 into a dataset by sampling a fixed seed budget for each generator. The release retains both the exported assets and their construction records, linking each sample to the program and configuration that produced it.

    4.1 Dataset Overview

    The RFW-A-400K release contains 402,410 articulated assets covering more than 500 semantic object categories. Alongside visual and collision geometry, each asset retains its selected components, resolved parameters, part hierarchy, joint parameters, and source provenance. Its generator version and seed identify a reproducible sample, while the recorded configuration exposes the choices used to construct it.

    Compared with existing articulated-object datasets, RFW-A-400K combines this scale with material assignments below the articulated-part level and associated physical-property annotations (Table 1). Each asset is represented through geometry, part structure, joint motion, and surface materials, which provide complementary views of asset quality in the qualitative comparison with Articraft and LAM (Figure 5).

    RFW-A pays the agentic authoring cost once per generator, then produces additional assets procedurally without further model calls or token charges. Amortizing the mean generator-authoring cost of $10.62 over 200 assets yields an API cost of $0.053 per asset, versus $1.237 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline, a 23-fold cost difference (Figure 6). We estimate these costs using ten category-level generators and 200 successful Articraft synthesis records [97], twenty from each of the same categories.

    4.2 Material Grounding and Directed Editing

    The procedural representation specifies how an asset is built and moves; material grounding extends it to the appearance and physical properties of its surfaces. To apply this grounding across the release, each validated generator records a material-class identifier for each visual surface and connects it to a shared library built once offline. The library supplies concrete instances that can be reused across generators and sampled across assets. After geometry and articulation validation, a single offline pass assigns each visual surface a class from the controlled taxonomy; performing this pass after repair ensures that added, removed, or renamed surfaces receive the correct identifiers.

    The library contains 8,295 curated PBR materials organized into 124 leaf classes across 18 families. Each entry associates a PBR appearance with six physical properties in SI units: density, Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, static and dynamic friction coefficients, and coefficient of restitution. These properties are estimated offline under fixed reference conditions; their uncertainty intervals and confidence estimates are retained in the library (Appendix A.9). Keeping appearance and physical annotations in the same entry lets both follow the material selected for a surface.

    During asset sampling, each surface’s class identifier selects a frozen material pool, and a seeded draw selects an entry from that pool. The selected appearance is bound to the surface and the corresponding physical properties are copied into the asset’s physics record (Figure 7). This lookup requires no per-asset model inference and is reproducible from the generator and seed. It also provides a direct control for material variation: a surface can receive a different entry from its pool or a different class assignment, while its appearance and physical annotations are resolved together.

    The generator representation also makes the release editable. An edit changes the configuration rather than a finished mesh and then re-executes the same program; no additional per-asset agent call is required. Figure 8 shows four examples: replacing a component, changing the number of repeated parts, assigning a different material, and changing a geometric dimension. Dependent placements, dimensions, and joint parameters are resolved again by the generator, keeping the edited asset internally consistent. Section 6 uses this control to adapt retrieved assets to real manipulation targets.

    We evaluate the dataset across five aspects: scale and structural diversity, asset validity, rest-pose assembly geometry, motion-induced collisions, and cross-simulator compatibility. Detailed protocols and results are deferred to Appendices A.3– A.8.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Downstream Articulation Estimation

    Experimental setup.

    We assess whether training with RFW-A-400K improves articulation estimation from a single 3D mesh. Following Articraft [97], we train Particulate-B [42] on PartNet-Mobility (PM) alone, PM+Articraft, and PM+RFW-A-400K. All models are trained from random initialization with identical optimizer settings and a global batch size of 128, and evaluated at 150K updates. For both augmented datasets, PM and the additional source are sampled with probabilities 0.1 and 0.9, respectively.

    Evaluation splits and metrics.

    All models share two evaluation splits. The in-domain split contains 255 objects from PM and Articraft together with additional released objects, covering six categories seen during training. The category out-of-distribution (OOD) split contains 774 objects from nine categories excluded from all three training sets.

    Following the Particulate evaluation protocol, we report mean IoU (mIoU), generalized IoU (gIoU), and part-wise Chamfer distance (PC) at rest, and part-wise gIoU, PC, and whole-object Chamfer distance (OC) at maximum articulation. Results aggregate three training seeds × five evaluation seeds per setting. Training and evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.16.

    Results.

    Table 2 shows that both generated datasets improve all six in-domain metrics over PM-only. PM+RFW-A-400K achieves the best in-domain results on all six metrics. Relative to PM+Articraft, rest-pose mIoU increases by 7.43 percentage points and articulated gIoU by 10.13 points; articulated PC falls from 0.10196 to 0.06268 and whole-object OC from 0.00778 to 0.00661. The larger part-level gains indicate that the added assets provide especially strong supervision for part correspondence and moved-part geometry, while also improving whole-object reconstruction.

    On the category-OOD split, PM+RFW-A-400K again leads on all five part-level metrics: articulated gIoU improves by 19.2% and rest-pose PC by 19.0% relative to PM+Articraft. The consistent part-level gains across both splits show that the dataset transfers beyond the categories used for training.

    Figure 9 compares articulation estimation results on six category-matched examples. Each column shows one case, with PM-only, PM+Articraft, PM+RFW-A-400K, and the ground-truth reference arranged by row. Red arrows and circles identify local regions where supports, attachments, or movable parts differ from the reference. The highlighted examples show that PM-only and PM+Articraft can omit or misplace articulated geometry, whereas the PM+RFW-A-400K outputs more closely preserve the reference structure.

    Generator component ablations are reported in Appendix A.17: the full configuration achieves the highest mean Judge score and passes all strict validity probes.

    6 Robotic Manipulation

    We further evaluate whether RFW-A-400K assets can serve as simulation surrogates for real-world robotic manipulation. For each real target object, we retrieve the most similar asset from RFW-A-400K and optionally edit its exposed procedural parameters to better match the target geometry. The resulting assets are used to train manipulation policies entirely in simulation, which are then deployed on the corresponding real objects without real-world training or fine-tuning.

    Tasks.

    We consider five real-world manipulation tasks with different articulation structures and interaction patterns: (1) opening and closing a cabinet door, where the left arm pushes the door open and the right arm closes it; (2) straightening a folding ruler; (3) folding a folding chair to its closed configuration; (4) pushing down the lever of a toaster; and (5) closing a pair of double doors. Together, these tasks cover revolute joints, multi-link articulation, and object-specific interaction geometries. Figure 10 shows the simulation training environments and the corresponding real-world evaluations for these five tasks.

    Simulation training.

    For each task, we compare three simulation-asset configurations (Table 3). Retrieval uses only the single retrieved RFW-A-400K asset. Retrieval + 4 Edit augments the retrieved asset with four edited variants, while Retrieval + 9 Edit augments it with nine edited variants. The edits modify task-relevant dimensions, part placement, and articulation parameters through the corresponding procedural generator while preserving a valid kinematic structure.

    Importantly, all three configurations use exactly 500 simulation demonstrations per task and the same policy architecture and training budget.

    Real-world evaluation.

    Each trained policy is evaluated for 10 trials on its corresponding real object. A trial is counted as successful when the task reaches its predefined target configuration. We report the number of successful trials for each task and the average across all five tasks.

    Results.

    Table 4 shows that real-world success improves from 6.2/10 with the retrieved asset alone to 7.2/10 with four edited variants and 8.0/10 with nine edited variants. The gains are largest on the cabinet, toaster, and folding-ruler tasks, whereas the double-door task remains unchanged. Since all settings use the same number of simulation demonstrations, policy architecture, and training budget, these results indicate that generator-based target adaptation and asset variation improve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without requiring additional training data.

    7 Conclusion

    We present RFW-A, an agentic procedural generation framework that constructs reusable category-level generators, enabling efficient asset sampling and editing without per-asset model inference. Using RFW-A, we build RFW-A-400K, comprising over 400K articulated assets across 500+ categories with explicit kinematics, fine-grained materials, and estimated physical properties. Our experiments demonstrate substantially reduced generation costs, high structural and kinematic validity, and reliable execution across four simulators. Beyond asset quality, RFW-A-400K improves articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories and enables zero-shot sim-to-real robotic manipulation through retrieved and procedurally edited assets. These results establish RFW-A as a scalable and controllable approach to articulated asset generation for embodied learning.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix Contents

    Appendix A Appendix

    A.1 Generator Construction and Validation

    A.2 Dataset Versions and Evaluation Sets

    Unless noted otherwise, the full-dataset evaluations contain 402,410 RFW-A-400K assets with 1,928,063 declared non-fixed joints, 2,347 PartNet-Mobility assets, 8,226 Infinigen-Articulated assets, 4,956 SketchMobility assets, 10,787 Articraft assets, 2,024 PhysX-Mobility assets, 3,544 Artiverse assets, and 3,217 LAM assets. The Articraft evaluation set combines 9,996 released packages with 791 GitHub-only source reconstructions.

    The structural-integrity and runtime evaluations use the same Core-200 set. For each source, we first retain assets with 1–20 declared movable joints and then sample 200 assets before running either test. Failed assets are not replaced. The free-standing center-of-mass panel applies an additional eligibility rule, so its N can be smaller than 200. In that panel, N_phys is the number of eligible assets with valid dataset-provided physics.

    A.3 Experimental Setup

    Comparison datasets.

    We compare RFW-A-400K with seven public datasets spanning three construction paradigms: (a) handcrafted datasets, including PartNet-Mobility [86], PhysX-Mobility [1], Artiverse [28], and SketchMobility [89]; (b) procedural datasets, represented by Infinigen-Articulated [34]; and (c) agentically generated datasets, including LAM [20] and Articraft [97].

    Evaluation protocol.

    We evaluate (a) dataset scale and structural diversity (Appendix A.4), (b) asset validity (Appendix A.5), (c) rest-pose assembly geometry (Appendix A.6), (d) collisions during articulation (Appendix A.7), and (e) simulation compatibility (Appendix A.8). We further assess the utility of RFW-A-400K as training data for articulation estimation (Section 5.1). Dataset size and asset validity are evaluated on the complete releases. For the more expensive geometry and simulation tests, we randomly sample 200 assets per source with 1–20 declared movable joints, forming a common evaluation subset that we refer to as Core-200. Dataset versions and evaluation sets are detailed in Appendix A.2.

一句话：高质量的带关节资产是感知、仿真与操作的基础，但规模化构建一直很难。

要点：

  • 需求侧：高质量的**带关节（articulated）资产**对具身感知、仿真与操作都不可或缺，但规模化构建仍然很难——人工标注与程序化建模都需要大量人力
  • 已有 agentic 系统的通病：通过程序合成来自动构建资产，但**每来一个新资产就要重复昂贵的推理与精修**
  • RFW-A 的关键观察是：同类资产可以**共享构建逻辑**（尽管外观各异），于是把逻辑复用起来，一次性生成覆盖 500 个类别的 40 万个带关节资产

为什么值得看：「带关节资产」正是物理仿真与游戏里最贵的资产类型（门、抽屉、铰链、机械）。把「同类共享构建逻辑」做成 agent 可复用的过程，规模从「手工几百个」变成「40 万」，这对做仿真环境或程序化关卡的团队是直接可用的方法论。

中文摘要：高质量的带关节资产对具身感知、仿真与操作都不可或缺，但规模化构建一直是难题：人工标注与程序化建模都需要大量人力。近年来有 agentic 系统尝试通过程序合成自动构建资产，但它们的通病是每遇到新资产就要重复一遍昂贵的推理与精修。RFW-A 的关键观察是，同一类别内的资产尽管外观各异，却可以共享构建逻辑；据此它把这部分逻辑复用起来，用 agentic 程序化生成的方式产出了覆盖 500 个类别、共 40 万个带关节资产。对需要大量可交互物体的仿真环境与程序化关卡，这条把「资产数量」从人力问题变成了流程问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-10-29

本期推送：2026-11-23

RFW-A: Agentic Procedural Generation of 400K Articulated Assets over 500 Categories

Abstract

High-quality articulated assets are essential for embodied perception, simulation, and manipulation, yet constructing them at scale remains difficult. Manual annotation and procedural modeling require substantial human effort. Recent agentic systems automate asset construction through program synthesis, but repeat costly reasoning and refinement for every new asset. Our key observation is that assets within a category can share construction logic despite variations in structure and appearance. Agentic synthesis and procedural generation are therefore complementary: agents can construct reusable programs, while procedural execution reuses the resulting logic across many samples. We therefore present RFW-A, which combines the two in a new articulated-asset generation paradigm. Starting from existing articulated programs, RFW-A organizes reusable components and their dependencies into category-level generators. Agents test and refine these generators across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generators produce diverse assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. The estimated API cost of generator authoring averages $10.62, amortizing to $0.05 per asset over 200 assets, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline. Using RFW-A, we built RFW-A-400K, containing over 400K sim-ready articulated assets across more than 500 categories. Experiments show high structural and kinematic validity and stable execution across physics simulators. Beyond asset validity, training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, while policies trained in simulation with retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

1 Introduction

Articulated objects are ubiquitous in everyday environments, ranging from cabinets and appliances to tools and mechanisms, as illustrated in Figure 1. Their functionality depends not only on shape, but also on how their parts are connected and move. High-quality articulated assets are therefore essential for learning part semantics, kinematics, and interaction affordances, as well as for training and evaluating manipulation policies in simulation [86, 57, 51, 58, 82, 91, 95]. Compared with static 3D models [2, 16, 17], these assets require additional specifications of part hierarchies, joint parameters, motion ranges, and physical properties. Producing and checking these annotations requires substantial human effort [86, 51, 89]; even with purpose-built interfaces, annotation can take around ten minutes per asset [51].

Procedural generation reduces per-asset effort by encoding construction rules in a reusable program that can produce many object variants [45]. Such generators can efficiently scale asset sampling within an object category, but their construction rules are still manually authored and are difficult to transfer across categories. Agentic program synthesis addresses the authoring problem by using language models to generate, execute, and refine articulated object programs [68, 20, 97]. However, existing systems typically synthesize assets one at a time, requiring a new round of reasoning and correction for every output. Thus, procedural generation scales sampling but not generator authoring, whereas agentic synthesis automates authoring but repeats the process at the asset level.

These paradigms are complementary because assets within a category often share construction logic. As shown in Figure 2, cabinets may vary in width, door type, and drawer count while sharing rules for part dimensions, placements, and joint attachments. Such logic can be encoded once in a category-level generator and reused across many configurations; Figure 19 in the appendix extends this example to four cabinet generator families. This motivates our central question: can agentic synthesis automate the construction of reusable category-level articulated object generators?

To answer this question, we present RoboFlywheel-Articulation (RFW-A), an agentic procedural generation framework that shifts agentic synthesis from individual assets to reusable category-level generators (Figure 3). To support variation, each generator specifies both what can change and which structural relationships must remain valid. RFW-A organizes these choices and dependencies into a category blueprint built from reusable components in existing articulated programs. Agents translate the blueprint into executable code, and iteratively test and refine it across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generator produces additional assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. As summarized in Figure 3, this amortizes agentic construction cost across many assets and enables broad and dense scaling across object categories: in our cost comparison, amortizing the mean generator-authoring API cost over 200 assets yields $0.05 per asset, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline (Figure 6).

Using RFW-A, we build RFW-A-400K, containing 402,410 articulated assets across more than 500 object categories, approximately 37 times the size of Articraft, the largest existing articulated-object dataset. Each asset includes part structure, kinematics, estimated physical properties, and the parameters needed to reproduce its construction. Our evaluation shows a 100% asset-level kinematic pass rate over the full release. On a 200-asset evaluation subset, 99.5% of assets pass a 1-second passive rollout with the root fixed in all four simulators: Genesis, PyBullet, MuJoCo, and Isaac Sim. Downstream experiments further show that training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories compared with PartNet-Mobility alone and Articraft augmentation. We further evaluate its utility for robot learning: across five manipulation tasks, policies trained from simulated demonstrations using retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce RFW-A, an agentic procedural generation framework that constructs and validates reusable category-level generators, enabling asset sampling without per-asset model inference.

  • •

    Using RFW-A, we release RFW-A-400K, comprising 402,410 articulated assets across more than 500 object categories. Each asset includes explicit part structure, kinematics, estimated physical properties, and reproducible generation parameters.

  • •

    We evaluate asset quality and cross-simulator compatibility, demonstrate improved part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, and show zero-shot sim-to-real manipulation using policies trained with retrieved and program-edited RFW-A-400K assets.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Articulated Object Datasets

    Large-scale 3D repositories provide broad geometric diversity, but most assets are static and lack reliable part and articulation annotations [2, 16, 17]. Datasets for articulated objects address this gap by adding part hierarchies, joint parameters, motion ranges, and actionable part labels to curated CAD models or real scans [75, 86, 51, 22]. More recent releases expand category and structural coverage, and some also include material or physical-property annotations [89, 28, 1]. Complementing these annotated collections, RFW-A-400K provides both assets and their executable construction programs. These programs support resampling and editing within each defined object family.

    2.2 Articulated Object Reconstruction and Generation

    Articulated reconstruction methods recover instance geometry and kinematics from interaction, single- or multi-state images, RGB-D observations, or videos [29, 48, 79, 94]. Recent methods use 3D Gaussian Splatting to improve reconstructed geometry and appearance [54, 80, 81, 53, 15, 67, 27, 19]. These approaches can produce detailed digital twins, but they reconstruct a particular observed object and must infer occluded geometry and ambiguous motion from the available observations.

    Generative methods instead learn distributions over part geometry, connectivity, and kinematics using graph-based, diffusion, autoregressive, or structured latent representations [38, 49, 18, 4, 30, 24]. Image-, text-, and sketch-conditioned methods provide additional control over articulated asset modeling [50, 55, 74, 89]. Another line of work adds articulation to existing geometry or assembles articulated assets from observed or retrieved components [11, 44, 37, 65, 42, 43, 88]. Related work on deformable assets considers skeleton and skinning generation [71, 72]. RFW-A instead constructs explicit category-level programs whose structural choices and parameters can be varied directly to generate new rigid-link object instances.

    2.3 Programmatic, Procedural, and Agentic Generation

    Programmatic representations encode 3D construction as CSG trees, assembly programs, or CAD command sequences. Their explicit operations and parameters support structured generation and editing [66, 31, 32, 83, 35, 3, 40]. Procedural generation reuses such programs across sampled configurations. Arti-PG synthesizes articulated objects by manipulating structure programs and propagating annotations [70], while Infinigen-Articulated and Infinite Mobility provide manually designed category-level generators [34, 45].

    LLMs and agents have also been used for code generation and structured 3D or motion synthesis through programmatic interfaces, tool use, and intermediate representations [69, 26, 56, 5, 8, 96]. For static shapes, ShapeLib uses LLMs to construct reusable procedural abstractions and refine a shape-sampling program [33]. Recent systems specialize agentic synthesis to articulated assets by jointly constructing geometry and kinematics as executable programs [20, 68, 97]. These systems broaden the range of objects that can be synthesized, but still run generation and refinement for each asset. RFW-A instead uses agents to construct category-level generators from existing articulated programs and refine them using configuration and motion tests. The resulting generators produce new assets through procedural execution without additional model inference.

    3 Method

    RFW-A combines agentic program synthesis with procedural generation, as shown in Figure 4. Given a category prompt c and source assets with executable CAD or 3D modeling programs A[97], RFW-A constructs a reusable category-level generator S_c. Four agents implement this workflow: the Source Agent extracts reusable component code, the Architect Agent constructs the category blueprint, the Code Agent implements the executable generator, and the Repair Agent revises the blueprint or generator using structured diagnostics. The Revision Module coordinates configuration and motion checks. We write construction and sampling as

    S_c=Build(c,A), x_z=S_c(z),

    where Build includes construction, validation, and release, and z is a random seed. After release, different seeds produce different assets through procedural sampling without further model inference. Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete loop.

    3.1 Agentic Generator Construction

    To construct S_c, we first extract reusable component code from A. We then build a category blueprint Σ_c to specify the available components, adjustable parameters, and assembly and joint rules. This blueprint guides code generation.

    Source component extraction.

    The Source Agent identifies relevant components in A based on the category prompt c. It extracts their construction code into a source map M_c:

    M_c=Extract(c,A).

    The map links each component to its construction code and source program. In Figure 4, the rover reuses wheel code from the mobile-robot program and arm code from the manipulator program.

    Blueprint construction.

    The Architect Agent constructs Σ_c from the components in M_c. We represent the blueprint as a graph G_c=(V_c,E_c). Each node specifies a component role, its available designs, and adjustable parameters. It also indicates whether the component is optional or repeated. Each edge specifies how two components attach, including joint parameters for movable connections. The blueprint also records rules for computing dependent dimensions and placements when component choices or parameters change. These construction rules are shared across configurations.

    3.2 Procedural Generator and Variant Sampling

    The Code Agent implements the blueprint Σ_c as an executable generator S_c, using the component code in M_c. Given a seed z, the generator selects components and samples free parameters. It computes dependent dimensions, placements, and joint parameters from the blueprint’s rules. The program then calls the component construction code to build and assemble the asset. The three execution steps in Figure 4 are

    χ_z=Sample(Σ_c;z), q_z=Resolve(Σ_c,χ_z), x_z=S_c(z)=Assemble(M_c,q_z).

    Here χ_z contains the sampled choices and free parameters, while q_z contains the selected components and all resolved construction parameters. These steps execute the rules encoded in S_c without further model inference. The program exports meshes, rigid links, collision geometry, joints, and a URDF file. It also records the source of each reused component.

    3.3 Validating, Repairing, and Releasing the Generator

    A generator that produces one valid asset may fail under other configurations or joint states. Before large-scale sampling, the Revision Module therefore checks blueprint–code consistency and tests assets across component choices, parameter settings, and joint states.

    Blueprint–code consistency.

    We check that each choice in Σ_c has a code path and that its dependent parameters can be computed. We run sampling and parameter resolution across seeds until each choice has been selected multiple times. These checks detect missing branches, unused parameters, and incomplete dependencies without constructing geometry.

    Configuration and motion testing.

    We test progressively larger batches generated with deterministic seeds. Each batch must pass before we increase its size. Additional tests target uncovered component choices, parameter boundaries, and selected component combinations. Each asset is checked for successful geometry construction, part connectivity, URDF export and parsing, and valid articulation. Collision checks cover the rest pose, multiple states across each joint’s range, and selected coupled-joint states.

    Let ℤₜₑₛₜ contain the current validation cases and all retained regression cases, and let V_c collect the component choices declared in Σ_c. The generator is released only when every retained case passes and every declared choice is covered by a passing case:

    Accept(S_c) \Longleftrightarrow [∀z∈ℤₜₑₛₜ, Valid(x_z)] ∧ [∀v∈V_c, ∃z∈ℤₜₑₛₜ:v∈q_z],

    where Valid(x_z) denotes that x_z passes the checks above.

    Failure localization and repair.

    For each failure, we record the failed check, sampled configuration, affected parts or joints, and responsible construction step. The report also includes measurements such as penetration depth. The Repair Agent uses these diagnostics to update the blueprint or generator, or both:

    (Σ_c⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾,S_c⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾)=Repair(Σ_c⁽ᵗ⁾,S_c⁽ᵗ⁾,Fₜ),

    where Fₜ is the structured diagnostics collected at iteration t. Blueprint errors are returned to the Architect Agent, and blueprint repairs are followed by recompilation of the generator. Implementation errors go to the Code Agent with the blueprint unchanged. The Revision Module then retests both failed and previously passed cases, retaining failures as regression tests until the release criterion is met.

    4 RFW-A-400K Dataset: Articulated Assets

    RFW-A turns the validated generators of Section 3.3 into a dataset by sampling a fixed seed budget for each generator. The release retains both the exported assets and their construction records, linking each sample to the program and configuration that produced it.

    4.1 Dataset Overview

    The RFW-A-400K release contains 402,410 articulated assets covering more than 500 semantic object categories. Alongside visual and collision geometry, each asset retains its selected components, resolved parameters, part hierarchy, joint parameters, and source provenance. Its generator version and seed identify a reproducible sample, while the recorded configuration exposes the choices used to construct it.

    Compared with existing articulated-object datasets, RFW-A-400K combines this scale with material assignments below the articulated-part level and associated physical-property annotations (Table 1). Each asset is represented through geometry, part structure, joint motion, and surface materials, which provide complementary views of asset quality in the qualitative comparison with Articraft and LAM (Figure 5).

    RFW-A pays the agentic authoring cost once per generator, then produces additional assets procedurally without further model calls or token charges. Amortizing the mean generator-authoring cost of $10.62 over 200 assets yields an API cost of $0.053 per asset, versus $1.237 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline, a 23-fold cost difference (Figure 6). We estimate these costs using ten category-level generators and 200 successful Articraft synthesis records [97], twenty from each of the same categories.

    4.2 Material Grounding and Directed Editing

    The procedural representation specifies how an asset is built and moves; material grounding extends it to the appearance and physical properties of its surfaces. To apply this grounding across the release, each validated generator records a material-class identifier for each visual surface and connects it to a shared library built once offline. The library supplies concrete instances that can be reused across generators and sampled across assets. After geometry and articulation validation, a single offline pass assigns each visual surface a class from the controlled taxonomy; performing this pass after repair ensures that added, removed, or renamed surfaces receive the correct identifiers.

    The library contains 8,295 curated PBR materials organized into 124 leaf classes across 18 families. Each entry associates a PBR appearance with six physical properties in SI units: density, Young’s modulus, Poisson’s ratio, static and dynamic friction coefficients, and coefficient of restitution. These properties are estimated offline under fixed reference conditions; their uncertainty intervals and confidence estimates are retained in the library (Appendix A.9). Keeping appearance and physical annotations in the same entry lets both follow the material selected for a surface.

    During asset sampling, each surface’s class identifier selects a frozen material pool, and a seeded draw selects an entry from that pool. The selected appearance is bound to the surface and the corresponding physical properties are copied into the asset’s physics record (Figure 7). This lookup requires no per-asset model inference and is reproducible from the generator and seed. It also provides a direct control for material variation: a surface can receive a different entry from its pool or a different class assignment, while its appearance and physical annotations are resolved together.

    The generator representation also makes the release editable. An edit changes the configuration rather than a finished mesh and then re-executes the same program; no additional per-asset agent call is required. Figure 8 shows four examples: replacing a component, changing the number of repeated parts, assigning a different material, and changing a geometric dimension. Dependent placements, dimensions, and joint parameters are resolved again by the generator, keeping the edited asset internally consistent. Section 6 uses this control to adapt retrieved assets to real manipulation targets.

    We evaluate the dataset across five aspects: scale and structural diversity, asset validity, rest-pose assembly geometry, motion-induced collisions, and cross-simulator compatibility. Detailed protocols and results are deferred to Appendices A.3– A.8.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Downstream Articulation Estimation

    Experimental setup.

    We assess whether training with RFW-A-400K improves articulation estimation from a single 3D mesh. Following Articraft [97], we train Particulate-B [42] on PartNet-Mobility (PM) alone, PM+Articraft, and PM+RFW-A-400K. All models are trained from random initialization with identical optimizer settings and a global batch size of 128, and evaluated at 150K updates. For both augmented datasets, PM and the additional source are sampled with probabilities 0.1 and 0.9, respectively.

    Evaluation splits and metrics.

    All models share two evaluation splits. The in-domain split contains 255 objects from PM and Articraft together with additional released objects, covering six categories seen during training. The category out-of-distribution (OOD) split contains 774 objects from nine categories excluded from all three training sets.

    Following the Particulate evaluation protocol, we report mean IoU (mIoU), generalized IoU (gIoU), and part-wise Chamfer distance (PC) at rest, and part-wise gIoU, PC, and whole-object Chamfer distance (OC) at maximum articulation. Results aggregate three training seeds × five evaluation seeds per setting. Training and evaluation details are provided in Appendix A.16.

    Results.

    Table 2 shows that both generated datasets improve all six in-domain metrics over PM-only. PM+RFW-A-400K achieves the best in-domain results on all six metrics. Relative to PM+Articraft, rest-pose mIoU increases by 7.43 percentage points and articulated gIoU by 10.13 points; articulated PC falls from 0.10196 to 0.06268 and whole-object OC from 0.00778 to 0.00661. The larger part-level gains indicate that the added assets provide especially strong supervision for part correspondence and moved-part geometry, while also improving whole-object reconstruction.

    On the category-OOD split, PM+RFW-A-400K again leads on all five part-level metrics: articulated gIoU improves by 19.2% and rest-pose PC by 19.0% relative to PM+Articraft. The consistent part-level gains across both splits show that the dataset transfers beyond the categories used for training.

    Figure 9 compares articulation estimation results on six category-matched examples. Each column shows one case, with PM-only, PM+Articraft, PM+RFW-A-400K, and the ground-truth reference arranged by row. Red arrows and circles identify local regions where supports, attachments, or movable parts differ from the reference. The highlighted examples show that PM-only and PM+Articraft can omit or misplace articulated geometry, whereas the PM+RFW-A-400K outputs more closely preserve the reference structure.

    Generator component ablations are reported in Appendix A.17: the full configuration achieves the highest mean Judge score and passes all strict validity probes.

    6 Robotic Manipulation

    We further evaluate whether RFW-A-400K assets can serve as simulation surrogates for real-world robotic manipulation. For each real target object, we retrieve the most similar asset from RFW-A-400K and optionally edit its exposed procedural parameters to better match the target geometry. The resulting assets are used to train manipulation policies entirely in simulation, which are then deployed on the corresponding real objects without real-world training or fine-tuning.

    Tasks.

    We consider five real-world manipulation tasks with different articulation structures and interaction patterns: (1) opening and closing a cabinet door, where the left arm pushes the door open and the right arm closes it; (2) straightening a folding ruler; (3) folding a folding chair to its closed configuration; (4) pushing down the lever of a toaster; and (5) closing a pair of double doors. Together, these tasks cover revolute joints, multi-link articulation, and object-specific interaction geometries. Figure 10 shows the simulation training environments and the corresponding real-world evaluations for these five tasks.

    Simulation training.

    For each task, we compare three simulation-asset configurations (Table 3). Retrieval uses only the single retrieved RFW-A-400K asset. Retrieval + 4 Edit augments the retrieved asset with four edited variants, while Retrieval + 9 Edit augments it with nine edited variants. The edits modify task-relevant dimensions, part placement, and articulation parameters through the corresponding procedural generator while preserving a valid kinematic structure.

    Importantly, all three configurations use exactly 500 simulation demonstrations per task and the same policy architecture and training budget.

    Real-world evaluation.

    Each trained policy is evaluated for 10 trials on its corresponding real object. A trial is counted as successful when the task reaches its predefined target configuration. We report the number of successful trials for each task and the average across all five tasks.

    Results.

    Table 4 shows that real-world success improves from 6.2/10 with the retrieved asset alone to 7.2/10 with four edited variants and 8.0/10 with nine edited variants.
