However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

  • •

    The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

  • •

    If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  • 11.

    Safeguards

  • Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  • Answer: [N/A]

  • Justification: No such risks.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

  • •

    Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

  • •

    Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

  • •

    We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  • 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  • Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We cite works of related assets.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有规划-控制系统的两种做法：要么开环执行，要么闭环但规划器固定——反馈永远改不了计划。

要点：

  • 需求侧：文本与目标条件下的人-物交互（HOI）为物理角色动画提供了直观的高层接口，但把意图映射成**物理上可信、接触丰富**的行为，天然需要一个生成式规划器加一个物理控制器
  • 现有系统的两种妥协：要么**开环执行计划**；要么闭环了但**规划器保持固定**，于是执行反馈永远无法重塑被规划的内容
  • InfCoiL 因此做**闭环**的规划器-控制器协同学习，让执行中的反馈回头修正规划

为什么值得看：「计划—执行」脱钩是物理驱动动画最常见的失败来源：手伸过去被挡住，计划却还在继续。让规划器吃执行反馈，等于把动画系统变成真正的闭环控制——这对做物理交互角色（推、拉、搬、开门）的团队是关键结构。

中文摘要：文本与目标条件驱动的人-物交互（HOI）为物理角色动画提供了直观的高层接口，但要把这类意图映射成物理上可信、接触丰富的行为，自然需要一个生成式规划器配合一个基于物理的控制器。已有系统分两类：一类开环地执行计划；另一类虽然闭环，却让规划器保持固定，于是执行中的反馈永远无法改变「计划什么」。InfCoiL 因此提出闭环的规划器-控制器协同学习，让执行反馈回头修正规划本身。对推、拉、搬运、开门这类接触丰富的交互，这种闭环结构正是让角色行为「有物理感」的前提。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-08

本期推送：2026-11-23

InfCoiL: Coordinated Planner-Controller Learning for Closed-Loop Physics-Based Human-Object Interaction

Abstract

Text- and goal-conditioned human-object interaction (HOI) provides an intuitive interface for specifying high-level intents in physics-based character animation. Mapping such intents to physically plausible, contact-rich behaviors naturally calls for a generative planner and a physics-based controller, yet existing planner-controller systems either execute plans open-loop or close the loop while keeping the planner fixed, so execution feedback never reshapes what is planned. We present InfCoiL, a closed-loop framework for physics-based HOI from coordinated planner-controller learning. InfCoiL couples a morphology-aware flow-matching planner with a unified multi-morphology controller through a shared morphology interface in an autoregressive plan-and-execute loop, and alternately fine-tunes both components with reinforcement learning from the same physical rollouts. To optimize the flow-matching planner online, we introduce Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which stochasticizes selected denoising transitions with channel-wise semantic covariance over heterogeneous HOI features and assigns group-relative, sequence-level rewards from complete closed-loop executions. On held-out OMOMO sequences, InfCoiL outperforms open-loop hierarchical baselines in goal-reaching task success and physical tracking accuracy. Project page: https://infcoil.github.io/.

1 Introduction

Text- and goal-conditioned physics-based human-object interaction (HOI) is an important step toward controllable character animation and embodied agents. Language specifies high-level intents, while spatial goals ground object-centric interactions geometrically, together forming an intuitive interface for specifying diverse, physically executable interaction. Realizing this interface requires bridging high-level semantic intent to low-level physical control for executable contact-rich interactions.

Existing approaches address different parts of this hierarchy. Kinematic generative models, such as diffusion-based interaction generators [Xu et al. (2023); Li et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2026)], learn diverse motion manifolds from large-scale mocap data and support flexible, text-conditioned synthesis. Lacking physical constraints, though, they often suffer from physical implausibility such as human-object penetration and foot skating. Physics-based imitation policies [Xu et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2026)] improve dynamic plausibility by tracking reference motions in simulation, yet depend on prescribed references and cannot directly infer fine-grained physical behaviors from high-level semantic conditions. Hierarchical planner-controller systems combine these strengths by using a generative planner to produce references for a physical controller. However, existing hierarchies still lack closed-loop planner-controller co-adaptation: SimGenHOI [Lin et al. (2025)] aligns its generator via supervised fine-tuning on simulator-executed trajectories but still executes generated plans open-loop, whereas CLoSD [Tevet et al. (2024)] replans online from simulated states for humanoid motion but adapts only the tracking controller while keeping the diffusion planner fixed.

A natural next step is to close this loop, allowing the planner to recurrently condition on the physical states reached by the controller and revise future interaction plans accordingly. In HOI, however, such coordination is not simply achieved by feeding simulator states back to a generative planner. Mocap-trained planners generate morphology-dependent interaction references, whereas controllers are often specialized to specific simulated embodiments, making physical feedback difficult to interpret across morphologies. Meanwhile, planner outputs may fall outside the controller’s executable distribution, and controller rollouts may visit physical states unseen during the planner’s supervised training. These gaps are further amplified by contact-rich object dynamics, where small errors in contact timing, position, or object pose can quickly lead to cascading failures. Together, these issues reveal a fundamental coordination problem between generative interaction planning and physical control.

To address this problem, we propose InfCoiL, a closed-loop framework for producing physics-based human-object interactions from coordinated planner-controller learning, as shown in Fig. 1. InfCoiL closes three coupled loops between a generative planner and a physics-based controller: an interface loop that maps realized human-object-contact states back into the planner’s conditioning across morphologies, an execution loop that replans from these states, and a learning loop that adapts both modules from the same physical rollouts. The first two loops are realized by an interface-compatible hierarchical architecture. A morphology-aware flow-matching planner trained on diverse mocap data generates short-horizon interaction references from textual instructions and spatial goals, conditioned on the target morphology and the realized execution history. A unified multi-morphology controller, rather than separate embodiment-specific policies, executes these references across body shapes.

To narrow the gap between planner-generated references and what the controller can execute, the learning loop alternately fine-tunes the controller to track these references and the planner to generate references that lead to better execution. Online planner fine-tuning, however, requires transition likelihoods that deterministic flow sampling lacks, and exploration suited to HOI tokens, whose body, object, and contact channels differ in physical sensitivity and error tolerance. We therefore propose Semantic Flow Policy Optimization (SFPO), which turns a fixed subset of denoising steps into Gaussian policy steps with semantic, channel-wise covariance. This yields tractable transition log-probabilities and channel-aware exploration while preserving efficient flow sampling. Together, SFPO and PPO controller fine-tuning align the planner’s generative distribution with the controller’s physical execution capability. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We formulate closed-loop physics-based HOI as a planner-controller coordination problem and propose InfCoiL, which closes interface, execution, and learning loops between a morphology-aware flow-matching planner and a unified multi-morphology controller.

  • •

    We propose SFPO, an online RL method for flow-matching HOI planners that stochasticizes selected denoising transitions with semantic channel-wise covariance and optimizes group-relative, sequence-level outcomes of complete closed-loop executions, and embed it in an alternating planner-controller learning scheme.

  • •

    Under a task-oriented evaluation on OMOMO [Li et al. (2023)] sequences held out from training, we show that InfCoiL improves task success over open-loop and SFT-aligned cascades, and provide component-wise ablations showing that replanning, controller learning, and planner learning address different failure sources, with planner learning most effective after the controller enlarges the executable region.

    • 2 Methodology

    We consider text- and goal-conditioned physics-based human-object interaction (HOI), where a simulated humanoid interacts with an object according to semantic and spatial task specifications. At simulation step t, the physical state sₜ consists of humanoid, object, and contact states. The task context is defined as

    cₜ=(ℓ,ξᵖₜ,ξᵒ,β,o,hₜ),

    		(1)

    where ℓ is the textual instruction, ξᵖₜ denotes the local pelvis sub-goal for the current planning window, ξᵒ specifies the final object goal, β represents the humanoid morphology using SMPL-X shape parameters [Pavlakos et al. (2019)], o encodes object geometry with BPS features [Prokudin et al. (2019)], and hₜ summarizes recent physical execution history. Given cₜ and sₜ, the system outputs low-level actions aₜ to realize the specified interaction while satisfying spatial goals and physical constraints.

    InfCoiL decomposes physics-based HOI into a high-level generative planner P_θ and a low-level physical controller π_φ, coupled through a closed-loop plan-and-execute interface, as detailed in Sec. 2.1. The planner predicts an N_f-frame reference window x̂_t:t+N_f-1, while the controller executes the first Nᵣ simulation steps before replanning, with Nᵣ≤N_f. Throughout the method, t denotes simulation time, t^′ denotes an execution step within a replanning segment, τ∈[0,1] is reserved for flow-matching time, and K denotes the number of flow denoising steps. To further align planning and control, InfCoiL jointly optimizes both components via coordinated reinforcement learning, mitigating the mismatch between generated references and executable behaviors (Sec. 2.2).

    2.1 Closed-loop Planner-Controller Framework for HOI

    2.1.1 Closed-loop versus Open-loop Design

    InfCoiL closes the planner-controller loop at the reference-trajectory level. In a conventional open-loop cascade, a generative model produces a complete kinematic interaction sequence, which is then tracked by a physics-based controller throughout the episode. This assumes that the simulated humanoid, object, and contacts remain close to the planned trajectory. However, contact-rich HOI easily violates this assumption: small errors in contact timing, object pose, root progress, or tracking accuracy accumulate over time and make the remaining reference physically infeasible.

    InfCoiL therefore adopts a receding-horizon replanning strategy, where the planner iteratively generates short-horizon reference windows and refines future plans using the controller’s realized physical states. Every Nᵣ simulation steps, the planner P_θ predicts x̂_t:t+N_f-1=P_θ(cₜ), where cₜ is the task context defined in Eq. (1). The controller π_φ executes the next segment by tracking these references, a_t^′=π_φ(s_t^′,x̂_t^′) for t^′∈[t,t+Nᵣ), after which the resulting body-object-contact states are fed back to update c_t+Nᵣ. This reference-level closed loop preserves the diversity and goal controllability of kinematic generation while enabling future plans to adapt to physical execution. Additional implementation details are provided in Appendix C.

    2.1.2 Morphology-aware Autoregressive Planner

    The high-level planner synthesizes short-horizon HOI references using a morphology-aware flow-matching model [Lipman et al. (2022)] trained on multi-subject, multi-object interaction data [Li et al. (2023)].

    Given task conditions and recent execution history, it recurrently predicts a short-horizon kinematic reference window for the controller to track. Each frame is represented as a structured HOI token containing body joints, hand joints, global body rotations, object translation and rotation, and hand contact labels. The planner is conditioned on text embeddings, local pelvis and object goals, object BPS features, temporal progress variables, fixed prefix frames, and a 16-dimensional SMPL-X shape code. The morphology condition allows the planner to adapt interaction references to different body shapes, since the same object-centric task may require different reaching poses, contact locations, and root motions across humanoid embodiments.

    During training, we interpolate between a clean reference window x₀ and Gaussian noise ε,

    x_τ=τε+(1-τ)x₀,\hskip20.00003ptτ∈(0,1],

    		(2)

    and train the planner to predict the clean state x̂₀=f_θ(x_τ,τ,c), where c denotes the full conditioning context, including text, goals, object geometry, morphology, progress, and prefix states. The supervised planning objective is

    Lₚₗₐₙ=∥f_θ(x_τ,τ,c)-x₀∥₂²+λ_objL_obj+λ_fkL_fk,

    		(3)

    where L_obj supervises object keypoints and L_fk supervises forward-kinematic hand and foot positions, and λ_* denotes corresponding hyperparameter. These auxiliary terms encourage the generated references to preserve object motion consistency and accurate end-effector geometry, which are critical for contact-rich HOI.

    At inference time, the planner samples a reference window by integrating the induced velocity

    v_θ(x_τ,τ,c)=(x_τ-f_θ(x_τ,τ,c))/(τ)

    		(4)

    from noise to data, while clamping the prefix frames from recent physical execution. Since x_τ is linear in x₀ and ε, Eq. (4) is the velocity induced by the clean-state prediction, so the trained network is exactly the one being integrated. Predicting x₀ rather than v=ε-x₀ regresses the structured HOI state instead of a noise-mixed target and avoids the 1/τ² reweighting of a velocity-space loss [Li and He (2025)]. The clean-state target directly supervises the positions, rotations, object states, and contact labels tracked by the controller, and Appendix B.6 shows that it reduces foot sliding and velocity error of the generated references compared with velocity prediction.

    2.1.3 Multi-morphology Controller

    The low-level controller provides a unified executable interface for morphology-conditioned planner references. This interface is essential for closed-loop HOI: since the planner generates references for the target humanoid morphology, the controller must execute them directly rather than retarget all motions to a canonical body. Unlike prior imitation frameworks such as InterMimic [Xu et al. (2025)], which consolidate embodiment-specific policies into a shared student with a unified output representation, InfCoiL learns a morphology-conditioned controller that adapts its tracking behavior to different SMPL body shapes while remaining compatible with planner-generated references.

    We initialize from morphology-specific InterMimic-style teachers trained for individual subjects and distill them into a single student controller through the distillation-to-RL curriculum of InterMimic [Xu et al. (2025)]. Each environment is assigned a subject-object pair, and the corresponding teacher labels every visited state with its action mean. Rollouts are initially driven by the teacher and gradually handed over to the student by mixing teacher and student actions with a decaying probability, so that expert labels are increasingly collected on student-induced states. After critic warm-up, PPO actor updates are enabled when a critic-reliability criterion is satisfied, with the actor weight gradually increased and the imitation weight reduced, allowing the student to inherit subject-specific tracking skills while adapting to its own induced state distribution.

    The student controller is conditioned on the same 16-dimensional SMPL-X shape code β used by the planner, together with a reference-tracking context x̂ over four lookahead steps. These inputs encode both body morphology and near-future interaction targets, enabling morphology-adaptive tracking under contact-rich dynamics. A compact transformer policy embeds the inputs and outputs a Gaussian action mean in the 153-dimensional action space. This yields a shared yet morphology-aware controller that supports closed-loop execution of planner-generated references across diverse humanoid shapes and object interactions.

    Extending reference state initialization [Peng et al. (2018)] and diverse resets [Yin et al. (2026)], we further introduce contact-aware state initialization (CSI) to focus controller pretraining on critical HOI phases. For each demonstration, reset weights are computed from hand-contact label transitions, so that rollouts are more frequently initialized near contact onset and release. This exposes the controller to diverse and challenging body-object configurations where tracking errors are most consequential, reducing the need to discover rare contact states through long rollouts and improving contact handling under planner-generated references. Appendix B.1 shows that removing CSI lowers SR by up to 25 points.

    2.2 Coordinated Planner-Controller Learning

    The closed-loop framework in Sec. 2.1 enables physical execution feedback for future planning, but does not by itself resolve the planner-controller distribution mismatch, i.e., generated references may be hard to execute and controller rollouts may reach states outside the planner’s pretraining distribution. To bridge this shift, InfCoiL introduces coordinated planner-controller learning with shared closed-loop rollout feedback. The controller is optimized to execute planner-generated references under simulation dynamics, while the planner is fine-tuned to improve downstream execution outcomes, forming a coupled optimization between generative planning and physical control. We realize this coordination with SFPO for the planner, PPO-based controller optimization, and interaction-centric rewards. Together, these updates align the planner’s generative distribution with the controller’s executable behavior distribution.

    2.2.1 SFPO for Planner Learning

    We fine-tune the flow-matching planner with physical execution feedback from the closed-loop controller. This is nontrivial because rectified-flow sampling is typically deterministic, and thus does not directly provide the transition likelihoods required by policy-gradient objectives [Zhang et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025); McAllister et al. (2025)]. Moreover, HOI references are high-dimensional and heterogeneous, containing body motion, object states, and contact labels, making naive stochastic perturbations unstable and inefficient.

    To address this, SFPO builds on the stochastic denoising path of Flow-GRPO [Liu et al. (2025)] rather than the flow-matching likelihood surrogate of FPO [McAllister et al. (2025)]. Let zₖ=x_τₖ (k=1,…,K+1) be the states of the K-step Euler sampler, from τ₁=1 to τ_K+1=0 with Δτₖ=τₖ₊₁-τₖ<0. SFPO turns a fixed subset S of S≤K steps into Gaussian policy steps by Euler–Maruyama discretization of the marginal-preserving flow SDE and keeps the deterministic Euler update at all other steps:

    π_θ(zₖ₊₁|zₖ,cₜ)=ℕ(μ_θ,k, (-Δτₖ)Γ_τₖΓ_τₖ^⊤),\hskip20.00003ptμ_θ,k=zₖ+v̄_θ(zₖ,τₖ,cₜ) Δτₖ,\hskip20.00003ptk∈S,

    		(5)

    where v̄_θ is a score-free drift computed from the velocity in Eq. (4). We use K=10 and make only the final step stochastic (S={K}), which reduces log-probability recomputation to a single denoising step per plan. To match exploration to heterogeneous HOI tokens, the diffusion coefficient is semantic rather than isotropic, Γ_τ=λₙ√τ/(1-τ)Diag(κ): fixed hand-set scales κ∈ℝ₊^D perturb object translation most and rotations least, and λₙ sets their global level.

    Planner updates are on-policy. A frozen snapshot θ_old generates the plans and stores their transition log-probabilities, which are recomputed under the current θ on the same denoising path. For a task condition cᵢ, we execute G closed-loop rollouts, and every replanning event t of the g-th rollout forms one training sample with ratio ρ_θ^i,g,t=\exp(ℓ̄_θ^i,g,t-ℓ̄_θ_old^i,g,t), where ℓ̄ denotes the transition log-probability averaged over the generated elements and clipped for numerical stability. Since each plan is scored only by the executed trajectory it leads to, all samples of a rollout share one group-relative advantage [Shao et al. (2024)] computed from the sequence reward Rᵢᵍ of rollout g (Eq. (10)):

    Aᵢᵍ=clip((Rᵢᵍ-R̄ᵢ)/(ςᵢ), -A_\max, A_\max),

    		(6)

    where R̄ᵢ and ςᵢ are the mean and standard deviation of Rᵢᵍ over the valid rollouts of group i, and groups with near-zero reward variance are skipped. The planner then maximizes the clipped surrogate J_clip with an optional fixed-reference penalty

    J_clip=𝔼_i,g,t[\min(ρ_θ^i,g,tAᵢᵍ, clip(ρ_θ^i,g,t,1-ε_c,1+ε_c)Aᵢᵍ)],(7)
    J_SFPO=J_clip-λ_KL 𝔼_i,g,t, k∈S[D_KL(π_θ(·|zₖ,cₜ) ∥ π_fix(·|zₖ,cₜ))].

    Here π_fix is a frozen pretrained planner, and λ_KL weights this optional penalty. We set λ_KL=0 in the reported experiments, so that J_SFPO=J_clip. Appendix E.1 gives the derivation of v̄_θ, the per-channel values of κ, the exact log-probability aggregation, and all hyperparameters.

    2.2.2 Human-Object Interaction-Centric Reward

    We design an HOI-centric reward to guide both local reference tracking and episode-level task completion, following the interaction-aware reward principles of InterMimic [Xu et al. (2025)]. The reward consists of a stepwise transition reward Rₜᵣₐₙₛᵗ and a task reward Rₜₐₛₖ triggered only at the end of the episode.

    The transition reward measures the consistency between the current simulated state and the reference interaction at each simulation step:

    Rₜᵣₐₙₛᵗ=wₕr_humanoidᵗ+wₒr_objectᵗ+wᵢₙₜr_interactionᵗ.

    		(8)

    Here, r_humanoidᵗ and r_objectᵗ are exponential tracking rewards based on the mean per-joint position error for the humanoid and the object center position error, respectively. The term r_interactionᵗ measures the interaction consistency between the human and the object based on hand-object contact labels, contact point distances, and interaction graph errors.

    The interaction term r_interactionᵗ is used only in the open-loop reinforcement learning of the controller and is disabled during closed-loop training. When the planner and the controller adapt to each other, rewarding interaction-graph consistency invites reward hacking toward trajectories with weak or negligible contact, which lowers task success. Closed-loop training therefore relies on the humanoid and object tracking rewards and the terminal task reward.

    The task reward is triggered only at the end of the episode:

    Rₜₐₛₖ=w_succR_success+wₜₑᵣₘRₜₑᵣₘ.

    		(9)

    In this formulation, R_success rewards episodes that successfully complete the target human-object interaction. The term Rₜₑᵣₘ penalizes episodes that terminate early due to infeasible humanoid motions or excessive object deviation from the reference trajectory, or that reach the timeout without completing the task. The overall reward therefore combines dense local tracking signals with sparse task-level evaluation, allowing the controller and planner to improve physical execution while remaining aligned with the intended HOI objective.

    2.2.3 Execution Feedback and Group-Relative Advantage

    The controller and the planner share these reward components but use them differently. The controller is a stepwise policy trained with PPO and a learned value function to maximize the expected return of the per-step reward Rₜᵣₐₙₛᵗ, with Rₜₐₛₖ added at the final step. The planner makes low-frequency decisions over long horizons whose quality is revealed only by the complete execution. Each rollout of length T is therefore scored by a sequence reward that averages the transition reward over time, so that the planner cannot gain reward merely by prolonging rollouts:

    R^seq=1/T∑ₜ₌₁ᵀRₜᵣₐₙₛᵗ+Rₜₐₛₖ.

    		(10)

    As described in Sec. 2.2.1, planner optimization in SFPO is critic-free and uses group-relative advantages. Rollouts in a group share the interaction conditions, such as the start state and task goals, and differ only in the semantic denoising noise. Normalizing the sequence scores Rᵢᵍ within each group therefore compares plans under identical conditions and removes reward offsets caused by task difficulty or object scale, which encourages references that the controller can execute. The reward terms, group construction, valid-set masking, and terminal advantage assignment are detailed in Appendix E.3.

    2.2.4 Coordinated Learning Paradigm

    Optimizing either component in isolation is insufficient. A controller trained alone adapts to fixed planner references but cannot change the motion generation itself, which bounds task success. A planner updated against a frozen controller instead explores references that the controller cannot execute, so it receives little useful feedback. InfCoiL therefore alternates planner and controller updates. After supervised pretraining of the planner and open-loop distillation and RL of the controller, the controller is first fine-tuned with PPO on closed-loop rollouts. Once its tracking quality or success rate plateaus, the controller is frozen and the planner is updated with SFPO until its sequence-level scores plateau, after which training returns to the controller. The controller phase thus resolves the physical executability of current references, and the planner phase moves references toward what the controller can stably track. Algorithm 1 and Appendix E.4 give the full procedure.

    3 Experiments

    3.1 Evaluation Settings

    Metrics and protocol. We evaluate all methods on a morphology-balanced re-split of OMOMO [Li et al. (2023)], which splits the sequences of every subject with the same train/test ratio. Planner training, controller training, and coordinated fine-tuning use only the training sequences, and all results are reported on the held-out test sequences. All methods share the same Isaac Gym environment, humanoid/object assets, physical parameters, and deterministic controller actions. Each test sequence is evaluated three times and metrics are averaged. SR@d counts an episode as successful when both the pelvis and the object end within d m of their goals. SR denotes SR@0.3 unless stated otherwise, and Table 2 and the appendix additionally report SR@0.2, SR@0.1, and their mean (Avg. SR). We also report pelvis/object goal errors and humanoid/object tracking errors Eₕ/Eₒ, all in centimeters. This protocol requires reaching the task goals, unlike the reference-tracking protocol of InterMimic [Xu et al. (2025)], which tracks references on a teacher-supported subset, counts episodes within a 0.5 m deviation as successful, and reports the best sampled rollout. Appendix B.2 explains how this difference affects the InterMimic student results, and Appendix A gives further protocol and metric details.

    Baselines and variants. We compare InfCoiL with two open-loop baselines and four internal variants. In all cases, the controller tracks reference trajectories produced by a high-level planner and the key difference is whether these references are generated once in an open-loop manner or repeatedly generated in a closed-loop manner with execution feedback. InterMimic [Xu et al. (2025)] student evaluates the distilled multi-morphology controller under the one-shot planner-reference protocol. SimGenHOI* [Lin et al. (2025)] follows an open-loop cascade with two-stage supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with the same network architecture of planner and controller as ours for fair comparison: the planner is first fine-tuned on trajectories produced by controller tracking, and the controller is then fine-tuned on trajectories generated by the updated planner. InfCoiL open-loop uses our planner and controller with one-shot reference generation and no closed-loop replanning. The closed-loop variant w/o FT P & C instead uses closed-loop online generation with receding-horizon feedback, but freezes both modules. Finally, w/o FT C fine-tunes only the planner, w/o FT P fine-tunes only the controller, and full InfCoiL alternates controller (C) and planner (P) fine-tuning phases. We report InfCoiL (C→P), with one controller phase followed by one planner phase, and InfCoiL (C→P→C), which adds a further controller phase. Unless otherwise stated, InfCoiL refers to the latter.

    3.2 Results and Analysis

    Table 1 shows that InfCoiL substantially improves task completion over open-loop baselines. Compared with InterMimic student, InfCoiL raises SR from 24.62% to 81.19% and reduces pelvis/object goal errors from 90.39/111.89 cm to 31.31/41.51 cm. Compared with SimGenHOI* (open-loop + SFT), InfCoiL increases SR from 52.14% to 81.19%, while reducing pelvis/object goal errors from 50.12/68.15 cm to 31.31/41.51 cm. These gains show that closed-loop planner-controller learning improves task completion beyond one-shot planner-reference generation. InfCoiL also improves physical tracking quality over open-loop baselines while achieving higher task success. Compared with InterMimic student and SimGenHOI*, InfCoiL reduces Eₕ from 9.23/9.69 cm to 8.87 cm and Eₒ from 16.89/18.00 cm to 14.21 cm. This indicates that closed-loop learning improves not only goal reaching, but also the executability of planner-generated references. As shown in Fig. 2, InfCoiL achieves more stable contacts and physically plausible object interactions, and Appendix B.8 analyzes the failure modes. Furthermore, Figs. 3 and 4 demonstrate the generalization to novel object-humanoid morphology combinations.

    3.3 Framework Ablation

    Component summary. Each component of InfCoiL is isolated by a controlled comparison. Closed-loop replanning alone raises SR from 49.23% to 56.09%, and lowers both goal errors and tracking errors, showing that replanning corrects part of the mismatch between generated references and realized physical states. Controller adaptation (w/o FT P) adds a further 17.28 points, and alternating updates are compared with controller-only training at a matched controller budget below. SFPO is compared with alternative planner RL objectives in Sec. 3.4, online RL is compared with supervised fine-tuning of the planner in Appendix B.4, and removing contact-aware state initialization lowers SR under the reference-tracking protocol of Appendix Table 3.

    Effect of coordinated learning. Table 1 shows that fine-tuning only one component exposes the asymmetry between planner and controller adaptation. Planner-only fine-tuning (w/o FT C) provides only a small SR gain over the frozen closed-loop system, from 56.09% to 56.98%, suggesting that a frozen controller restricts the executable support and thus the useful reward signal for planner learning. Controller-only fine-tuning (w/o FT P) is much stronger, raising SR to 73.37% and reducing object-goal error to 49.45 cm, but it still leaves the planner distribution fixed. Alternating the two phases yields consistent gains: a subsequent SFPO planner phase raises SR to 77.24% (C→P), and a further controller phase reaches 81.19% (C→P→C) while reducing pelvis/object goal errors to 31.31/41.51 cm. In contrast, the matched-budget comparison in Appendix B.3 shows that continuing controller-only training to the same 14k controller iterations lowers SR to 71.99%, indicating that the gain comes from planner-controller co-adaptation rather than additional controller updates. Although the lowest humanoid tracking error Eₕ is attained by the frozen closed-loop variant, full InfCoiL achieves the best task success, goal accuracy, and object tracking error, suggesting that coordinated learning optimizes executable task completion rather than tracking fidelity alone.

    3.4 Planner RL Ablation

    We compare SFPO with planner-side reinforcement learning baselines under the same closed-loop setting. All methods start from the same controller-adapted checkpoint, keep the controller frozen, and update the planner with the same number of iterations. The baselines cover critic-based single-step updates, namely FPO++ [Yi et al. (2026)], an improved variant of FPO [McAllister et al. (2025)], and ReinFlow PPO [Zhang et al. (2025)], each with and without a behavior-cloning (BC) anchor, as well as Flow-GRPO [Liu et al. (2025)] with isotropic noise. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B.5.

    Table 2 shows that critic-based updates do not improve on this strong starting point: without a BC anchor, FPO++ and ReinFlow PPO degrade to 12.83% and 70.06% SR@0.3, and with the anchor they at most preserve the initial policy (73.45% and 73.61% vs. 73.37%). Making the flow sampler stochastic with isotropic noise is also insufficient, as Flow-GRPO drops to 22.52%. In contrast, SFPO improves SR@0.3 over the starting point at every tested noise level (λₙ∈{0.05,0.1,0.2}, 74.66–77.24%), and the default λₙ=0.1 achieves the best success at all thresholds together with the lowest goal errors, while a larger noise level trades strict-threshold success (SR@0.1) for coarse-threshold gains. These results indicate that channel-wise exploration matched to heterogeneous HOI tokens is what makes sequence-level planner RL stable in this setting. Appendix B.4 further compares online RL with supervised fine-tuning of the planner.

    4 Related Works

    Generative Models for Human-Object Interaction. Kinematic generative models have become a dominant approach for synthesizing human-object interactions (HOI). Diffusion-based methods incorporate various conditions to support object-guided manipulation and text-controllable interaction synthesis [Xu et al. (2023); Li et al. (2023); Diller and Dai (2024); Li et al. (2024)]. Subsequent work improves conditioning and representation design through semantic-geometric context [Cong et al. (2025)], object relations [Xue et al. (2025)], kinematic-chain structures [Zeng et al. (2025)], unseen-object generalization [Li et al. (2025)], and interaction dynamics [Wu et al. (2025a)]. Other studies accelerate or refine the generative process itself, including asynchronous denoising for classifier-free interaction guidance [Wang et al. (2026)] and consistency-based motion generators for fast inference [Dai et al. (2024); Jiang et al. (2025); Zou et al. (2026a)]. However, flow-based HOI generation remains underexplored. Moreover, existing generators are typically trained without physical execution feedback, limiting their ability to adapt plans to the states reached by the controller.

    Physics-based Human-Object Interaction. Physics-based HOI methods aim to execute interactions under contact-rich dynamics rather than only synthesize kinematic trajectories. A direct paradigm is to learn task policies with reinforcement learning from manually designed rewards, which can produce executable behaviors for sports, games, and object manipulation but often depends on task-specific engineering and lacks demonstration-level realism [Merel et al. (2020); Liu and Hodgins (2018); Xu et al. (2024)]. Imitation-based methods reduce this burden by tracking human-object demonstrations in simulation, enabling contact-rich and reusable interaction skills [Wang et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2025); Yu et al. (2025)]. However, these skills remain bounded by the objects, motions, and interaction modes covered by demonstrations, limiting their ability to synthesize diverse long-horizon behaviors from fine-grained textual and spatial instructions. Recent large-scale methods improve coverage by learning whole-body controllers from broader and imperfect mocap interaction data, including unified controllers for heterogeneous objects and sparse-intention-conditioned control [Xu et al. (2025); Xu et al. (2026)]. These methods ground HOI in simulation, but they remain less expressive than text-conditioned generative planners in semantic controllability and motion diversity. Hierarchical systems further combine interaction generators with imitation policies to connect planning and physical tracking [Lin et al. (2025)], but they still generate static references before tracking, leaving the planner essentially open-loop. In contrast, InfCoiL addresses this gap with a closed-loop planner-controller framework, where the planner repeatedly conditions on language, goals, morphology, object states, and recent physical feedback, and coordinated reinforcement learning adapts both modules to each other.

    5 Conclusion and Limitation

    This work studies how high-level generative interaction planning can be coordinated with low-level physical control for text- and goal-conditioned human-object interaction. A series of validations on the OMOMO benchmark shows that the closed-loop planner-controller framework enables adaptive replanning from physical execution feedback, while coordinated learning further aligns motion-capture-based generation with executable simulated behavior. The ablations also indicate when each component matters: closed-loop replanning corrects recoverable drift from the generated references, controller adaptation enlarges the physically executable region, and planner learning is most effective once this region has expanded, where it raises the final task-success ceiling. Together, these findings suggest that physics-based HOI animation requires not only diverse and controllable generative priors, but also their closed-loop adaptation to the physical controller and contact-rich execution dynamics.

    While InfCoiL demonstrates strong performance in simulation, several limitations remain. First, InfCoiL is a physics-based character animation system. All experiments use simulated SMPL-X humanoids, whose shape variation is not equivalent to the kinematics, actuation, and sensing of real humanoid robots, so real-robot deployment would require adaptation to hardware constraints, sensing noise, and real contact dynamics. Second, the current setting assumes structured object states and goal specifications, which offers a controlled testbed for studying planner-controller coordination but leaves perception-driven inputs and more complex scenes to future work. Third, the effective semantic range of language conditioning follows the OMOMO/CHOIS annotations, and we have not evaluated paraphrased or out-of-distribution instructions. Appendix F.2 discusses possible extensions.

    Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding

    This work was supported in part by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grant 62401367 and in part by Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  • 1.

    Claims

  • Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: The paper’s contributions and scope are specifically claimed in the abstract and introduction. Our key contributions are summarized in the last paragraph of Section 1.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

  • •

    The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

  • •

    The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

  • •

    It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  • 2.

    Limitations

  • Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We discuss the limitations of our work in Section 5.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

  • •

    The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

  • •

    The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

  • •

    The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

  • •

    The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

  • •

    The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

  • •

    If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

  • •

    While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  • 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  • Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  • Answer: [N/A]

  • Justification: The paper does not present theorems. The derivation of the SFPO transition likelihood is given in Section 2.2.1 and Appendix E.1.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

  • •

    All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

  • •

    All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

  • •

    The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

  • •

    Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

  • •

    Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  • 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  • Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We fully describe our architecture settings, simulation and training parameters in Section 3 and Appendices A, C, and D, and the provided information is sufficient to reproduce our main experimental results.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

  • •

    If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

  • •

    If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

  • •

    Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

  • •

    While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

  • (a)

    If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

  • (b)

    If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

  • (c)

    If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

  • (d)

    We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  • 5.

    Open access to data and code

  • Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We provide sufficient material in supplemental material.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

  • •

    Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

  • •

    While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

  • •

    The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

  • •

    The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

  • •

    The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

  • •

    At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

  • •

    Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  • 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  • Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We specify our training and test details in Section 3.1 and Appendices A, D, and E.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

  • •

    The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

  • •

    The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  • 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  • Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We define the evaluation metrics in Section 3.1. And then we compare our method with other baselines, showing statistical results in Sections 3.2 and 3.3.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

  • •

    The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

  • •

    The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

  • •

    The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

  • •

    The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

  • •

    It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

  • •

    It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

  • •

    For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

  • •

    If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  • 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  • Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: Please see our experimental details in Section 3 and Appendices C and D. Training InfCoiL takes about one week on four NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs (Appendix D).

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

  • •

    The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

  • •

    The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

  • •

    The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  • 9.

    Code of ethics

  • Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We read the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, and make sure that our research conducted in the paper conform with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics in every respect.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

  • •

    If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

  • •

    The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  • 10.

    Broader impacts

  • Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We discuss the societal impacts in Appendix F.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

  • •

    If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

  • •

    Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

  • •

    The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

  • •

    The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

  • •

    If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  • 11.

    Safeguards

  • Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  • Answer: [N/A]

  • Justification: No such risks.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

  • •

    Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

  • •

    Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

  • •

    We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

  • 12.

    Licenses for existing assets

  • Question: Are the creators or original owners of assets (e.g., code, data, models), used in the paper, properly credited and are the license and terms of use explicitly mentioned and properly respected?

  • Answer: [Yes]

  • Justification: We cite works of related assets.

  • Guidelines:

  • •

    The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not use existing assets.

item.title: 游戏是采 VLA 数据最便宜的地方，但现有数据集不够用：AceAction 用多层目标标出「技能组合」与「子目标切换」 ｜ AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
item.description:
一句话：限制有三处：游戏覆盖窄、语言监督稀疏、时间层级并不反映任务目标的变化。

要点：

  • 前提：视频游戏为采集视觉-语言-动作（VLA）数据提供了实用场景，因为物理环境里采数据太贵
  • 现有数据集的三处限制：**游戏覆盖面窄**、**语言监督稀疏**，以及**时间层级并不必然反映任务目标的变化**
  • AceAction 因此构建跨多个 3D 游戏的人类游玩数据集，用**层级目标**来标注技能组合与子目标切换，规模在 5M 量级

为什么值得看：「层级目标」是这块缺失的关键监督：只标「这一段在干什么」学不到技能组合。对要做游戏内 agent 或自动化测试的团队，这份数据的标注方式比数据本身更值得借鉴。

中文摘要：视频游戏为采集视觉-语言-动作（VLA）数据提供了很实用的场景，因为在物理环境里采集这类数据成本过高。但现有数据集受限于三处：覆盖的游戏种类有限、语言监督稀疏，以及其时间层级并不一定反映任务目标本身的改变。AceAction 因此构建了一个跨多个 3D 游戏的人类游玩数据集，专门用于学习技能组合与子目标切换，并用层级化的目标标注来刻画这两件事。对需要训练游戏内 agent、或做自动化回归测试的团队，它提供的「层级目标」标注口径比数据规模更值得借鉴。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-06

本期推送：2026-11-23

AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for
Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds

Abstract

Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision–language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.

**footnotetext: Equal contribution.

1 Introduction

Learning vision-language-action (VLA) models requires demonstrations that connect language goals, visual observations, and executable actions [2, 11, 16, 12]. Collecting such data at scale in the physical world is costly, requiring robotic hardware, human supervision, and repeated environment setup [10]. Video games offer a practical setting for collecting large-scale interaction data: human players can perform diverse tasks in rich virtual environments, while visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions can be recorded together [20]. Paired with language annotations, these trajectories support learning to translate task instructions into actions grounded in visual observations. In particular, 3D games demand close coordination between high-level decision-making and low-level control, requiring agents to navigate, scout, engage opponents, and interact with the environment through rapid and precise keyboard-and-mouse actions. Under partial observability and continuously changing conditions, agents must continually adapt their decisions and actions to environmental feedback.

Tasks in 3D games often require agents to combine multiple skills across successive stages. For example, an agent asked to approach the building, scout the entrance, engage the enemy, and fall back to cover to recover may fight effectively yet continue chasing an opponent when it should retreat. Successful task completion therefore requires agents to understand how each skill serves the current subgoal and to select, compose, and switch skills as the task progresses. This motivates two complementary data requirements. First, hierarchical annotations linking tasks, subgoals, and skill-level instructions: demonstrations should connect overall objectives to local goals and concrete instructions, making explicit what to achieve and how to act, with temporal boundaries indicating subgoal transitions. Second, large-scale action data covering diverse goals and tasks: extensive keyboard-and-mouse trajectories should span varied scenarios and skill combinations, capturing how navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery are executed and composed for different objectives. Together, these properties support learning both task structure and the behaviors needed to realize it.

Existing game-interaction datasets exhibit limitations in both behavioral coverage and supervision for task structure. EgoCS-400K [7] provides detailed replay-grounded actions and multi-granularity captions, but remains confined to Counter-Strike and primarily describes local clips and action chains. Open-P2P [23] broadens game coverage, yet its sparse, goal-oriented instructions provide limited supervision for connecting fine-grained skill execution with intermediate and overall objectives. GameHorizon [22] introduces multi-horizon instructions aligned with action recordings, but constructs its instruction hierarchy under predefined duration ranges for operations, goals, and strategies. These constraints may split a sustained subgoal or combine several brief subgoals, making temporal hierarchy an imperfect proxy for task-stage structure. These limitations motivate demonstrations with broader behavioral coverage and explicit, objective-driven stage annotations, linking each task to its constituent skills and marking when execution transitions between subgoals.

To bridge this gap, we introduce AceAction-5M, a dataset that unifies multi-game tasks, fine-grained hierarchical instructions, and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. Each episode pairs a global task description with temporally bounded stage-level subgoals, and aligns local action instructions frame by frame with the keyboard-and-mouse actions that realize them. The resulting trajectories capture how navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery are composed and switched, providing a data foundation for learning to map complex task instructions to continuous, fine-grained control. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    A hierarchically annotated, multi-game action dataset. AceAction covers 42 games and 5,027.87 hours of play, with 5,476,222 episodes in which task descriptions, stage-level subgoals, and local action instructions are jointly aligned with frame-level keyboard-and-mouse trajectories.

  • •

    An annotation scheme that makes stage structure explicit. We define 43 skill categories spanning navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, and mark the start and end of every stage, turning when to switch from an implicit property of the data into an explicit, learnable signal.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Game Data and Benchmarks for World Modeling

    Gameplay data supports action-conditioned world modeling by aligning visual observations, actions, and environment states. GameNGen [21] learns video prediction from DOOM trajectories collected by a reinforcement learning agent, while DIAMOND [1] demonstrates interactive world modeling using recorded CS:GO gameplay. WildWorld [13] provides frame-level annotations of skeletons, camera poses, and depth for evaluating action following and state consistency.

    EgoCS-400K [7] synchronizes player states, actions, and events extracted from CS:GO/CS2 replays with over 10,000 hours of first-person video. Its multi-granularity captions and video generation prompts link visual changes to replay information, providing language supervision for world modeling. GameVerse [9] provides minute-scale gameplay videos with temporally coherent camera trajectories and event-aligned structured captions, supporting long-horizon interactive world modeling.

    GameHorizon [22] combines 5,000 hours of gameplay from 21 games with synchronized keyboard-and-mouse actions and three levels of instructions: operations, goals, and strategies. Its offline benchmark evaluates action understanding, goal decomposition, and cross-horizon consistency through multiple-choice questions, with predicted action sequences matched to answer options for scoring. Our work links subtask instructions to waypoints and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories within multi-stage tasks, providing supervision for subgoal transitions and continuous control.

    2.2 Game Action Data for Instruction Following

    Large-scale gameplay demonstrations support action policy learning [24, 25]. MineRL [8] provides human demonstrations in Minecraft with automatically annotated states and actions. VPT [3] uses inverse dynamics to infer keyboard-and-mouse actions from Minecraft videos, while NitroGen [15] extracts gamepad actions from online videos for cross-game behavior cloning.

    Language-based supervision further connects gameplay behaviors to task goals. MineDojo [5] combines an open-ended task suite specified in natural language with an internet-scale multimodal knowledge base of videos, tutorials, wiki pages, and forum discussions. Open-P2P [23] provides cross-game keyboard-and-mouse trajectories with sparse goal-oriented instructions. SIMA [18] learns to follow language instructions across 3D environments, focusing primarily on short-horizon tasks, while SIMA 2 [4] extends this setting to complex instructions and instruction chaining. STEVE-1 [14] supports text- and visual-goal control in Minecraft and composes multi-step behaviors through sequential subgoal prompts.

    AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete multi-stage tasks, with annotations spanning overall goals, stage-level subgoals, and local skill instructions. Each subtask is associated with a waypoint, explicit temporal boundaries, and aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. This structure connects individual skill execution to task progression, providing supervision for action execution and the timing of subgoal transitions.

    3 Dataset

    3.1 Data Source

    Our dataset comprises two complementary components: directly collected gameplay and publicly sourced gameplay. The directly collected gameplay was recorded from full-time in-house staff who held a Gold rank and consented to participate. These recordings were transcribed in anonymized form during data collection. Together, these components provide approximately 5,180 hours of gameplay recordings paired with keyboard-and-mouse actions.

    Directly collected gameplay. We collected gameplay recordings and corresponding keyboard-and-mouse actions from human players. This component includes approximately 1,891 hours of Game for Peace, including combat scenarios, and 261.17 hours of Valorant. These recordings pair gameplay observations with the actions performed by human players.

    Publicly sourced gameplay. To broaden coverage across games and tasks, we incorporate 2,103.05 hours of CS:GO and CS2 gameplay from match recordings collected online, 811.50 hours of annotated 3D gameplay from Open-P2P, and 113.25 hours of Minecraft gameplay from VPT. These durations refer to the portions included in our dataset rather than the complete upstream datasets.

    Action representation and sampling rates. Across both components, we use a common action representation that encodes keyboard and mouse-button states, together with horizontal and vertical mouse displacement. Our directly collected gameplay is recorded at 16 Hz, corresponding to one action step every 62.5 ms. For publicly sourced gameplay, we CS:GO and CS2 action sequences are 16 Hz, while retaining the original 20 Hz sampling rate for Open-P2P and VPT.

    3.2 Construction Pipeline

    We construct hierarchical annotations from gameplay observations and actions recorded from human players (Figure 2). The pipeline first identifies skill-based subgoals and uses visually recognizable waypoints to construct navigation subgoals. Adjacent subgoals are then composed into overall instructions. Throughout this process, source indices preserve the correspondence between semantic annotations and the original image–action sequences.

    Skill-based subgoal annotation. We group every four consecutive actions into an annotation unit with a corresponding visual observation. Each trajectory is processed in consecutive windows of up to 32 units. Given the ordered observations and actions, a vision–language model jointly predicts a skill category, start and end indices, and a subgoal description for each segment. The skill category identifies the type of behavior, while the subgoal description specifies its concrete objective. Multiple subgoals can therefore share the same skill category while referring to different targets or objectives.

    Segmentation follows continuity of purpose. An activity remains within one segment while it serves the same objective. A new segment begins when the primary objective or interaction target changes. To preserve this continuity across window boundaries, each subsequent window receives the previous window’s final observation, skill category, and subgoal description. The model also predicts a continuation flag indicating whether its first segment extends the preceding subgoal. We merge the two segments only when this flag is positive, their skill categories match, and their sequence indices are adjacent. This allows a subgoal to span multiple annotation windows. After normalizing category labels, descriptions, and boundaries, we remove residual airborne segments and map the retained subgoals back to their original image–action sequences using source indices.

    Waypoint-based subgoal annotation. Navigation subgoals are constructed around arrival events at visually recognizable locations. We identify these events using a sliding window containing up to eight recent observations. The window advances by one observation at each step, and the model evaluates whether the newest frame shows arrival at a specific location. Its input includes the observations, recorded actions, associated skill annotations, previously accepted waypoint names, and the most recent waypoint. Visual observations provide the evidence for arrival, while actions and skill annotations provide behavioral context.

    For each accepted arrival event, the model assigns a descriptive waypoint name and associates it with the source frame. Previously accepted names are reused when the same location is recognized again. Continued activity within an already reached location does not produce repeated arrival annotations. Each waypoint thus identifies a destination and the observation at which it is reached.

    We then sample clips of varying lengths that end at the waypoint frame. This creates navigation examples with a shared destination but different starting points and intervening actions. For each clip, the model receives sampled keyframes, including the first and arrival frames, together with the complete action sequence, skill context, and target waypoint name. It generates a navigation subgoal that includes the waypoint name and describes the observed route or movement toward that destination. Although annotation uses sampled keyframes, the resulting subgoal retains the complete image–action sequence.

    Instruction composition. We combine adjacent subgoals from the same trajectory in execution order to form an overall instruction. The overall instruction summarizes the task defined by this sequence, while the constituent subgoals retain its intermediate objectives. A composed task can include successive subgoals of the same skill or transitions between different skills. For example, navigation subgoals may lead to a destination where the player subsequently performs an interaction.

    For each composed sample, we retain the overall instruction, ordered subgoal descriptions, skill categories, segment boundaries, and corresponding image–action sequence. These boundaries identify the observations and actions associated with each intermediate objective, preserving the relationship between the complete task and its execution stages.

    Before export, we check that descriptions are non-empty, skill categories are valid, and segment boundaries are ordered and within the source sequence. We also verify image–action correspondence and confirm that each navigation clip ends at its designated waypoint frame. The resulting samples explicitly connect overall instructions, intermediate subgoals, and executable actions.

    3.3 Quality Control

    We apply a two-stage quality-control procedure consisting of model-based verification and human inspection.

    Model-based verification.

    We use Qwen3.8-27B [17] and GLM-5.3-FLASH [6] to review each annotated sample against its gameplay clip and recorded actions. Both models perform bottom-up verification across three annotation levels. First, they check whether each action description matches the visible behavior and recorded controls. Second, they assess whether each subgoal accurately describes the objective supported by its associated observations and actions. Finally, they verify that the overall instruction is consistent with the constituent subgoals and the complete trajectory. At every level, the review checks both visual grounding and action consistency. A sample is retained only when both models approve all annotation levels. A rejection at any level by either model leads to its exclusion.

    Human inspection.

    Following model-based verification, eight human reviewers inspect 500 trajectories, with each trajectory assessed by at least two reviewers. The inspection checks whether action descriptions match the observed operations, subgoals reflect the corresponding execution stages, and overall instructions accurately describe the complete tasks. Reviewers assess these annotations against both the gameplay clips and recorded actions. The pass rate across independent review records is 95.8%, where each record represents one reviewer’s assessment of one trajectory.

    3.4 Compared with other benchmark

    Table 1 compares gameplay datasets in terms of instruction annotations and supervision characteristics. Our dataset emphasizes two aspects for training and evaluating game agents, including vision–language–action (VLA) models. First, trajectory segmentation is grounded in both player-view videos and recorded keyboard–mouse actions. Each annotated segment preserves the temporal correspondence between visual observations, language instructions, and control inputs, providing aligned supervision for instruction following and action prediction. Second, our dataset provides extensive subgoal descriptions and second-scale skill annotations within an explicit task–subgoal–skill hierarchy. Overall task instructions are linked to ordered subgoals and action description, with temporal boundaries marking subgoal transitions. These annotations provide structured textual supervision for reasoning about task decomposition, skill composition, and subgoal transitions, supporting both training and evaluation on multi-stage tasks.

    4 Conclusion

    We introduce AceAction-5M, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for training and evaluating game agents and vision–language–action (VLA) models. Combining directly collected and publicly sourced gameplay, AceAction links player-view observations and aligned keyboard–mouse actions through a task–subgoal–skill instruction hierarchy. Explicit temporal boundaries connect overall task objectives to local skill execution and mark subgoal transitions. Model-based verification and human inspection assess consistency among language annotations, visual observations, and actions. AceAction provides structured supervision for studying task decomposition, skill composition, and subgoal transitions in dynamic game environments.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：限制有三处：游戏覆盖窄、语言监督稀疏、时间层级并不反映任务目标的变化。

要点：

  • 前提：视频游戏为采集视觉-语言-动作（VLA）数据提供了实用场景，因为物理环境里采数据太贵
  • 现有数据集的三处限制：**游戏覆盖面窄**、**语言监督稀疏**，以及**时间层级并不必然反映任务目标的变化**
  • AceAction 因此构建跨多个 3D 游戏的人类游玩数据集，用**层级目标**来标注技能组合与子目标切换，规模在 5M 量级

为什么值得看：「层级目标」是这块缺失的关键监督：只标「这一段在干什么」学不到技能组合。对要做游戏内 agent 或自动化测试的团队，这份数据的标注方式比数据本身更值得借鉴。

中文摘要：视频游戏为采集视觉-语言-动作（VLA）数据提供了很实用的场景，因为在物理环境里采集这类数据成本过高。但现有数据集受限于三处：覆盖的游戏种类有限、语言监督稀疏，以及其时间层级并不一定反映任务目标本身的改变。AceAction 因此构建了一个跨多个 3D 游戏的人类游玩数据集，专门用于学习技能组合与子目标切换，并用层级化的目标标注来刻画这两件事。对需要训练游戏内 agent、或做自动化回归测试的团队，它提供的「层级目标」标注口径比数据规模更值得借鉴。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-06

本期推送：2026-11-23

AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for

Abstract

Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions.
