To construct these annotations, we develop a vision–language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. Learning vision-language-action (VLA) models requires demonstrations that connect language goals, visual observations, and executable actions [2, 11, 16, 12]. Collecting such data at scale in the physical world is costly, requiring robotic hardware, human supervision, and repeated environment setup [10]. Video games offer a practical setting for collecting large-scale interaction data: human players can perform diverse tasks in rich virtual environments, while visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions can be recorded together [20]. Paired with language annotations, these trajectories support learning to translate task instructions into actions grounded in visual observations. In particular, 3D games demand close coordination between high-level decision-making and low-level control, requiring agents to navigate, scout, engage opponents, and interact with the environment through rapid and precise keyboard-and-mouse actions. Under partial observability and continuously changing conditions, agents must continually adapt their decisions and actions to environmental feedback.

Tasks in 3D games often require agents to combine multiple skills across successive stages. For example, an agent asked to approach the building, scout the entrance, engage the enemy, and fall back to cover to recover may fight effectively yet continue chasing an opponent when it should retreat. Successful task completion therefore requires agents to understand how each skill serves the current subgoal and to select, compose, and switch skills as the task progresses. This motivates two complementary data requirements. First, hierarchical annotations linking tasks, subgoals, and skill-level instructions: demonstrations should connect overall objectives to local goals and concrete instructions, making explicit what to achieve and how to act, with temporal boundaries indicating subgoal transitions. Second, large-scale action data covering diverse goals and tasks: extensive keyboard-and-mouse trajectories should span varied scenarios and skill combinations, capturing how navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery are executed and composed for different objectives. Existing game-interaction datasets exhibit limitations in both behavioral coverage and supervision for task structure. Open-P2P [23] broadens game coverage, yet its sparse, goal-oriented instructions provide limited supervision for connecting fine-grained skill execution with intermediate and overall objectives. GameHorizon [22] introduces multi-horizon instructions aligned with action recordings, but constructs its instruction hierarchy under predefined duration ranges for operations, goals, and strategies. These constraints may split a sustained subgoal or combine several brief subgoals, making temporal hierarchy an imperfect proxy for task-stage structure. These limitations motivate demonstrations with broader behavioral coverage and explicit, objective-driven stage annotations, linking each task to its constituent skills and marking when execution transitions between subgoals.

To bridge this gap, we introduce AceAction-5M, a dataset that unifies multi-game tasks, fine-grained hierarchical instructions, and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories. Each episode pairs a global task description with temporally bounded stage-level subgoals, and aligns local action instructions frame by frame with the keyboard-and-mouse actions that realize them. Our work links subtask instructions to waypoints and temporally aligned keyboard-and-mouse trajectories within multi-stage tasks, providing supervision for subgoal transitions and continuous control.

item.title: DiT 特征缓存省算力，但短采样下误差更大：CalibCache 用一次离线校准把外推拉回正轨 ｜ CalibCache: Cache-to-Full Feature Dynamics Calibration for Diffusion Transformers
item.description:
一句话：采样步数越少、网格越粗，基于历史的外推就越不可靠。

要点：

  • 矛盾：扩散 transformer 采样开销大，**特征缓存**能减少完整网络评估次数，但在**短采样计划**下误差会变得更严重
  • 原因是结构性的：完整计算步更少、采样网格更粗，导致**基于历史的外推**不可靠
  • CalibCache 提出一种**轻量离线校准**方法，把缓存结果对齐到完整计算的动态，从而在少步设置下保持质量

为什么值得看：实时渲染与实时生成的交集就是「少步 + 缓存」，而这两者叠在一起最容易崩。一次离线校准换来少步下的可用性，是可插进现有 DiT 管线的最小改动。

中文摘要：扩散 transformer 能生成高质量图像，但迭代采样仍然昂贵。特征缓存可以减少完整网络评估的次数，问题在于它的近似误差在短采样计划下会更严重：完整计算步更少、采样网格更粗，使基于历史的外推变得不可靠。CalibCache 因此提出一种轻量的离线校准方法，把缓存得到的特征动态校准到完整计算的特征动态上，从而在少步设置下维持质量。对需要把扩散模型压进实时预算的管线，这类「一次性离线校准 + 运行时缓存」的组合是最小侵入的加速方式。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-23

CalibCache: Cache-to-Full Feature Dynamics Calibration for Diffusion Transformers

Abstract

Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals N=3,4,5. At N=5, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from 0.563 to 0.429 while achieving a 2.86× denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from 16.39 to 10.37 relative to TaylorSeer.

1 Introduction

Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a central backbone for image generation [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)]. Although recent models can generate high-quality images with only a few tens of sampling steps, inference remains expensive because each step requires costly Transformer attention and feed-forward computations. Training-free feature caching reduces this cost by reusing intermediate features across adjacent sampling steps [(Ma et al., 2023; Selvaraju et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025)], but reused features can deviate from their full-compute counterparts as the reuse interval grows.

Short sampling schedules can exacerbate this discrepancy. Fewer sampling steps provide fewer full-compute observations overall, while a cache interval of fixed N spans a larger fraction of the rollout. History-based extrapolation can therefore become less reliable under coarse sampling, where sparse historical observations provide a weaker basis for estimating local feature dynamics and prediction errors can accumulate across reused steps.     For a fixed model and cache schedule, CalibCache calibrates discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature acceleration.     3.1 Feature acceleration

    Consider a diffusion or flow-matching sampler with T sampling steps, indexed by τ=0,…,T-1 in execution order from noise to data. A branch refers to a residual-producing submodule within a Transformer layer, such as an attention or MLP submodule. Let r_τ,ℓ,b^F and r_τ,ℓ,b^C denote the residual features of branch b in layer ℓ at sampling step τ along the full-compute and naive-cache trajectories, respectively. Let S denote a prescribed cache schedule that specifies which branch evaluations are skipped, and let N denote its nominal cache interval. The full-compute trajectory evaluates every branch at every step. The naive-cache trajectory follows S, evaluating branches normally at full-compute steps and directly reusing their latest full-compute residuals at cache steps. For either trajectory, suppressing the layer and branch indices, define the first- and second-order finite differences for τ≥1 and τ≥2, respectively, as

    v_τ=r_τ-r_τ-1, a_τ=Δ²r_τ=r_τ-2r_τ-1+r_τ-2.

    		(1)

    We refer to a_τ as feature acceleration. This term denotes a second finite difference of features and does not imply a continuous-time derivative. The superscripts F and C distinguish full-compute and naive-cache quantities: a_τ,ℓ,b^F and a_τ,ℓ,b^C are computed from the residual sequences of their respective trajectories using Equation (1).

    Acceleration calibration.

    We address the discrepancy between naive-cache and full-compute feature accelerations introduced by residual reuse. We fit grouped scalar maps from naive-cache accelerations to their full-compute counterparts using paired calibration trajectories. The fitted maps are then used to correct cached residuals at the first cache step of each interval. We compare acceleration supervision with residual and velocity supervision in Table 4; the fitting targets and shared deployment protocol are specified in Appendix A.4.

    We fix one conditioning signal (a text prompt or class label), initial noise, guidance, solver, and timestep schedule, then record a full-compute trajectory and a naive-cache trajectory under the prescribed cache schedule. The trajectories evolve independently; at the first cache step of each interval, accelerations computed from their respective residual sequences are paired for the same sampling step τ, layer ℓ, and branch b, as in Figure 2(a). This pairing matches the step, layer, and branch indices across trajectories, without requiring their intermediate latent states to coincide: each observation is extracted from the state reached by its own rollout.

    Centered scalar fitting.

    We group observations by sampling step and computational branch, g=G(τ,b), and share each scalar across layers and tokens in its group. Let I_g index the paired channel vectors (aⱼ^C,aⱼ^F) at corresponding layers and token positions. Each layer and token position contributes a paired vector, so a single trajectory pair supplies many observations for estimating one scalar. This sharing retains dependence on the sampling step and computational branch while restricting the fitted map to a common scale within each group. Define the group means as ā_g^⋆=|I_g|⁻¹∑_j∈I_gaⱼ^⋆ for ⋆∈{F,C}. We estimate a shared scale from centered observations:

    s_g=*arg min_s∈ℝ∑_j∈I_g∥(aⱼ^F-ā_g^F)-s(aⱼ^C-ā_g^C)∥₂².

    		(2)

    For nonzero centered input energy, the closed-form solution is

    s_g=(∑_j∈I_g⟨aⱼ^C-ā_g^C,aⱼ^F-ā_g^F⟩)/(∑_j∈I_g∥aⱼ^C-ā_g^C∥₂²).

    		(3)

    The numerator measures alignment between centered accelerations, normalized by the cached energy in the denominator. Thus, the shared scale is estimated from within-group co-variation rather than group means. The deployed map is scalar multiplication by s_g; the means are used only during fitting. We write s_g=s_τ,b for g=G(τ,b) and suppress the branch index as s_τ in Figure 2 and the online equations below. The fitted scalars remain frozen for all subsequent samples under the same deployment configuration.

    3.3 Online correction

    Let r_τ,ℓ,b^O denote the online reference residual supplied to the calibration operator, equal to the current pre-correction residual at a correction step. The preceding r_τ-1,ℓ,b^O and r_τ-2,ℓ,b^O belong to this reference sequence for the same layer and branch, while r̃_τ,ℓ,b is the corrected residual feature. The superscript O distinguishes online references from the offline full-compute (F) and naive-cache (C) trajectories. Suppressing layer and branch indices, at an eligible first cache step with two preceding references, we compute a_τ^O=Δ²r_τ^O using Equation (1). Following Figure 2(b), the frozen map gives a full-compute acceleration estimate, whose discrepancy from the reference acceleration corrects the current residual:

    â_τ^F=s_τa_τ^O, Δa_τ=â_τ^F-a_τ^O,(4)
    r̃_τ=r_τ^O+Δa_τ=r_τ^O+(s_τ-1)a_τ^O.

    Here Δa_τ is the correction discrepancy and â_τ^F is a mapped estimate, not an additional full-compute evaluation. With the preceding references fixed, adding Δa_τ changes the current residual’s second difference by the same amount. This local relation is defined relative to the reference sequence; the residual sequence actually used by the network also reflects the deployment policy. The correction remains sample-dependent through a_τ^O, while s_τ=1 leaves the current residual unchanged.

    The correction operator itself uses a three-point finite difference and elementwise scaling and addition, costing O(d) for a d-dimensional residual token. The coefficient storage is O(|G|) for step–branch groups G, with one scalar per group; runtime feature buffers are separate. The operator preserves the full/cache schedule and requires neither additional full-network evaluations nor online optimization.     4.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and benchmarks.

    We evaluate 20-step sampling at cache intervals N∈{3,4,5} on three diffusion Transformers.     The model-named baseline rows use full computation at all 20 sampling steps. Calibration and deployment details are given in Appendix A.1.

    Baselines.

    We compare CalibCache with FORA direct reuse [(Selvaraju et al., 2024)] and two history-based forecasting baselines, TaylorSeer [(Liu et al., 2025b)] and HiCache [(Feng et al., 2026)], both at order O=2. A separate predictor history records the latest full-compute anchor at every cache step, supplying the references r^O in Section 3.3 and isolating direct feedback from corrected reuse. Full-compute steps refresh both the anchor and the reuse buffer on the deployed rollout. At N=4, the final step (logical step 0) is a first cache step; we skip its correction to avoid a large terminal perturbation that could degrade image quality. Appendix A.1 lists the exact step positions.

    Metrics and efficiency.

    PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] compare each final image with the full-compute output generated from the same prompt and seed, measuring full-compute fidelity. We measure per-image denoising latency on one NVIDIA H800 GPU at batch size one, averaging 30 CUDA-event measurements after ten benchmark warmup runs. Model weights and calibration parameters are GPU-resident before timing, which excludes text encoding, VAE decoding, pack preparation, and disk I/O. FLOPs cover the same 20-step denoising-only region as latency. We use torch.profiler for profiler-visible tensor operations, including linear projections, and analytically add fused attention matrix multiplications, custom Triton correction kernels, and TaylorSeer/HiCache predictor arithmetic omitted by the profiler. Conditioning, VAE decoding, device-to-host transfer, and disk I/O are excluded for all three models. The accounting scope is specified in Appendix A.3.

    4.2 FLUX DrawBench

    Table 1 compares the deployed implementations of CalibCache, FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache. Across N=3,4,5, CalibCache achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and IR among the evaluated caching methods. It also obtains the highest CLIP score at N=4,5.

    At N=5, CalibCache increases PSNR from 17.2693 for TaylorSeer and 17.9516 for HiCache to 19.1014 and increases IR from 0.77485 and 0.84138, respectively, to 0.89891. Its denoising speedup reaches 2.86×, compared with 2.69× for TaylorSeer and 2.43× for HiCache. Across all three intervals, CalibCache is faster than TaylorSeer; its latency is comparable to HiCache at N=3 and lower at N=4,5. The reported FLOPs include the additional single-stream projections in the FLUX implementation. Table 5 further compares CalibCache with uncorrected reuse at matched full/cache positions.

    4.3 Qwen-Image DrawBench

    On Qwen-Image, CalibCache improves all five reported alignment, preference, and fidelity metrics over FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache at N=3,4,5 (Table 2). At N=5, LPIPS decreases from 0.50306 for TaylorSeer and 0.47577 for HiCache to 0.30412, corresponding to reductions of 39.5% and 36.1%. ImageReward increases from 0.45596 and 0.52504, respectively, to 1.00084. CalibCache also has lower denoising latency than both TaylorSeer and HiCache at every interval, reaching 2.27× speedup at N=5 versus 2.01× and 1.80×, respectively.

    4.4 DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256

    Table 3 evaluates class-conditional generation under the unified deployment policy in Section 4.1. Each CalibCache setting uses one calibration trajectory pair. Across N=3,4,5, CalibCache outperforms FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache on all five reported distributional metrics. At N=5, FID decreases from 16.3916 for TaylorSeer and 24.1568 for HiCache to 10.3691, while sFID decreases from 17.5930 and 26.8663, respectively, to 6.4061.

    CalibCache is also faster than both TaylorSeer and HiCache at all three intervals, reaching 1.81× speedup at N=5 compared with 1.64× and 1.21×, respectively. FORA offers higher speedup but has substantially worse FID and sFID.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：采样步数越少、网格越粗，基于历史的外推就越不可靠。

要点：

  • 矛盾：扩散 transformer 采样开销大，**特征缓存**能减少完整网络评估次数，但在**短采样计划**下误差会变得更严重
  • 原因是结构性的：完整计算步更少、采样网格更粗，导致**基于历史的外推**不可靠
  • CalibCache 提出一种**轻量离线校准**方法，把缓存结果对齐到完整计算的动态，从而在少步设置下保持质量

为什么值得看：实时渲染与实时生成的交集就是「少步 + 缓存」，而这两者叠在一起最容易崩。一次离线校准换来少步下的可用性，是可插进现有 DiT 管线的最小改动。

中文摘要：扩散 transformer 能生成高质量图像，但迭代采样仍然昂贵。特征缓存可以减少完整网络评估的次数，问题在于它的近似误差在短采样计划下会更严重：完整计算步更少、采样网格更粗，使基于历史的外推变得不可靠。CalibCache 因此提出一种轻量的离线校准方法，把缓存得到的特征动态校准到完整计算的特征动态上，从而在少步设置下维持质量。对需要把扩散模型压进实时预算的管线，这类「一次性离线校准 + 运行时缓存」的组合是最小侵入的加速方式。

    		(1)

    We refer to a_τ as feature acceleration. This term denotes a second finite difference of features and does not imply a continuous-time derivative. The superscripts F and C distinguish full-compute and naive-cache quantities: a_τ,ℓ,b^F and a_τ,ℓ,b^C are computed from the residual sequences of their respective trajectories using Equation (1).

    Acceleration calibration.

    We address the discrepancy between naive-cache and full-compute feature accelerations introduced by residual reuse. We fit grouped scalar maps from naive-cache accelerations to their full-compute counterparts using paired calibration trajectories. The fitted maps are then used to correct cached residuals at the first cache step of each interval. We compare acceleration supervision with residual and velocity supervision in Table 4; the fitting targets and shared deployment protocol are specified in Appendix A.4.

    3.2 Offline calibration

    We fix one conditioning signal (a text prompt or class label), initial noise, guidance, solver, and timestep schedule, then record a full-compute trajectory and a naive-cache trajectory under the prescribed cache schedule. The trajectories evolve independently; at the first cache step of each interval, accelerations computed from their respective residual sequences are paired for the same sampling step τ, layer ℓ, and branch b, as in Figure 2(a). This pairing matches the step, layer, and branch indices across trajectories, without requiring their intermediate latent states to coincide: each observation is extracted from the state reached by its own rollout.

    Centered scalar fitting.

    We group observations by sampling step and computational branch, g=G(τ,b), and share each scalar across layers and tokens in its group. Let I_g index the paired channel vectors (aⱼ^C,aⱼ^F) at corresponding layers and token positions. Each layer and token position contributes a paired vector, so a single trajectory pair supplies many observations for estimating one scalar. This sharing retains dependence on the sampling step and computational branch while restricting the fitted map to a common scale within each group. Define the group means as ā_g^⋆=|I_g|⁻¹∑_j∈I_gaⱼ^⋆ for ⋆∈{F,C}. We estimate a shared scale from centered observations:

    s_g=*arg min_s∈ℝ∑_j∈I_g∥(aⱼ^F-ā_g^F)-s(aⱼ^C-ā_g^C)∥₂².

    		(2)

    For nonzero centered input energy, the closed-form solution is

    s_g=(∑_j∈I_g⟨aⱼ^C-ā_g^C,aⱼ^F-ā_g^F⟩)/(∑_j∈I_g∥aⱼ^C-ā_g^C∥₂²).

    		(3)

    The numerator measures alignment between centered accelerations, normalized by the cached energy in the denominator. Thus, the shared scale is estimated from within-group co-variation rather than group means. The deployed map is scalar multiplication by s_g; the means are used only during fitting. We write s_g=s_τ,b for g=G(τ,b) and suppress the branch index as s_τ in Figure 2 and the online equations below. The fitted scalars remain frozen for all subsequent samples under the same deployment configuration.

    3.3 Online correction

    Let r_τ,ℓ,b^O denote the online reference residual supplied to the calibration operator, equal to the current pre-correction residual at a correction step. The preceding r_τ-1,ℓ,b^O and r_τ-2,ℓ,b^O belong to this reference sequence for the same layer and branch, while r̃_τ,ℓ,b is the corrected residual feature. The superscript O distinguishes online references from the offline full-compute (F) and naive-cache (C) trajectories. Suppressing layer and branch indices, at an eligible first cache step with two preceding references, we compute a_τ^O=Δ²r_τ^O using Equation (1). Following Figure 2(b), the frozen map gives a full-compute acceleration estimate, whose discrepancy from the reference acceleration corrects the current residual:

    â_τ^F=s_τa_τ^O, Δa_τ=â_τ^F-a_τ^O,(4)
    r̃_τ=r_τ^O+Δa_τ=r_τ^O+(s_τ-1)a_τ^O.

    Here Δa_τ is the correction discrepancy and â_τ^F is a mapped estimate, not an additional full-compute evaluation. With the preceding references fixed, adding Δa_τ changes the current residual’s second difference by the same amount. This local relation is defined relative to the reference sequence; the residual sequence actually used by the network also reflects the deployment policy. The correction remains sample-dependent through a_τ^O, while s_τ=1 leaves the current residual unchanged.

    The correction operator itself uses a three-point finite difference and elementwise scaling and addition, costing O(d) for a d-dimensional residual token. The coefficient storage is O(|G|) for step–branch groups G, with one scalar per group; runtime feature buffers are separate. The operator preserves the full/cache schedule and requires neither additional full-network evaluations nor online optimization. Implementation details and deployment-policy analyses are provided in Section 4 and Appendix A.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and benchmarks.

    We evaluate 20-step sampling at cache intervals N∈{3,4,5} on three diffusion Transformers. FLUX.1-dev [(Black Forest Labs, 2024)] uses shifted flow-matching steps and guidance 3.5; Qwen-Image [(Wu and others, 2025)] uses true classifier-free guidance (CFG) 4.0. Both text-to-image models are evaluated on DrawBench-200 [(Saharia et al., 2022)] at 1024² resolution. DiT-XL/2 [(Peebles and Xie, 2023)] is evaluated on ImageNet-256 using DDIM-20 [(Song et al., 2021)], CFG 1.5, and 50K generated images per configuration. Each model–interval configuration uses one calibration condition (a COCO [(Lin et al., 2014)] caption disjoint from evaluation prompts, or a class label) and fixed initial noise to generate a full-compute/naive-cache trajectory pair. The centered estimator in Equation (3) fits one scalar per correction step and branch, reused across the entire evaluation set.

    The model-named baseline rows use full computation at all 20 sampling steps. Calibration and deployment details are given in Appendix A.1.

    Baselines.

    We compare CalibCache with FORA direct reuse [(Selvaraju et al., 2024)] and two history-based forecasting baselines, TaylorSeer [(Liu et al., 2025b)] and HiCache [(Feng et al., 2026)], both at order O=2. HiCache uses the authors’ official scaled-Hermite predictor (commit 4d0839f) with scale 0.6.

    Unified deployment policy.

    Across all three models, TaylorSeer, HiCache, and CalibCache share the same full/cache schedule: warmup-2 at N=3 and warmup-3 at N=4,5, followed by full evaluations every N steps from the last warmup step. FORA instead refreshes every N steps from the initial full-compute step, without extra warmup. CalibCache applies Equation (4) only at the first cache step of each interval, writes the corrected residual into the reuse buffer, and reuses it until the next full-compute step. A separate predictor history records the latest full-compute anchor at every cache step, supplying the references r^O in Section 3.3 and isolating direct feedback from corrected reuse. Full-compute steps refresh both the anchor and the reuse buffer on the deployed rollout. At N=4, the final step (logical step 0) is a first cache step; we skip its correction to avoid a large terminal perturbation that could degrade image quality. Appendix A.1 lists the exact step positions.

    Metrics and efficiency.

    PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS [(Zhang et al., 2018)] compare each final image with the full-compute output generated from the same prompt and seed, measuring full-compute fidelity. CLIP [(Radford et al., 2021)] and ImageReward (IR) [(Xu et al., 2023)] assess semantic alignment and learned human-preference scores, respectively. For DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, we report FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)], sFID, IS, precision, and recall. We measure per-image denoising latency on one NVIDIA H800 GPU at batch size one, averaging 30 CUDA-event measurements after ten benchmark warmup runs. Model weights and calibration parameters are GPU-resident before timing, which excludes text encoding, VAE decoding, pack preparation, and disk I/O. FLOPs cover the same 20-step denoising-only region as latency. We use torch.profiler for profiler-visible tensor operations, including linear projections, and analytically add fused attention matrix multiplications, custom Triton correction kernels, and TaylorSeer/HiCache predictor arithmetic omitted by the profiler. Conditioning, VAE decoding, device-to-host transfer, and disk I/O are excluded for all three models. The accounting scope is specified in Appendix A.3.

    4.2 FLUX DrawBench

    Table 1 compares the deployed implementations of CalibCache, FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache. Across N=3,4,5, CalibCache achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and IR among the evaluated caching methods. It also obtains the highest CLIP score at N=4,5.

    At N=5, CalibCache increases PSNR from 17.2693 for TaylorSeer and 17.9516 for HiCache to 19.1014 and increases IR from 0.77485 and 0.84138, respectively, to 0.89891. Its denoising speedup reaches 2.86×, compared with 2.69× for TaylorSeer and 2.43× for HiCache. Across all three intervals, CalibCache is faster than TaylorSeer; its latency is comparable to HiCache at N=3 and lower at N=4,5. The reported FLOPs include the additional single-stream projections in the FLUX implementation. Table 5 further compares CalibCache with uncorrected reuse at matched full/cache positions.

    4.3 Qwen-Image DrawBench

    On Qwen-Image, CalibCache improves all five reported alignment, preference, and fidelity metrics over FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache at N=3,4,5 (Table 2). At N=5, LPIPS decreases from 0.50306 for TaylorSeer and 0.47577 for HiCache to 0.30412, corresponding to reductions of 39.5% and 36.1%. ImageReward increases from 0.45596 and 0.52504, respectively, to 1.00084. CalibCache also has lower denoising latency than both TaylorSeer and HiCache at every interval, reaching 2.27× speedup at N=5 versus 2.01× and 1.80×, respectively.

    4.4 DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256

    Table 3 evaluates class-conditional generation under the unified deployment policy in Section 4.1. Each CalibCache setting uses one calibration trajectory pair. Across N=3,4,5, CalibCache outperforms FORA, TaylorSeer, and HiCache on all five reported distributional metrics. At N=5, FID decreases from 16.3916 for TaylorSeer and 24.1568 for HiCache to 10.3691, while sFID decreases from 17.5930 and 26.8663, respectively, to 6.4061.

    CalibCache is also faster than both TaylorSeer and HiCache at all three intervals, reaching 1.81× speedup at N=5 compared with 1.64× and 1.21×, respectively. FORA offers higher speedup but has substantially worse FID and sFID.

item.title: 第三人称转第一人称要能「直播」：StreamEgo 解决操作区域劣化与固定片段两头的毛病 ｜ StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
item.description:
一句话：做成流式才能支撑实时应用，但现有方法在操作区域劣化、过拟合，且被固定长度片段与高延迟卡住。

要点：

  • 用途明确：外中心→自我中心（Exo2Ego）视频生成把第三人称录像转成第一人称视角，可支撑沉浸式 AR/VR 体验，并为具身机器人**规模化合成演示**
  • 做成流式才能支撑实时应用，但现有方法有三处问题：**操作区域劣化**、过拟合，以及被**固定长度片段与高延迟**限制
  • StreamEgo 因此面向流式设置重新设计，目标是持续、低延迟地生成第一人称视角

为什么值得看：「同一次演示，一次拍摄，多视角复用」对 VR 录制与机器人数据合成都有价值。把固定长度片段的限制去掉、改成流式，才可能进直播或实时管线。

中文摘要：外中心到自我中心（Exo2Ego）的视频生成把第三人称录像转换为第一人称视角，可用于沉浸式 AR/VR 体验，也能为具身机器人规模化合成演示数据。把它扩展到流式设置，本应进一步支撑实时应用；但已有方法存在三个问题：操作区域质量劣化、过拟合，以及被固定长度的片段与过高的延迟限制。StreamEgo 因此针对流式场景重新设计这一任务，目标是持续、低延迟地生成第一人称视角画面，从而让这项能力从离线工具走向实时应用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-23

StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

Abstract

Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

1 Introduction

Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation [(Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2026)] converts third-person recordings into dynamic first-person viewpoints. For embodied AI, Exo2Ego unlocks massive web-scale video repositories as a scalable and diverse data source. Real-time streaming Exo2Ego further extends this capability to live applications such as AR-based tutorials and surgical demonstrations.

To achieve accurate Exo2Ego video generation, recent studies [(Kang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025)] formulate Exo2Ego by decomposing the egocentric canvas into three functional regimes (Fig. 1:Left): the hand-object interaction area (H), the shared view (S), and the unseen view (U). By leveraging geometric reprojections from the exocentric view to construct appearance priors, existing methods [(Kang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)] achieve robust alignment and satisfactory visual fidelity in S.

However, they fall short across the remaining domains. Firstly, accurate hand-object interaction remains challenging in H, as projective geometric priors break down under complex foreground dynamics, while existing mask- [(Xu et al., 2025)] or pose-based [(Park et al., 2026)] remedies are fragile due to their reliance on ground-truth first-frame or noisy hand pose estimates (Fig. 1:Right, red box). Meanwhile, existing approaches suffer from benchmark memorization on paired datasets [(Grauman et al., 2024)], artificially replicating ground-truth details in U and impairing generalization (Fig. 1:Right, yellow box). Finally, existing methods rely on full-sequence offline scanning for appearance priors [(Shi et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)] and full-sequence bidirectional attention, implicitly assuming access to future frames. This non-causal paradigm is fundamentally incompatible with streaming, where the future is unknown (Fig. 1:Right, 0.08 FPS).

In this paper, we propose StreamEgo, a real-time, streaming, and generalizable framework for Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve fine-grained manipulation in H under the streaming setting, we establish a pixel-aligned conditioning scheme via streaming dual-branch priors. A dynamic ego prior maintains an incremental 3D world cache for the static background and tracks moving entities to render ego-aligned appearance anchors, while a human pose prior provides structural guidance for hand interactions. To improve the quality in U, we propose a region-aware training curriculum. It progressively shifts the optimization focus from S to U and then to H. This curriculum stabilizes training while improving generalization. To support streaming under a causal setting, we adapt a chunk-wise autoregressive architecture, where each chunk is generated only from past chunks, and distill the diffusion backbone into a high-throughput causal student with 3 steps. This removes the reliance on full-sequence offline scanning and bidirectional attention. Meanwhile, we propose a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum to improve the quality for the streaming rollouts. As a result, StreamEgo can process unbounded exocentric video streams and generate high-quality egocentric videos at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present StreamEgo, the first streaming framework for Exo2Ego video generation, reformulating the task from full-sequence generation to causal generation.

  • •

    We introduce a streaming dual-branch prior and a region-aware training curriculum, which respectively improve interaction fidelity in H and generalization in U.

  • •

    We introduce a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enhancing the visual quality for StreamEgo, achieving high-quality real-time Exo2Ego generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

    Paired Exo-Ego datasets [(Grauman et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2021; Sener et al., 2022)] have catalyzed exocentric-to-egocentric synthesis. Early attempts simplify the setup via multi-view inputs [(Liu et al., 2024; Mahdi et al., 2025)], initial ego guidance [(Xu et al., 2025)], or static image translation [(Park et al., 2026)]. Concurrently, novel-view synthesis methods inject camera encodings [(Bai et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025)] or condition on rendered 3D/4D geometry [(Ren et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025; Bahmani et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026)], but falter under extreme perspective shifts. Structured conditions, such as sketches for video instance repainting [(Weng et al., 2025b)], multi-stream audio cues for temporal control [(Weng et al., 2025a)], and latitude/longitude-aware mechanisms for 360∘ generation [(Xia et al., 2025)], have also proven effective in steering video diffusion models toward precise spatial and temporal control. Recent single-exo works incorporate geometry guidance [(Kang et al., 2026)] or semantic grounding [(Wang et al., 2026)], yet uniform canvas supervision causes benchmark memorization and hand drift across short, fixed-length clips. In contrast, StreamEgo addresses these problems with streaming dual-branch priors and region-aware curriculum scheduling, enabling generalizable, real-time streaming synthesis.

    2.2 Streaming Video Generation Models

    To break the temporal limits of short-clip diffusion, training-free noise rescheduling [(Qiu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024)] and training-based autoregressive conditioning [(Chen et al., 2024; Ruhe et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025)] have been proposed to mitigate exposure bias. Subsequent frameworks scale temporal length via predictive modelling, long-context architectures, and causal forcing [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Gu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2026)]. Streaming generation has also been extended to joint audio-video synthesis, now with a dedicated benchmark [(Liu et al., 2026a)], and to panoramic world models for language-guided navigation [(Liu et al., 2026b)]. However, these methods focus on text-, audio-, or action-conditioned generation rather than asymmetric cross-view streaming. Built upon streaming long-video designs and few-step distillation paradigms [(Yuan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2025)], StreamEgo achieves chunk-wise autoregressive modelling for the Exo2Ego task.

    2.3 Video World Models for Embodied Learning

    Video world models facilitate embodied learning via interactive simulation [(Yang et al., 2023)], recently extended to multiple agents [(Cai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026)], visual planning [(Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024)], and synthetic demonstrations [(Bharadhwaj et al., 2024)]. Subsequent methods couple video with action prediction [(Li et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c)], adapt video priors via inverse dynamics [(Feng et al., 2025)], or incorporate causal history for online control [(Li et al., 2026a)]. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models are being developed on modular open-source codebases [(StarVLA Community, 2026)] and extended with spatial memory [(Li et al., 2026b)] and fast reflexive control [(Guo et al., 2026)]; like world models, they rely on large-scale embodied demonstrations. Although cross-view conversion can furnish training data for egocentric world models [(Tran et al., 2026)], synthesizing continuous, structurally faithful streams remains challenging. StreamEgo bridges this gap by streaming third-person observations into structurally consistent egocentric trajectories, providing scalable first-person training data for embodied AI.

    3 Method

    Given an input exocentric video stream along with known exocentric and target egocentric camera intrinsics, and the target egocentric camera trajectory, the goal for StreamEgo is to synthesize the corresponding egocentric video from the target viewpoint with the same frame rate as the input.

    We develop StreamEgo in three stages: formulating streaming priors (Sec. 3.1), building the base system with the priors (Sec. 3.2), and making the system real-time (Sec. 3.3).

    3.1 Streaming Dual-Branch Priors

    Exo2Ego is intrinsically underconstrained because of extreme perspective disparities. This challenge is worse in H, where motion is rapid and occlusions are frequent. The model therefore benefits from pixel-aligned conditions that provide visual context and structural guidance. At the same time, practical online deployment requires these conditions to be built causally and in a streaming manner. To this end, we introduce streaming dual-branch priors (Fig. 2a): (1) a streaming dynamic ego prior for appearance cues, paired with (2) a streaming human pose prior for structural guidance.

    Streaming dynamic ego prior. Unlike existing methods [(Kang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026)] that rely on offline, full-video inputs with prohibitive latency, we introduce a streaming geometric conditioning scheme to construct causal pixel-aligned visual priors in real-time.

    As is shown in Fig. 2a, we decouple the environment into persistent static background surfaces and transient interaction geometry, following CamDirector [(Shi et al., 2026)]. Using the stationary exocentric camera, each rectified pixel corresponds to a fixed physical ray in world space. We maintain an incremental, ray-indexed 3D world cache that stores the first valid depth and color observed along each ray. The cache updates at sparse keyframes. MoGe-2 [(Wang et al., 2025b)] predicts metric depth, while SAM3.1 [(Meta AI, 2026)] segments dynamic entities to isolate the interaction region. Static rays outside dynamic masks are committed to the cache and remain fixed once initialized. Depth is propagated via backward optical flow between keyframes.

    At frame t, the retrieved static background points Aₜ and the current dynamic foreground points Dₜ are unified in world space. The ego-aligned prior Pₜ is synthesized via:

    Pₜ=ℝ_ℂ_g,t(T_g,t⁻¹(Aₜ∪Dₜ)),

    		(1)

    where T_g,t is the transformation from target egocentric coordinates to world space, and ℝ_ℂ_g,t is a calibrated splatting renderer parameterized by target camera intrinsics ℂ_g,t. This formulation provides stable anchors for region S and dynamic visual cues for contacts in H in a streaming fashion.

    Streaming human pose prior. While dynamic ego priors supply visual context, accurately synthesizing complex interactions in H requires explicit structural guidance [(Park et al., 2026)]. Prior attempts either rely on ground-truth egocentric first frames for interaction masks [(Xu et al., 2025)], or condition directly on isolated hand poses [(Park et al., 2026)]; the latter induces severe spatial misalignment on the egocentric canvas because monocular depth estimation on small, dynamic hand regions is highly ill-posed. Inspired by human proprioception, we introduce skeletal constraints by kinematically bonding hand estimation to the upper-body pose.

    At sampled exocentric frames, SMPLer-X [(Cai et al., 2023)] estimates and ViTPose [(Xu et al., 2022)] refines full-body topology and upper-limb joints. Wrist joints derived from the upper-body chain define zoom-in bounding boxes for WiLoR [(Potamias et al., 2025)] to recover wrist-relative finger articulation. For each hand s∈{L,R} (left and right) at frame t, the predicted j-th local finger joint Ĵˢ_t,j is kinematically anchored to the refined 3D wrist joint position Bˢ_t,wrist:

    Jˢ_t,j=Bˢ_t,wrist+(Ĵˢ_t,j-Ĵˢ_t,root), s∈{L,R},

    		(2)

    where Ĵˢ_t,root is the canonical root position of the predicted hand model. This locks the hand’s global coordinate to the physical arm chain Bˢ_t,wrist while preserving local finger articulation. Bˢ_t,wrist is obtained in the calibrated exocentric camera frame by anchoring the root-relative 3D skeleton of SMPLer-X [(Cai et al., 2023)] to the known 3D position of the egocentric camera cₜ (Eq. 1) and fitting its metric scale via 2D reprojection against the ViTPose [(Xu et al., 2022)] keypoints (Appendix D.1). The resulting upper-limb skeletons are causally interpolated and rasterized into both exocentric and egocentric views as skeletal guidance maps (Qᵉₜ,Qᵍₜ) using calibrated camera parameters ℂ, with joint confidence scores modulating stroke intensities to suppress hallucinated joints.

    3.2 Bidirectional Teacher

    With the streaming dual-branch priors established, we construct the teacher model with bidirectional attention to master Exo2Ego [(Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2026)]. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, all visual inputs and condition priors are encoded into latent representations via a frozen video VAE. Following EgoX [(Kang et al., 2026)], we concatenate the streaming priors with video latents along the channel dimension for pixel-aligned conditioning, while concatenating the clean exocentric video and the noisy egocentric latent along the width dimension. The composite latents are then fed into a pretrained Wan backbone. The model is trained using LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] with our proposed region-aware training curriculum.

    Region-aware loss weight scheduling. Uniform supervision across the egocentric canvas is suboptimal due to disparate learning difficulties across functional domains: S offers stable visual anchors, U requires plausible completion vulnerable to overfitting, and H exhibits complex dynamics that destabilize early training. We therefore propose a region-aware curriculum (Fig. 2b): first anchoring cross-view alignment in S, gradually introducing completion in U, and finally ramping up supervision in H to refine manipulation fidelity.

    Let r_S(p),r_U(p),r_H(p)∈{0,1} denote binary regional indicators on the egocentric latent grid Ω_g. At training progress u∈[0,1], the unnormalized spatial weight at position p is linearly combined as aᵤ(p)=∑_r∈{S,U,H}wᵣ(u)rᵣ(p), where wᵣ(u) follows the region-aware curriculum. To stabilize gradient scales, we normalize aᵤ(p) across the canvas into ωᵤ(p)=aᵤ(p)/((1)/(|Ω_g|)∑_q∈Ω_gaᵤ(q)+δ) (δ>0). Denoting the flow-matching prediction error as e_σ(p), our training objective is:

    L=𝔼[(1)/(|Ω_g|)∑_p∈Ω_gωᵤ(p)e_σ(p)].

    		(3)

    3.3 Real-Time Autoregression

    To enable streaming from our bidirectional teacher, we adapt the framework into a causal, chunk-wise autoregressive student distilled for few-step inference. Following Helios [(Yuan et al., 2026)], this adaptation proceeds in three stages: causal attention across chunks, pyramid token compression, and few-step distillation with DMD [(Yin et al., 2024b)] and adversarial training (Appendix D.3). As illustrated in Fig. 3, the video stream is processed chunk by chunk; the k-th chunk (which denotes the current chunk) is denoised via intra-chunk bidirectional attention conditioned on current-chunk priors (Sec. 3.1) and a historical memory buffer Mₖ which maintains exclusively clean egocentric latents from past chunks and compresses distant context via multi-term memory patchification [(Yuan et al., 2026)]. To address Exo2Ego task-specific challenges in autoregressive training, we introduce two dedicated strategies: region-aware corruption to mitigate exposure bias and motion drift in H, and a first-chunk curriculum to handle the initial chunk without historical conditioning, improving the student’s rollout robustness in U.

    Region-aware corruption. The exposure bias induced by teacher forcing is highly uneven across regions: S is continuously anchored through the proposed streaming dynamic ego prior, resilient to drift. By contrast, the dynamic and complex nature of region H makes it susceptible to self-occlusions and motion blur, under which the streaming priors can degrade. In such unconstrained cases, synthesis in H refers to historical context and thus prone to error accumulation.

    We inject stochastic perturbations into H on historical latents zₜᵍ∈Mₖ:

    z̃ₜᵍ=zₜᵍ+bₜmₜ^H⊙εₜ,

    L_critic=L_reg(D_ψ)+λ_DL_adv^D(G_φ,D_ψ)+λ_RL_R1(D_ψ),

    where L_DMD aligns the generative distribution, and the adversarial objective with discriminator D_ψ sharpens fine details. We refer the readers to the Appendix for more details.

    Training. We train both our bidirectional teacher and autoregressive student on 4,400 curated clips from Ego-Exo4D [(Grauman et al., 2024)], with each clip spanning 5 seconds at 24 FPS. (2024)]). We evaluate only qualitatively on Assembly101 [(Sener et al., 2022)], as its egocentric views provide only monochromatic ground truth within a single indoor scene.

Other related works [(Xu et al., 2025; Mahdi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2026)] are omitted since they are not open-source.

一句话：做成流式才能支撑实时应用，但现有方法在操作区域劣化、过拟合，且被固定长度片段与高延迟卡住。

要点：

  • 用途明确：外中心→自我中心（Exo2Ego）视频生成把第三人称录像转成第一人称视角，可支撑沉浸式 AR/VR 体验，并为具身机器人**规模化合成演示**
  • 做成流式才能支撑实时应用，但现有方法有三处问题：**操作区域劣化**、过拟合，以及被**固定长度片段与高延迟**限制
  • StreamEgo 因此面向流式设置重新设计，目标是持续、低延迟地生成第一人称视角

为什么值得看：「同一次演示，一次拍摄，多视角复用」对 VR 录制与机器人数据合成都有价值。把固定长度片段的限制去掉、改成流式，才可能进直播或实时管线。

中文摘要：外中心到自我中心（Exo2Ego）的视频生成把第三人称录像转换为第一人称视角，可用于沉浸式 AR/VR 体验，也能为具身机器人规模化合成演示数据。把它扩展到流式设置，本应进一步支撑实时应用；但已有方法存在三个问题：操作区域质量劣化、过拟合，以及被固定长度的片段与过高的延迟限制。StreamEgo 因此针对流式场景重新设计这一任务，目标是持续、低延迟地生成第一人称视角画面，从而让这项能力从离线工具走向实时应用。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-20

本期推送：2026-11-23

StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

Abstract

Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

1 Introduction

Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation [(Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2026)] converts third-person recordings into dynamic first-person viewpoints. For embodied AI, Exo2Ego unlocks massive web-scale video repositories as a scalable and diverse data source. Real-time streaming Exo2Ego further extends this capability to live applications such as AR-based tutorials and surgical demonstrations.

To achieve accurate Exo2Ego video generation, recent studies [(Kang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2025)] formulate Exo2Ego by decomposing the egocentric canvas into three functional regimes (Fig. 1:Left): the hand-object interaction area (H), the shared view (S), and the unseen view (U). By leveraging geometric reprojections from the exocentric view to construct appearance priors, existing methods [(Kang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)] achieve robust alignment and satisfactory visual fidelity in S.

However, they fall short across the remaining domains. Firstly, accurate hand-object interaction remains challenging in H, as projective geometric priors break down under complex foreground dynamics, while existing mask- [(Xu et al., 2025)] or pose-based [(Park et al., 2026)] remedies are fragile due to their reliance on ground-truth first-frame or noisy hand pose estimates (Fig. 1:Right, red box). Meanwhile, existing approaches suffer from benchmark memorization on paired datasets [(Grauman et al., 2024)], artificially replicating ground-truth details in U and impairing generalization (Fig. 1:Right, yellow box). Finally, existing methods rely on full-sequence offline scanning for appearance priors [(Shi et al., 2026; Kang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026)] and full-sequence bidirectional attention, implicitly assuming access to future frames. This non-causal paradigm is fundamentally incompatible with streaming, where the future is unknown (Fig. 1:Right, 0.08 FPS).

In this paper, we propose StreamEgo, a real-time, streaming, and generalizable framework for Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve fine-grained manipulation in H under the streaming setting, we establish a pixel-aligned conditioning scheme via streaming dual-branch priors. A dynamic ego prior maintains an incremental 3D world cache for the static background and tracks moving entities to render ego-aligned appearance anchors, while a human pose prior provides structural guidance for hand interactions. To improve the quality in U, we propose a region-aware training curriculum. It progressively shifts the optimization focus from S to U and then to H. This curriculum stabilizes training while improving generalization. To support streaming under a causal setting, we adapt a chunk-wise autoregressive architecture, where each chunk is generated only from past chunks, and distill the diffusion backbone into a high-throughput causal student with 3 steps. This removes the reliance on full-sequence offline scanning and bidirectional attention. Meanwhile, we propose a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum to improve the quality for the streaming rollouts. As a result, StreamEgo can process unbounded exocentric video streams and generate high-quality egocentric videos at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We present StreamEgo, the first streaming framework for Exo2Ego video generation, reformulating the task from full-sequence generation to causal generation.

  • •

    We introduce a streaming dual-branch prior and a region-aware training curriculum, which respectively improve interaction fidelity in H and generalization in U.

  • •

    We introduce a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enhancing the visual quality for StreamEgo, achieving high-quality real-time Exo2Ego generation.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation

    Paired Exo-Ego datasets [(Grauman et al., 2024; Kwon et al., 2021; Sener et al., 2022)] have catalyzed exocentric-to-egocentric synthesis. Early attempts simplify the setup via multi-view inputs [(Liu et al., 2024; Mahdi et al., 2025)], initial ego guidance [(Xu et al., 2025)], or static image translation [(Park et al., 2026)]. Concurrently, novel-view synthesis methods inject camera encodings [(Bai et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2025)] or condition on rendered 3D/4D geometry [(Ren et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2025; Bahmani et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026)], but falter under extreme perspective shifts. Structured conditions, such as sketches for video instance repainting [(Weng et al., 2025b)], multi-stream audio cues for temporal control [(Weng et al., 2025a)], and latitude/longitude-aware mechanisms for 360∘ generation [(Xia et al., 2025)], have also proven effective in steering video diffusion models toward precise spatial and temporal control. Recent single-exo works incorporate geometry guidance [(Kang et al., 2026)] or semantic grounding [(Wang et al., 2026)], yet uniform canvas supervision causes benchmark memorization and hand drift across short, fixed-length clips. In contrast, StreamEgo addresses these problems with streaming dual-branch priors and region-aware curriculum scheduling, enabling generalizable, real-time streaming synthesis.

    2.2 Streaming Video Generation Models

    To break the temporal limits of short-clip diffusion, training-free noise rescheduling [(Qiu et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024)] and training-based autoregressive conditioning [(Chen et al., 2024; Ruhe et al., 2024; Sun et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025)] have been proposed to mitigate exposure bias. Subsequent frameworks scale temporal length via predictive modelling, long-context architectures, and causal forcing [(Zhang et al., 2025b; Gu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2026)]. Streaming generation has also been extended to joint audio-video synthesis, now with a dedicated benchmark [(Liu et al., 2026a)], and to panoramic world models for language-guided navigation [(Liu et al., 2026b)]. However, these methods focus on text-, audio-, or action-conditioned generation rather than asymmetric cross-view streaming. Built upon streaming long-video designs and few-step distillation paradigms [(Yuan et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a; Yin et al., 2025)], StreamEgo achieves chunk-wise autoregressive modelling for the Exo2Ego task.

    2.3 Video World Models for Embodied Learning

    Video world models facilitate embodied learning via interactive simulation [(Yang et al., 2023)], recently extended to multiple agents [(Cai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026)], visual planning [(Du et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024)], and synthetic demonstrations [(Bharadhwaj et al., 2024)]. Subsequent methods couple video with action prediction [(Li et al., 2025b; Zhu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026c)], adapt video priors via inverse dynamics [(Feng et al., 2025)], or incorporate causal history for online control [(Li et al., 2026a)]. In parallel, vision-language-action (VLA) models are being developed on modular open-source codebases [(StarVLA Community, 2026)] and extended with spatial memory [(Li et al., 2026b)] and fast reflexive control [(Guo et al., 2026)]; like world models, they rely on large-scale embodied demonstrations. Although cross-view conversion can furnish training data for egocentric world models [(Tran et al., 2026)], synthesizing continuous, structurally faithful streams remains challenging. StreamEgo bridges this gap by streaming third-person observations into structurally consistent egocentric trajectories, providing scalable first-person training data for embodied AI.

    3 Method

    Given an input exocentric video stream along with known exocentric and target egocentric camera intrinsics, and the target egocentric camera trajectory, the goal for StreamEgo is to synthesize the corresponding egocentric video from the target viewpoint with the same frame rate as the input.

    We develop StreamEgo in three stages: formulating streaming priors (Sec. 3.1), building the base system with the priors (Sec. 3.2), and making the system real-time (Sec. 3.3).

    3.1 Streaming Dual-Branch Priors

    Exo2Ego is intrinsically underconstrained because of extreme perspective disparities. This challenge is worse in H, where motion is rapid and occlusions are frequent. The model therefore benefits from pixel-aligned conditions that provide visual context and structural guidance. At the same time, practical online deployment requires these conditions to be built causally and in a streaming manner. To this end, we introduce streaming dual-branch priors (Fig. 2a): (1) a streaming dynamic ego prior for appearance cues, paired with (2) a streaming human pose prior for structural guidance.

    Streaming dynamic ego prior. Unlike existing methods [(Kang et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026)] that rely on offline, full-video inputs with prohibitive latency, we introduce a streaming geometric conditioning scheme to construct causal pixel-aligned visual priors in real-time.

    As is shown in Fig. 2a, we decouple the environment into persistent static background surfaces and transient interaction geometry, following CamDirector [(Shi et al., 2026)]. Using the stationary exocentric camera, each rectified pixel corresponds to a fixed physical ray in world space. We maintain an incremental, ray-indexed 3D world cache that stores the first valid depth and color observed along each ray. The cache updates at sparse keyframes. MoGe-2 [(Wang et al., 2025b)] predicts metric depth, while SAM3.1 [(Meta AI, 2026)] segments dynamic entities to isolate the interaction region. Static rays outside dynamic masks are committed to the cache and remain fixed once initialized. Depth is propagated via backward optical flow between keyframes.

    At frame t, the retrieved static background points Aₜ and the current dynamic foreground points Dₜ are unified in world space. The ego-aligned prior Pₜ is synthesized via:

    Pₜ=ℝ_ℂ_g,t(T_g,t⁻¹(Aₜ∪Dₜ)),

    		(1)

    where T_g,t is the transformation from target egocentric coordinates to world space, and ℝ_ℂ_g,t is a calibrated splatting renderer parameterized by target camera intrinsics ℂ_g,t. This formulation provides stable anchors for region S and dynamic visual cues for contacts in H in a streaming fashion.

    Streaming human pose prior. While dynamic ego priors supply visual context, accurately synthesizing complex interactions in H requires explicit structural guidance [(Park et al., 2026)]. Prior attempts either rely on ground-truth egocentric first frames for interaction masks [(Xu et al., 2025)], or condition directly on isolated hand poses [(Park et al., 2026)]; the latter induces severe spatial misalignment on the egocentric canvas because monocular depth estimation on small, dynamic hand regions is highly ill-posed. Inspired by human proprioception, we introduce skeletal constraints by kinematically bonding hand estimation to the upper-body pose.

    At sampled exocentric frames, SMPLer-X [(Cai et al., 2023)] estimates and ViTPose [(Xu et al., 2022)] refines full-body topology and upper-limb joints. Wrist joints derived from the upper-body chain define zoom-in bounding boxes for WiLoR [(Potamias et al., 2025)] to recover wrist-relative finger articulation. For each hand s∈{L,R} (left and right) at frame t, the predicted j-th local finger joint Ĵˢ_t,j is kinematically anchored to the refined 3D wrist joint position Bˢ_t,wrist:

    Jˢ_t,j=Bˢ_t,wrist+(Ĵˢ_t,j-Ĵˢ_t,root), s∈{L,R},

    		(2)

    where Ĵˢ_t,root is the canonical root position of the predicted hand model. Bˢ_t,wrist is obtained in the calibrated exocentric camera frame by anchoring the root-relative 3D skeleton of SMPLer-X [(Cai et al., 2023)] to the known 3D position of the egocentric camera cₜ (Eq. 1) and fitting its metric scale via 2D reprojection against the ViTPose [(Xu et al., 2022)] keypoints (Appendix D.1). The resulting upper-limb skeletons are causally interpolated and rasterized into both exocentric and egocentric views as skeletal guidance maps (Qᵉₜ,Qᵍₜ) using calibrated camera parameters ℂ, with joint confidence scores modulating stroke intensities to suppress hallucinated joints.

    3.2 Bidirectional Teacher

    With the streaming dual-branch priors established, we construct the teacher model with bidirectional attention to master Exo2Ego [(Liu et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024; Kang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Mahdi et al., 2026)]. As illustrated in Fig. 2b, all visual inputs and condition priors are encoded into latent representations via a frozen video VAE. Following EgoX [(Kang et al., 2026)], we concatenate the streaming priors with video latents along the channel dimension for pixel-aligned conditioning, while concatenating the clean exocentric video and the noisy egocentric latent along the width dimension. The composite latents are then fed into a pretrained Wan backbone. The model is trained using LoRA [(Hu et al., 2022)] with our proposed region-aware training curriculum.

We therefore propose a region-aware curriculum (Fig. 2b): first anchoring cross-view alignment in S, gradually introducing completion in U, and finally ramping up supervision in H to refine manipulation fidelity.

    Let r_S(p),r_U(p),r_H(p)∈{0,1} denote binary regional indicators on the egocentric latent grid Ω_g.     L=𝔼[(1)/(|Ω_g|)∑_p∈Ω_gωᵤ(p)e_σ(p)].

    		(3)

    3.3 Real-Time Autoregression

    To enable streaming from our bidirectional teacher, we adapt the framework into a causal, chunk-wise autoregressive student distilled for few-step inference. In such unconstrained cases, synthesis in H refers to historical context and thus prone to error accumulation.

    z̃ₜᵍ=zₜᵍ+bₜmₜ^H⊙εₜ,

    4.2.1 Short video
